subtopic_detail: Plasma level change after smoking cessation
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 41-year-old man with treatment resistant schizophrenia stable on clozapine 450 mg at night for four years. Nine days ago he was admitted to a surgical ward after an appendicectomy and has not smoked since, having previously smoked 25 cigarettes a day.

He is now drowsy, unsteady when walking to the bathroom and has been hypersalivating more than usual. He has had no fever, his blood pressure is unchanged from baseline and his creatine kinase is within normal limits. His neutrophil count is unchanged from his last monitoring result and no other new medicine has been started.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96, BP 118/74, RR 14, SpO2 97% room air, temperature 36.7
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable, no rigidity, no tremor, unsteady gait, no focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: Neutrophils 3.4 x10^9/L (2.0-7.5); creatine kinase 96 U/L (less than 200); C-reactive protein 6 mg/L (less than 5); troponin within normal limits; clozapine level pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Reduce the clozapine dose now and monitor levels and mental state closely
Cease clozapine immediately and start an alternative antipsychotic at equivalent dose
Withhold clozapine and treat presumptively for neuroleptic malignant syndrome
Continue the current dose and add hyoscine for the increased salivation overnight
Order urgent echocardiography with repeat troponin and inflammatory markers

subtopic_detail: Treatment of a bipolar depressive episode
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 32-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder who has had six weeks of low mood, hypersomnia, weight gain and profound fatigue. She has had two manic episodes, the most recent two years ago, and takes lithium with a level in the therapeutic range.

Eight months ago a serotonin reuptake inhibitor was added during a similar episode and was followed within three weeks by a period of reduced sleep, rapid speech and overspending that resolved when it was stopped. She has no psychotic features now and no suicidal intent. Her thyroid function and renal function are within normal limits and she is using reliable contraception.

data_table.Examination: Psychomotor retardation, reactive affect, no psychotic features, cognition intact
data_table.Investigations: Lithium level 0.8 mmol/L (0.6-0.8); thyroid function, renal function and full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next treatment step?

options.text: Add sertraline at a low dose with close monitoring for elevated mood symptoms
Increase the lithium dose to reach a level at the upper end of the range
Add sodium valproate to the lithium and review her mood in four weeks
Refer for electroconvulsive therapy as the next step in this depressive episode
Add quetiapine to the lithium and review her mood and tolerability in four weeks

subtopic_detail: Declining renal function during long term therapy
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 59-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder who has taken lithium for nineteen years. She has had no episode of any polarity for twelve years, and two attempts to stop lithium in her thirties were each followed by mania within four months.

Her estimated glomerular filtration rate has fallen from 78 to 51 mL/min/1.73 m2 over six years, with the last three annual values 61, 56 and 51. She takes no anti-inflammatory drugs or diuretics, her lithium levels have never exceeded the therapeutic range, and her blood pressure and HbA1c are within normal limits. Urine albumin to creatinine ratio is normal and renal ultrasound shows no obstruction.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72, BP 124/76, RR 14, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 36.5
data_table.Examination: Euthymic, no tremor, no oedema, no goitre
data_table.Investigations: Lithium level 0.7 mmol/L (0.6-0.8); estimated glomerular filtration rate 51 mL/min/1.73 m2; calcium 2.58 mmol/L (2.10-2.60); thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits; urine albumin to creatinine ratio normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Stop lithium now and start sodium valproate as maintenance therapy instead
Continue the current regimen unchanged and repeat renal function in twelve months
Halve the lithium dose immediately and accept levels below the therapeutic range
Refer to nephrology and review the risks and benefits of continuing with her
Add amiloride for nephrogenic diabetes insipidus and continue the current dose

subtopic_detail: Persistent grief after bereavement
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar seeing a 62-year-old woman fourteen months after her husband died. She thinks about him for most of the day, has kept his room exactly as it was, and cannot listen to certain music because it is unbearable.

She says life feels meaningless without him and that she does not know who she is now, and she avoids their friends because seeing couples is painful. Her appetite and weight are stable, she sleeps six to seven hours, and she still enjoys her grandchildren's visits and her garden. She has no guilt about matters unrelated to the death and no suicidal intent, and she describes wishing she could be with him rather than wanting to end her life.

data_table.Examination: Tearful when discussing her husband, affect otherwise reactive, no psychomotor change, cognition intact
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, thyroid function, B12 and iron studies within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence sertraline for a major depressive episode and review her in four weeks
Reassure her that this is normal bereavement and review her again in six months
Refer for grief focused psychotherapy targeting avoidance and restoration of function
Refer for eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing for traumatic bereavement
Refer to a peer support bereavement group as the sole intervention for now

subtopic_detail: Pharmacotherapy choice with a history of stimulant misuse
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar seeing a 27-year-old man newly diagnosed with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder after a structured assessment that confirmed childhood onset from school reports and a parent interview. He has lost two jobs through disorganisation and missed deadlines.

He used methamphetamine two to three times weekly for three years and has been abstinent for seven months with fortnightly drug and alcohol keyworker support and negative urine screens. He describes strong cravings when stressed and lives with two former using friends. His electrocardiogram is normal, his blood pressure is normal, and he has no tics, seizures or cardiac history.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 74, BP 122/76, RR 14, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Examination: No psychomotor agitation, no psychotic features, cognition intact
data_table.Investigations: Electrocardiogram normal with corrected QT 410 ms; liver function, renal function and thyroid function within normal limits; urine drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate pharmacological treatment to start?

options.text: Immediate release dexamfetamine twice daily with weekly dispensing arranged
Atomoxetine daily with the drug and alcohol keyworker involvement continued
Defer all pharmacotherapy until he has completed two years of documented abstinence
Modafinil daily with monitoring of his mood and his substance use at each review
Bupropion daily with monitoring of his mood and his substance use at each review

subtopic_detail: Relapse prevention pharmacotherapy with liver disease
stem:
You are the consultation liaison psychiatry registrar asked to see a 51-year-old man on the gastroenterology ward. He has alcohol related cirrhosis with a resolving episode of ascites and completed a supervised withdrawal five days ago without seizure or delirium.

He drinks about twenty standard drinks daily when using and has relapsed twice in two years, each time within a fortnight of discharge. He wants pharmacological help to stay abstinent. His bilirubin is elevated with a prolonged international normalised ratio, his renal function is preserved and he takes no opioid.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84, BP 108/64, RR 16, SpO2 97% room air, temperature 36.5
data_table.Examination: Mild jaundice, resolving ascites, no asterixis, no tremor
data_table.Investigations: Bilirubin 62 micromol/L (less than 20); alanine aminotransferase 74 U/L (less than 40); international normalised ratio 1.6 (0.8-1.2); albumin 29 g/L (35-50); creatinine 74 micromol/L (60-110)

lead_in: Which relapse prevention pharmacotherapy is most appropriate?

options.text: Naltrexone daily with liver function monitoring every four weeks after discharge
Disulfiram daily with a supervised dosing arrangement organised before discharge
Acamprosate three times daily with renal function checked before starting treatment
Baclofen three times daily with review of sedation and dose at each outpatient visit
Diazepam tapering over four weeks with counselling arranged in the community

subtopic_detail: Sequencing therapy where the threat is ongoing
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar seeing a 34-year-old man from a refugee background who arrived in Australia three years ago and describes nightmares, hypervigilance and flashbacks to detention and torture. He has never disclosed the detail of what happened to anyone.

He is on a temporary visa with a protection claim under review, has had two extensions in eighteen months, and does not know whether he will be returned. He sleeps two to three hours a night, is in insecure short term housing with income from casual work only, and his wife and two children remain overseas. He uses no substances and has no suicidal intent, and he asks for something to stop the nightmares.

data_table.Examination: Hypervigilant, startles at door noise, no psychotic features, cognition intact
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, thyroid function, B12 and vitamin D within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial approach?

options.text: Begin trauma-focused exposure therapy at weekly sessions starting this fortnight
Provide stabilisation and psychosocial support with an interpreter and specialist referral
Prescribe quetiapine at night for the nightmares and review him in four weeks
Prescribe prazosin for nightmares and defer any psychological treatment until settled
Ask him to describe the detail of the torture today to establish the diagnosis

subtopic_detail: Hoarding disorder distinguished from obsessive compulsive disorder
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 58-year-old man referred after a council fire safety inspection found his home filled to shoulder height with newspapers, containers and unopened mail, leaving only narrow paths between rooms. He has lived alone since his mother died twelve years ago.

He tells you the items will be useful one day and becomes visibly distressed when you ask what would happen if a skip were brought in. He describes no fear of contamination, no repeated washing or checking, and no intrusive thoughts that he tries to neutralise. His mood is reactive and he sleeps and eats normally. His score on a cognitive screening test is 29 out of 30 and there is no history of stroke or head injury.

data_table.Examination: Well groomed, no psychomotor change, no thought disorder, insight limited into the extent of the risk
data_table.Investigations: Cognitive screening 29 out of 30; full blood count, electrolytes, thyroid function and B12 within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Start fluvoxamine at a high dose as used for compulsive disorder
Arrange a compulsory house clearance through the local council now
Apply to the tribunal for a financial administration order for him
Refer for hoarding specific cognitive behavioural therapy for him
Start risperidone at a low dose to address the poor insight shown

subtopic_detail: Management threshold for a tic disorder in a school aged child
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 9-year-old boy whose parents are worried about movements that started about eighteen months ago. He blinks hard and shrugs one shoulder, and for the past six months he has also made a repeated throat clearing sound.

His parents say the movements come and go in waves, are worse when he is tired or excited, and disappear when he is absorbed in building models. He can hold them back briefly at school but says the urge builds until he has to let go. He is doing well academically, has friends, and denies any low mood, although two boys in another class have started imitating the sounds. He has no repetitive rituals, no compulsions and no difficulty concentrating in class.

data_table.Examination: Observed eye blinking, unilateral shoulder shrug and throat clearing, suppressible on request, normal neurological examination
data_table.Investigations: No investigations performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start low dose risperidone and monitor his weight and prolactin
Provide psychoeducation and refer for behavioural tic therapy for him
Start clonidine at night and review the tics again in four weeks
Arrange an electroencephalogram to exclude a seizure disorder in him
Refer for botulinum toxin injection into the affected muscle groups

subtopic_detail: First line treatment for binge eating disorder in adulthood
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 34-year-old woman who describes eating enormous amounts in the evening after her children are asleep, getting through a family sized block of chocolate and several packets of biscuits within two hours. She says she cannot stop once she starts and feels disgusted with herself afterwards.

This has happened about three times a week for eight months and she hides the wrappers from her partner. She does not make herself vomit, does not use laxatives or diuretics, does not fast between episodes and exercises only by walking the dog. Her body mass index is 34 kg/m2 and her weight has risen 9 kg over the year. Her mood is low only in the hours after an episode and she has no thoughts of self-harm.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 34 kg/m2, no parotid swelling, no dental erosion, no Russell sign on the knuckles
data_table.Investigations: Electrolytes, full blood count, thyroid function and fasting glucose within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment?

options.text: Start lisdexamfetamine as the initial treatment for the binge episodes
Refer for bariatric surgery assessment given her current body weight
Start fluoxetine 60 mg daily as the sole initial treatment for her
Refer to a dietitian for a structured energy restricted weight loss diet
Refer for eating disorder focused cognitive behavioural therapy for her

subtopic_detail: Body dysmorphic disorder presenting as a request for cosmetic surgery
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 23-year-old man who asks for a referral to a surgeon to have his nose reshaped. He says it is crooked and takes up his whole face, and that people stare at it on the train.

He checks his profile in reflective surfaces for about four hours a day, angles his head in conversation to hide one side, and has stopped going to gatherings where photographs might be taken. He has already had a septorhinoplasty and a chin filler elsewhere, and says neither made any difference. He describes his appearance as ruining his life but sleeps and eats normally, enjoys his job and has no anhedonia or thoughts of self-harm. His nose appears entirely unremarkable to you.

data_table.Examination: Nose of normal appearance with no deformity, no skin excoriation, mood euthymic with reactive affect
data_table.Investigations: No investigations indicated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer to a plastic surgeon for an independent second opinion for him
Start olanzapine at a low dose to address the fixed belief he holds
Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy rather than to a surgeon
Arrange a psychology referral for social anxiety focused therapy for him
Start a low dose of sertraline and review him again in six months

subtopic_detail: New behaviour change in a non verbal adult with intellectual disability
stem:
You are the general practitioner asked to visit a group home for a 24-year-old man with moderate intellectual disability who communicates with gestures and a small set of signs. Over the past three weeks he has begun hitting the side of his head with his palm and shouting, sometimes for an hour at a time, and staff have requested something to settle him.

Staffing, housemates and his weekly routine are unchanged, and his family visits as usual. He has been leaving most of his dinner, has lost 2 kg, and staff have noticed him holding his right cheek and pulling at that ear. He last saw a dentist four years ago. He takes no regular medication and his bowels have been opening normally.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 92, blood pressure 122/76, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 37.2
data_table.Examination: Guards the right side of his face on approach, will not allow full oral examination, no external ear discharge, chest and abdomen unremarkable
data_table.Investigations: Weight down 2 kg over three weeks, no investigations performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Examine for an untreated physical cause including dental disease
Start regular low dose risperidone and review him again in four weeks
Prescribe as needed diazepam for staff to give when he is agitated
Admit him to the acute psychiatric inpatient unit for observation
Ask the service to write a positive behaviour support plan for him

subtopic_detail: Behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia presenting as late onset mood change
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 58-year-old accountant brought in by his wife, who says he is not the man she married. Over eighteen months he has spent nearly forty thousand dollars on equipment he has never used, has begun making blunt remarks about strangers' weight in the supermarket, and no longer seems to notice when she is upset.

He now eats two packets of sweet biscuits a day when he never had a sweet tooth, and he sits in the same chair for hours unless prompted. He sleeps soundly through the night, wakes at his usual hour and denies feeling sad. He has no personal or family history of mood disorder and takes no medication. His recall of three items at five minutes is intact and his score on a cognitive screening test is 28 out of 30, with difficulty only on a verbal fluency task.

data_table.Examination: No focal neurological deficit, no tremor or rigidity, affect fatuous with reduced concern about the consultation
data_table.Investigations: Cognitive screening 28 out of 30 with reduced verbal fluency and intact delayed recall; full blood count, electrolytes, liver function, thyroid function, B12 and folate within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start sertraline for a late onset depressive episode and review him
Start quetiapine for a first manic episode occurring at this age
Repeat cognitive screening in six months before making any referral
Refer for psychology to address the recent stress in his marriage
Arrange neuroimaging and refer to a cognitive disorders clinic

subtopic_detail: Psychosis persisting a month after abstinence from methamphetamine
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar planning discharge for a 22-year-old man admitted four weeks ago. He arrived believing his housemates were filming him for a syndicate and hearing two voices discussing him in the third person, after three months of using crystal methamphetamine several times a week.

His urine drug screen was positive on admission and has been negative on weekly testing since, and the ward is a locked unit with no access to substances. He was started on olanzapine 10 mg at night and his agitation settled within days, but he still believes the filming occurred and still hears the voices most days. He has no blunting of affect, no social withdrawal and remains motivated to return to his apprenticeship. His mood is euthymic with no manic or depressive features.

data_table.Examination: Persecutory delusion of being filmed held with full conviction, third person auditory hallucinations most days, no negative symptoms, no thought disorder
data_table.Investigations: Weekly urine drug screens negative for four weeks; full blood count, electrolytes, liver function and thyroid function within normal limits; computed tomography of the brain normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan on discharge?

options.text: Stop the antipsychotic at discharge as the drug screen is now clear
Continue the antipsychotic and refer to an early psychosis service
Switch him to clozapine because of the incomplete symptom response
Reduce and cease the antipsychotic over the next fortnight after discharge
Add sodium valproate for mood stabilisation before he is discharged

subtopic_detail: Eligibility screening before ketamine treatment for resistant depression
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar in a mood disorders clinic seeing a 44-year-old woman with a nine year history of recurrent major depression. She has completed adequate trials of sertraline, venlafaxine and mirtazapine at therapeutic doses for at least eight weeks each, plus quetiapine augmentation, with only partial benefit and a current score in the severe range.

She has no psychotic symptoms, no history of mania and no current substance use. She has read about ketamine and asks whether she can start it. She has never seen a doctor about her blood pressure and takes no antihypertensive. Her blood pressure today is 168 over 104, repeated after ten minutes seated at 166 over 102, and a reading taken at her pharmacy last month was similar.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 84, blood pressure 168/104 repeated at 166/102, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 29 kg/m2, no cardiac murmur, no papilloedema, no focal neurological signs
data_table.Investigations: Electrolytes, liver function, thyroid function and full blood count within normal limits; electrocardiogram shows sinus rhythm with voltage criteria for left ventricular hypertrophy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start esketamine nasal spray at the next available clinic appointment
Refer for electroconvulsive therapy as the only remaining option for her
Add lithium augmentation and review her response again in six weeks
Control the blood pressure before considering any ketamine therapy
Refer for transcranial magnetic stimulation instead of ketamine therapy

subtopic_detail: Sequencing trauma focused therapy alongside alcohol dependence
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar seeing a 38-year-old woman with nightmares, flashbacks and hypervigilance since a violent assault four years ago. She avoids the suburb where it happened and has not travelled on public transport since.

She drinks about twelve standard drinks daily, starting mid morning, and describes shaking hands and sweating until the first drink. She has never had a withdrawal seizure or delirium. She has read about eye movement therapy and asks to start it, and says a previous service told her she had to be dry for six months before they would see her. She has no psychotic symptoms and no current suicidal intent, and her liver function shows a mildly raised gamma glutamyl transferase with normal synthetic function.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 96, blood pressure 138/86, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7
data_table.Examination: Fine tremor of the outstretched hands, no asterixis, no stigmata of chronic liver disease, no jaundice
data_table.Investigations: Gamma glutamyl transferase 180 U/L (5-50); albumin, bilirubin and international normalised ratio within normal limits; full blood count shows mean cell volume 101 fL (80-100)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment plan?

options.text: Require six months of abstinence before starting any trauma therapy
Start sertraline alone and defer any trauma-focused therapy for now
Offer withdrawal management and trauma-focused therapy together
Begin eye movement therapy without addressing her daily drinking
Refer to residential rehabilitation and review her in twelve months

subtopic_detail: Medical instability threshold before outpatient family based treatment
stem: A 15-year-old girl has lost 14 kg over 8 months and her periods stopped 4 months ago. She fainted last week. Her parents want to start family based treatment at home this week.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 38 /min awake, BP 88/54 lying and 66/40 standing, T 35.4 degrees C
data_table.Examination: BMI 15.1 kg/m2, cannot rise from squatting unaided
data_table.Investigations: Potassium 3.3, phosphate 0.8, glucose 3.4 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Admit for medical stabilisation before family based treatment
Start outpatient family based treatment with weekly weighing
Refer for individual cognitive behavioural therapy
Start low-dose olanzapine to assist weight restoration
Arrange dietitian review and repeat observations in a week

subtopic_detail: First line treatment for chronic insomnia disorder in a patient requesting a hypnotic
stem:
You are the general practice registrar. A 46-year-old accountant has had trouble sleeping for eight months. He takes about 90 minutes to fall asleep, wakes at 3 am and lies awake for an hour or more, and this happens five or six nights a week. He is irritable and unproductive at work.

He has started going to bed at 8.30 pm to give himself the best chance, spends time in bed reading work emails, and naps for an hour most afternoons. He drinks two coffees before midday and no alcohol. He denies low mood, anhedonia, worry or panic, and he does not snore, has no restless sensations in his legs and his partner has seen no breathing pauses. His thyroid function and full blood count taken last week were normal. He asks directly for a script for zolpidem.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 24 kg/m2, Mallampati class 1 airway, normal mental state examination with euthymic mood and full affect
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone and full blood count within normal limits; Epworth Sleepiness Scale score 6 of 24

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment?

options.text: Prescribe zolpidem nightly for four weeks with a plan to taper it after that period
Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia including sleep restriction and stimulus control
Prescribe low dose amitriptyline at night and review the effect on his sleep in six weeks
Arrange an overnight polysomnogram before making any decision about treatment for him
Start an antidepressant at a standard dose and review his sleep and mood in four weeks

subtopic_detail: Sequencing iron replacement before dopaminergic therapy in restless legs syndrome
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 39-year-old woman who describes a crawling discomfort deep in both calves every evening. She says she has to get up and walk around to make it go away, that it is worst when she sits still after dinner, and that it settles completely while she is moving.

It has been present for a year and is now delaying her sleep by two hours most nights. She is a vegetarian with heavy periods. Her mood is normal, she takes no antidepressant or antipsychotic, and her renal function is normal. Neurological examination of the legs is normal with preserved reflexes, power and sensation, and there is no calf tenderness or swelling.

data_table.Examination: Normal lower limb power, tone, reflexes and sensation, no oedema or calf tenderness, no peripheral pulse deficit
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 118 g/L (115-165); ferritin 22 mcg/L (15-200); transferrin saturation 14 per cent (15-45); urea, electrolytes and creatinine within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first step in management?

options.text: Start pramipexole at a low nightly dose and titrate it against her symptom response
Begin oral iron replacement aiming for a ferritin above 75 mcg/L and reassess symptoms
Prescribe gabapentin at night and review both her sleep and her symptoms in four weeks
Arrange nerve conduction studies of both lower limbs before starting any specific treatment
Prescribe temazepam at night for four weeks and review her sleep pattern after that time

subtopic_detail: Detecting and responding to disordered gambling presenting as an unexplained financial and mood crisis
stem:
You are the general practice registrar. A 34-year-old man presents asking for a mental health care plan for stress. He has taken out a second personal loan, has been borrowing from family with vague explanations, and has stopped seeing friends. He has lost 6 kg and sleeps four hours a night.

When you ask what the money went on, he becomes evasive, then says he has been using an online sports betting app since it was advertised during the football and that he has been chasing his losses for about a year. He drinks two standard drinks a week and uses no other substances. He says he has thought that his family would be better off without him but has no plan and does not want to die.

data_table.Examination: Anxious, reactive affect, no psychomotor retardation, oriented with intact cognition, no psychotic features
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, liver function tests and thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start an antidepressant for his low mood and review both symptoms in four weeks
Arrange an urgent psychiatric admission because of the passive suicidal thoughts he described
Reassure him that the debt is the problem and refer him only to a financial counsellor
Make a safety plan, refer for gambling specific psychological therapy, and discuss self exclusion
Prescribe naltrexone at an anticraving dose and review his gambling behaviour in six weeks

subtopic_detail: Distinguishing a stressor linked disorder from major depression when function is preserved
stem:
You are the general practice registrar. A 51-year-old woman was made redundant five weeks ago after 20 years with the same employer. Since then she has felt flat and tearful, worries about money and sleeps poorly in the first half of the night. She asks whether she should start an antidepressant.

She still walks the dog daily, enjoys her book club and laughed several times during the consultation when talking about her grandchildren. Her appetite and weight are unchanged, and she describes no diurnal variation in mood, early morning waking or psychomotor slowing. She denies thoughts of self-harm, and neither she nor her family has ever been treated for a mood disorder. She scores 11 on the Patient Health Questionnaire 9. She is applying for jobs and has an interview next week.

data_table.Examination: Tearful at times but reactive affect, normal speech rate, no psychomotor change, no psychotic features, cognition intact
data_table.Investigations: Patient Health Questionnaire 9 score 11 of 27; thyroid stimulating hormone and full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start sertraline at an antidepressant dose and review her symptoms again in four weeks
Refer for electroconvulsive therapy assessment given the severity of her low mood score
Prescribe temazepam for her sleep and review the situation once she has found new work
Diagnose major depressive disorder and refer for psychological therapy plus an antidepressant
Offer structured psychological support with a mental health care plan and review in two weeks

subtopic_detail: Pharmacotherapy decision for nicotine dependence acquired through vaping in an adolescent
stem:
You are the general practice registrar. A 16-year-old girl attends alone and asks for help stopping vaping. She has used a disposable nicotine vape daily for 18 months, now vapes within ten minutes of waking, and gets headaches and irritability by mid morning at school if she does not use it.

She has tried to stop three times, the longest for two days. She has never smoked cigarettes. She has no psychiatric history, no low mood or suicidal thoughts, takes no medication and is not pregnant. You have assessed her as a mature minor who understands the treatment being discussed. She scores 7 on a nicotine dependence questionnaire.

data_table.Examination: Normal cardiorespiratory examination, normal mental state examination, no oral lesions
data_table.Investigations: Urine pregnancy test negative; no other investigations indicated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Offer behavioural support with nicotine replacement therapy and arrange structured follow up
Start varenicline at the standard adult dose and review her tolerance of it in two weeks
Advise abrupt cessation with behavioural support alone and review her progress in four weeks
Recommend switching to a lower nicotine concentration vape and gradually reducing over time
Start bupropion at a cessation dose and review both her mood and her cravings in two weeks

subtopic_detail: Separating persistent bereavement related distress from a depressive episode more than a year after a death
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar in a consultation clinic. A 62-year-old woman was referred 15 months after her husband died suddenly. She thinks about him for most of the day, keeps his clothes laid out and his phone charged, and cannot bring herself to enter their bedroom. She says she feels that part of her died with him and that she has no idea who she is now.

She has stopped seeing the friends they had together because being with couples is unbearable, and she has not returned to the volunteering she loved. She eats and sleeps reasonably and her weight is unchanged. She feels intense yearning that comes in waves triggered by reminders rather than a constant flat mood, and she still laughs with her granddaughter. Her guilt centres on things she wishes she had said to him rather than on her own worthlessness, and she denies psychomotor slowing or thoughts of self-harm.

data_table.Examination: Reactive affect with tearfulness on discussing her husband, normal speech and psychomotor activity, no psychotic features, cognition intact
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, urea and electrolytes, liver function tests and thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start mirtazapine at night and review her sleep, appetite and mood in four weeks
Refer for grief focused psychotherapy addressing avoidance and restoration of daily roles
Reassure her that grief has no timetable and review her again in six months if needed
Start an antidepressant with a mood stabiliser and review her response again in six weeks
Arrange cognitive testing and neuroimaging to investigate her sense of altered identity

subtopic_detail: Excessive daytime sleepiness with emotionally triggered weakness misattributed to a mood disorder
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar. A 19-year-old university student is referred with two years of overwhelming daytime sleepiness that a previous doctor treated as depression, without benefit from two adequate antidepressant trials.

He falls asleep in lectures and once at the dinner table, and says a 15 minute nap leaves him refreshed for a couple of hours. When he laughs hard at a joke his knees buckle and his jaw sags for a few seconds while he stays fully aware of what is happening. On waking he sometimes cannot move for half a minute and has seen figures at the end of his bed while otherwise awake. His mood is reactive, he enjoys his sport and friends, and he denies anhedonia, guilt or suicidal thoughts. His body mass index is 23 kg/m2, he does not snore and his Epworth Sleepiness Scale score is 19.

data_table.Examination: Normal neurological examination, Mallampati class 1 airway, reactive affect with no depressive cognitions
data_table.Investigations: Epworth Sleepiness Scale 19 of 24; full blood count, iron studies and thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Switch to a serotonin noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor and review his energy in six weeks
Prescribe modafinil for daytime sleepiness and review his alertness again in four weeks
Refer for polysomnography followed by a multiple sleep latency test the next day
Arrange an electroencephalogram to investigate the episodes of collapse he describes
Arrange overnight oximetry at home and start positive airway pressure if it is abnormal

subtopic_detail: Mood and behavioural change from androgen misuse presenting as a primary psychiatric disorder
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 24-year-old man brought by his partner because of four months of irritability, verbal aggression and jealous accusations. He has been sleeping five hours a night, feels unusually confident and has been training at the gym twice a day.

He has gained 9 kg of muscle in that time, has acne across his back and shoulders, and his partner has noticed tender swelling under both nipples. He denies grandiose delusions and there are no hallucinations or thought disorder. He drinks little and uses no illicit stimulants, and a urine drug screen for amphetamines, cocaine and cannabis is negative. There is no personal or family history of bipolar disorder. When asked specifically what he takes for training, he says only protein powder and a testosterone booster from an overseas website.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 92, blood pressure 152/94, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8
data_table.Examination: Marked muscle bulk, truncal acne, bilateral tender gynaecomastia, small testes, no tremor or hyperreflexia
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen negative for amphetamines, cocaine and cannabis; haematocrit 0.54 (0.40-0.52); alanine aminotransferase 78 U/L (less than 40); high density lipoprotein cholesterol 0.7 mmol/L (greater than 1.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start olanzapine for the irritability and arrange psychiatric review again in two weeks
Start lithium for a first manic episode and arrange monitoring of his serum concentrations
Refer for couples counselling to address the jealousy and review his mood in six weeks
Take a targeted history of injectable androgen use and measure testosterone and gonadotrophins
Admit him involuntarily under the mental health act for assessment of his aggression

subtopic_detail: Treatment choice when attention symptoms and a chronic tic disorder coexist in a school aged child
stem:
You are the paediatric psychiatry registrar. A 9-year-old boy has been assessed as meeting criteria for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder with impairment at school and at home documented on teacher and parent rating scales.

For the past two years he has also had bouts of eye blinking and shoulder shrugging, and for the last eight months a repeated throat clearing sound. His mother says these wax and wane, are worse when he is tired or anxious, and that he can hold them back briefly at the cost of building tension. He is teased about the throat clearing. His growth, cardiovascular examination and sleep are normal, and there is no family history of sudden cardiac death. His mother has read that stimulants cause tics and does not want him to have one.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 84, blood pressure 104/64, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7
data_table.Examination: Intermittent eye blinking and shoulder shrugs during interview, audible throat clearing, normal cardiovascular examination, height and weight on the 50th centile
data_table.Investigations: Teacher and parent rating scales in the clinical range for inattention and hyperactivity; electrocardiogram not yet performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start guanfacine and provide behavioural intervention with review of both sets of symptoms
Start risperidone to suppress the tics and defer any treatment of the attention symptoms
Provide behavioural intervention alone and review both sets of symptoms in six months
Start atomoxetine and refer for comprehensive behavioural intervention for tics as well
Start methylphenidate at a low dose and stop it immediately if any tics become worse

subtopic_detail: Dosing strategy for a serotonergic antidepressant in cyclical premenstrual mood symptoms
stem:
You are the general practice registrar. A 31-year-old woman describes irritability, tearfulness and a sense of being out of control that starts about six days before each period and lifts within two days of bleeding starting. She has snapped at her children and nearly resigned from her job during these episodes.

She has kept a daily symptom chart for three consecutive cycles which shows a clear symptom-free interval from day 4 to day 16 of each cycle. Her cycles are regular at 28 days. She has no depressive or anxiety symptoms outside the premenstrual window, no history of a depressive episode and no thyroid disease. She uses condoms for contraception and does not want to start a hormonal method.

data_table.Examination: Euthymic and reactive on the day of review, which is day 9 of her cycle, with normal mental state examination
data_table.Investigations: Three cycles of prospective daily symptom rating showing a symptom-free follicular phase; thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line pharmacological treatment?

options.text: Prescribe a serotonin reuptake inhibitor taken only from ovulation until menstruation starts
Prescribe a serotonin reuptake inhibitor taken continuously every day of the cycle instead
Prescribe oral micronised progesterone during the luteal phase of each menstrual cycle
Prescribe a gonadotrophin releasing hormone agonist with add back oestrogen and progestogen
Prescribe a low dose benzodiazepine taken as required during the premenstrual week only

subtopic_detail: Choosing between light therapy and pharmacotherapy in recurrent winter pattern depression
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar in a clinic in Hobart. A 29-year-old woman has had four episodes of low mood, each beginning in late May and remitting by early October, with full return to normal function over summer in every year. She is now three weeks into this year's episode.

During episodes she sleeps ten hours and still feels unrefreshed, craves carbohydrate and has gained 5 kg each winter. She has never had an episode outside these months, has never been elevated, and there is no seasonal shift work or travel. She responded to sertraline two winters ago but stopped it because of sexual side effects and says she will not take it again. Her thyroid function and full blood count are normal, and her vitamin D is 58 nmol per litre.

data_table.Examination: Mildly slowed speech, reactive affect, no psychotic features, no suicidal ideation, cognition intact
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone and full blood count within normal limits; serum 25 hydroxyvitamin D 58 nmol/L (50-150)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment to recommend?

options.text: Prescribe high dose vitamin D supplementation and review her mood again in six weeks
Start bright light therapy each morning with review of her response after two weeks
Start lithium as a mood stabiliser given the regular recurrence of her mood episodes
Restart sertraline at the dose that worked before and manage the side effects as they arise
Start agomelatine at night and review her sleep pattern and mood again in four weeks

subtopic_detail: Acute assessment of volatile substance use in an adolescent and the hazard of catecholamine provocation
stem:
You are the emergency registrar. A 15-year-old boy is brought in by ambulance after being found in a park unsteady, giggling and slurring his words. Paramedics found aerosol cans nearby and noted a chemical smell on his breath. Twenty minutes later he is drowsy but rousable and oriented.

There is a rash of small red spots around his mouth and nose and his clothing smells of solvent. His breath alcohol is zero and a urine drug screen is negative for amphetamines, opioids, benzodiazepines and cannabis. He becomes agitated when the nursing staff try to attach the monitoring leads and wants to leave. His mother has been contacted and is on her way.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 112, blood pressure 124/72, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Examination: Perioral erythematous rash, solvent odour, dysarthria and gait ataxia, pupils 4 mm and reactive, no focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: Breath alcohol zero; urine drug screen negative; capillary glucose 5.4 mmol/L (4.0-7.8); electrocardiogram shows sinus tachycardia with normal QT interval

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Give intramuscular droperidol for the agitation and repeat the dose if he remains unsettled
Give intravenous flumazenil to reverse the sedation and reassess his conscious state
Give activated charcoal now and admit him to the short stay unit for overnight observation
Nurse him calmly in a quiet area with cardiac monitoring and supplemental oxygen as needed
Discharge him to his mother once he is fully alert with advice to see his own doctor

subtopic_detail: Atypical features in a first psychotic presentation that redirect the workup away from a primary disorder
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 21-year-old woman admitted three days ago with a two week history of paranoid beliefs about her housemates, disorganised speech and severe anxiety. She has no personal or family psychiatric history and uses no substances, and a urine drug screen is negative.

Over the last 48 hours the nursing staff report she has become intermittently mute and then floridly agitated within the same hour. She has developed repetitive lip smacking and choreiform movements of both hands that were not present on admission and that persist during sleep observation. She has been febrile to 38.2 twice without a source, and her pulse has swung between 48 and 140 while lying still in bed. She has received two doses of olanzapine only.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate fluctuating 48 to 140, blood pressure 96/58 to 158/94, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 38.2
data_table.Examination: Orofacial dyskinesia and hand chorea persisting in sleep, fluctuating conscious state, no neck stiffness, no rigidity or clonus
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 8.4 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0); C-reactive protein 9 mg/L (less than 5); creatine kinase 210 U/L (less than 200); urine drug screen negative; computed tomography of the brain reported as normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Cease olanzapine and start bromocriptine with active cooling and intravenous fluid support
Increase the olanzapine dose and add regular lorazepam for the fluctuating agitation
Arrange lumbar puncture with paired serum and cerebrospinal fluid autoantibody testing
Arrange urgent electroconvulsive therapy for a presumed catatonic presentation of psychosis
Start intravenous ceftriaxone and aciclovir empirically and repeat the computed tomography scan

subtopic_detail: Cyclical mood symptoms confined to the luteal phase and the evidence needed before treatment
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 31-year-old woman who describes becoming a different person for about a week each month. She is irritable to the point of shouting at her children, tearful, bloated and exhausted, and has twice taken sick leave because she could not face work.

She says the symptoms lift within a day or two of her period starting and that she feels entirely well for the following fortnight. This has happened for at least six months. She has no history of mental illness, drinks two standard drinks a week, and is not using hormonal contraception. Her thyroid function and full blood count taken last month were normal, and today, on day 8 of her cycle, her mental state examination is entirely unremarkable.

data_table.Examination: Mental state examination normal today with euthymic mood, no psychomotor change, no suicidal ideation
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone 1.8 mIU/L (0.4-4.0); haemoglobin 132 g/L (115-165); ferritin 46 mcg/L (30-200)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start sertraline 50 mg daily continuously and review her in four weeks
Start a combined oral contraceptive taken continuously without a break
Refer to psychiatry for assessment of possible bipolar II disorder now
Ask her to complete daily symptom ratings over two menstrual cycles
Advise calcium and vitamin B6 supplements and review her in three months

subtopic_detail: Body focused repetitive behaviour and the treatment that comes before medication
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 19-year-old university student who has been wearing a beanie indoors for three months. She tells you she pulls hair from her scalp while studying and watching television, sometimes without noticing she has started.

She describes a build up of tension beforehand and a sense of relief afterwards, and she has tried repeatedly to stop. She does not eat the hair. She denies any belief that her hair is abnormal or that she looks disfigured, and she is not checking mirrors or seeking cosmetic procedures. On examination there is an irregular patch of hair loss over the right parietal scalp containing hairs of varying lengths, with normal skin, no scaling, no scarring and no broken exclamation mark hairs.

data_table.Examination: Irregular right parietal patch of hair loss with hairs of differing lengths, normal underlying scalp skin, no scaling or scarring, no abdominal mass
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, iron studies and thyroid stimulating hormone all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line management?

options.text: Start fluoxetine 20 mg daily and review her response after six weeks
Refer to dermatology for a scalp biopsy to clarify the pattern of loss
Start low dose olanzapine at night and monitor her weight monthly
Reassure her that the habit is common and review her again in six months
Refer for habit reversal training with a trained psychologist

subtopic_detail: Persisting bereavement reaction beyond the diagnostic time threshold
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 58-year-old woman 15 months after her husband died of pancreatic cancer. She tells you she thinks about him for most of the day, longs for him constantly, and still cannot bring herself to enter the room where he died or to give away his clothes.

She says she feels that part of her died with him and that she no longer knows who she is without him. She has stopped seeing the friends they had as a couple. She sleeps and eats reasonably and has not lost weight. She has no pervasive anhedonia, no feelings of worthlessness unrelated to the loss, and no suicidal ideation, although she says she would not mind if she did not wake up. She is still doing her job but has taken no interest in it.

data_table.Examination: Tearful when speaking about her husband, reactive affect at other times, no psychomotor retardation, no psychotic features, no plan or intent to harm herself
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, urea and electrolytes and thyroid stimulating hormone all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reassure her that this is normal grief and offer review in six months
Start mirtazapine at night to address her sleep and appetite as well
Refer for structured grief focused psychotherapy with a psychologist
Prescribe short term temazepam to help her sleep and review in a month
Refer her to a community bereavement support group run by volunteers

subtopic_detail: Somatic complaints confined to school mornings in early adolescence
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 12-year-old boy brought by his mother because he has missed 14 of the last 20 school days with stomach aches and nausea. The symptoms begin as he is getting dressed and are severe enough that he cries and refuses to get in the car.

Once the decision is made that he can stay home he settles within an hour, and he is entirely well at weekends and through the recent school holidays. His mother has been working from home so that she can stay with him. He tells you he worries that something bad will happen to his mother while he is at school and that he cannot concentrate for thinking about it. He denies being bullied and his teachers report he is academically capable. His growth is normal and his abdomen is soft and non-tender.

data_table.Examination: Soft non-tender abdomen, no organomegaly, growth tracking along the 50th centile, normal general examination
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, C-reactive protein, coeliac serology and faecal calprotectin all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Arrange a graded return to school with the school and family together
Start sertraline 25 mg daily and review his symptoms in four weeks
Refer to gastroenterology for endoscopy to investigate the abdominal pain
Support a period of home schooling until his anxiety symptoms settle
Notify the education department of unauthorised absence from school

subtopic_detail: Treating attention deficit hyperactivity disorder when a tic disorder coexists
stem:
You are the paediatrician reviewing a 9-year-old boy who has had eye blinking and shoulder shrugging for two years, with intermittent throat clearing. The movements come and go in intensity, do not hurt him, and he says other children have stopped commenting on them.

His parents' concern today is different. He cannot stay in his seat, loses his belongings weekly, and his teacher reports he completes about a third of set work. Structured rating scales completed by parents and two teachers meet criteria for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, combined presentation, with impairment at home and at school. His father asks you directly whether starting a stimulant will make the movements worse, because a relative told him it would.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 84, blood pressure 100/62, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Examination: Intermittent eye blinking and shoulder shrugs suppressible on request, normal neurological examination, growth on the 60th centile for height and weight
data_table.Rating scales: Parent and two teacher scales meet criteria for combined presentation with cross setting impairment; tic severity rated mild with no functional impact

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Treat the movements first with comprehensive behavioural intervention
Start methylphenidate for the attentional symptoms and monitor his tics
Start clonidine as a single agent to cover both sets of symptoms
Start risperidone at a low dose and review his movements in six weeks
Defer all medication and reassess both problems again in six months

subtopic_detail: Behavioural addiction presenting as insomnia and anxiety in primary care
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 45-year-old man who asks for something to help him sleep. He works as a plumber and says he lies awake with his heart racing.

On questioning he tells you he has been betting on sport through an app for three years. Over the past eight months the stakes have grown, he returns the next day to win back what he lost, and he has taken out a personal loan and a credit card that his wife does not know about. He has twice promised her he had stopped. He drinks four standard drinks a week, uses no other substances, and has no previous psychiatric history. He looks tired and says quietly that his family would be better off without him, although he has no plan and wants help.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 92, blood pressure 138/86, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7
data_table.Examination: Anxious and tired appearing, reactive affect, no psychotic features, no intoxication or withdrawal signs
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, liver function tests and thyroid stimulating hormone all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Prescribe a short course of temazepam and review his sleep in two weeks
Start sertraline for anxiety and arrange to see him again in one month
Advise him to self exclude from betting apps and review him in one month
Assess suicide risk today and refer to a gambling specific psychology service
Refer him to a financial counsellor to consolidate his debts and review later

subtopic_detail: Withdrawing long term hypnotic treatment in an older person after a fall
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 74-year-old woman two weeks after she fell in her hallway at 2 am and fractured her wrist. She has been taking temazepam 20 mg every night for six years, started after her husband's death, and says she no longer knows whether it helps but is frightened of nights without it.

She takes perindopril and atorvastatin, drinks no alcohol, and lives alone. Her cognitive screening score is in the normal range and her orthostatic blood pressure drop is 8 mmHg. Her renal function and vitamin D are normal and her most recent bone density showed osteopenia. She tells you she would like to come off the tablet but has tried twice before and lasted two nights each time.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 72, blood pressure 132/78, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 36.5
data_table.Examination: Steady tandem gait in a wrist cast, no focal neurology, cognitive screening within the normal range, postural blood pressure drop 8 mmHg
data_table.Investigations: Estimated glomerular filtration rate greater than 60 mL/min/1.73m2; sodium 139 mmol/L (135-145); 25 hydroxyvitamin D 68 nmol/L (greater than 50)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Stop the temazepam now and provide written sleep hygiene instructions
Substitute zopiclone at an equivalent nightly dose and continue it long term
Reduce the dose by about a quarter every two to four weeks with review
Add prolonged release melatonin nightly and continue the temazepam as well
Refer her for inpatient withdrawal management at the local drug service

subtopic_detail: Progressive household accumulation in later life and its differential
stem:
You are the doctor on a community aged care assessment visit to a 68-year-old retired librarian, requested by her daughter after the council issued a notice about the state of the property.

Only a narrow path runs through each room, the kitchen bench and the stove cannot be used, and newspapers are stacked to shoulder height. She has bought items she does not need for years and cannot let anything go because she believes each item may be needed later, and she becomes acutely distressed and tearful when her daughter removes anything. She is embarrassed by the mess and will not let neighbours in. Her personal hygiene is good, she pays her bills on time, and she gives a detailed and coherent account of her finances. Her cognitive screening is in the normal range, and there is no disinhibition, no change in food preference, no rituals such as washing or checking, and no delusions or hallucinations.

data_table.Examination: Well kempt, coherent and detailed history, cognitive screening within the normal range, no frontal release signs, no disinhibition, no psychotic features
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, urea and electrolytes, thyroid stimulating hormone and vitamin B12 all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Obsessive compulsive disorder with predominant hoarding symptoms
Behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia with collecting behaviour
Severe self neglect syndrome associated with social isolation
Very late onset schizophrenia like psychosis with delusional beliefs
Hoarding disorder with excessive acquisition and limited insight

subtopic_detail: Request for a cosmetic referral where the appearance concern is the disorder
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 22-year-old man who asks for a referral to a plastic surgeon because his nose is crooked and, in his words, ruins his face. He had a rhinoplasty 18 months ago and says the surgeon did not fix it properly.

He tells you he checks his profile in reflective surfaces for around three hours a day, photographs his face from set angles each evening, and now leaves the house only after dark. He has stopped attending his apprenticeship two days a week and has lost contact with most of his friends. He denies low mood as his main problem, saying he would be fine if his nose were fixed. On examination there is minimal residual nasal asymmetry that is difficult to appreciate at conversational distance.

data_table.Examination: Minimal residual nasal asymmetry, no functional nasal obstruction, no septal deviation on inspection, reactive affect, no psychotic features
data_table.Investigations: No abnormality on routine screening bloods taken by the previous surgeon

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Explain the underlying disorder and refer for cognitive behavioural therapy
Write the referral to a plastic surgeon and review him after the operation
Arrange a second surgical opinion to assess the technical adequacy of the repair
Start low dose olanzapine because his belief about his nose is held firmly
Reassure him that his nose looks normal and review him again in three months

subtopic_detail: Daytime sleepiness referred as depression with a symptom that redirects the diagnosis
stem:
You are the doctor in a youth mental health service seeing a 17-year-old girl referred with a provisional diagnosis of depression. Her school reports that she sleeps in class most days and her marks have fallen from A grades to passes over the past year.

Her sleep diary shows a consistent bedtime of 10 pm, sleep onset within five minutes, and waking at 6:30 am, and she still falls asleep on the bus and during afternoon lessons. She naps for 20 minutes and wakes refreshed. She says she is flat about school but still enjoys her netball training and her friendships, and she has no suicidal thoughts or weight change. Her mother adds that for the past few months her knees have buckled and her jaw has gone slack for a few seconds when she laughs hard, which they had put down to clumsiness. She uses no substances and takes no medication.

data_table.Examination: Normal neurological examination, body mass index 22 kg per square metre, no goitre, reactive affect with preserved interest in activities
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, ferritin, thyroid stimulating hormone, iron studies and glucose all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start fluoxetine 20 mg daily and review her mood in four weeks' time
Provide sleep hygiene education and a fixed schedule with review in a month
Repeat her iron studies and thyroid function and review in six weeks
Refer for polysomnography followed by a multiple sleep latency test
Start modafinil for her daytime sleepiness and arrange follow up in clinic

subtopic_detail: Escalating gabapentinoid use in a patient stabilised on opioid agonist treatment
stem:
You are the doctor at an opioid treatment clinic reviewing a 34-year-old man who has been stable on methadone 90 mg daily for two years, with negative urine drug screens and steady employment.

He was prescribed pregabalin for sciatica 10 months ago at 150 mg daily. He now asks you to increase it to 600 mg daily, telling you it is the only thing that quietens his anxiety and that he sometimes takes several days worth at once for the buzz. Real time prescription monitoring shows he has obtained pregabalin from three prescribers in the past two months. Two weeks ago his partner found him asleep and unrousable for several minutes on the couch after an evening of drinking. His sciatica has settled and straight leg raise is now negative.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 72, blood pressure 118/74, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Examination: Alert and oriented, mildly slurred speech late in the consultation, negative straight leg raise, no focal neurological deficit
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen positive for methadone only; liver function tests and renal function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Increase the pregabalin to 600 mg daily and review him again in one month
Decline the increase, consolidate prescribing with you and plan a taper
Stop the pregabalin today and provide a letter for the other prescribers
Switch him to gabapentin at an equivalent dose and continue the same plan
Add diazepam at night for his anxiety and continue the current pregabalin

subtopic_detail: Limits of confidentiality when a specific threat is made to an identifiable person
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar seeing a 29-year-old man in the community clinic. He stopped his risperidone six weeks ago and has slept poorly since.

He tells you that the man in the flat below is transmitting signals into his head through the ceiling and that he has worked out this will only stop if the neighbour is dealt with. He names the neighbour, describes his work hours, and says he bought a hunting knife last week and has it in his kitchen drawer. He is not intoxicated. He asks you to keep what he has told you between the two of you because his mother would be upset, and he declines admission and declines to restart medication.

data_table.Examination: Suspicious and guarded, persecutory delusions with a passivity phenomenon, no cognitive impairment, no intoxication, expressed intent with an identified means and a named target
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen negative for amphetamines and cannabis

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Respect his request and document the threat carefully in the clinical record
Telephone the neighbour yourself to warn him before taking any other step
Arrange urgent involuntary assessment and inform police of the specific threat
Seek his written consent to disclose before contacting anyone about the threat
Restart oral risperidone today and bring him back to the clinic tomorrow

subtopic_detail: Which legal instrument authorises treatment of a physical illness in a patient who lacks capacity
stem:
You are the consultation liaison psychiatry registrar asked to see a 78-year-old man admitted with a community-acquired pneumonia. He has severe depression with psychotic features and is already an involuntary patient under mental health legislation for that illness.

He is refusing intravenous antibiotics. When you assess him he tells you that his lungs rotted away years ago, that he has no blood left in his body, and that treatment is pointless because he is already dead. He cannot repeat back or weigh any of the information you give him about the infection or the consequences of not treating it, and his account does not change when the information is repeated. His oxygen saturation is 89 per cent on room air. There is no advance care directive and his daughter is available and is his nominated substitute decision maker.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 104, blood pressure 118/70, respiratory rate 26, SpO2 89 per cent on room air, temperature 38.6
data_table.Examination: Nihilistic delusions, psychomotor retardation, unable to retain or weigh information about the infection, oriented to person only
data_table.Investigations: C-reactive protein 180 mg/L (less than 5); white cell count 16.2 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0); chest radiograph shows right lower lobe consolidation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate way to authorise the antibiotic treatment?

options.text: Treat under the existing involuntary order because he is already detained
Accept his refusal and document that he has declined treatment for pneumonia
Apply to a tribunal for a guardianship order before giving any antibiotic
Sedate him and give the antibiotics under restraint as an emergency measure
Obtain consent from his substitute decision maker after documenting incapacity

subtopic_detail: Formed visual hallucinations with retained insight in a patient with severe visual loss
stem:
You are the general practitioner making a home visit to an 81-year-old woman with advanced age related macular degeneration whose corrected acuity is 6/60 in both eyes. For three months she has seen small figures in old fashioned clothing standing near her armchair, and repeating brick patterns across her lounge room wall, several times a day for a few minutes at a time.

She tells you she knows they cannot really be there and finds them more puzzling than frightening. She hears no voices, smells nothing unusual and holds no unusual beliefs. She sleeps well, has started no new medicines, and her daughter says her memory and conversation are unchanged.

data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, calcium, thyroid stimulating hormone and urinalysis within normal limits
data_table.Cognitive assessment: Mini Mental State Examination 28 out of 30, with points lost on the copying task

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence risperidone 0.5 mg at night and review in four weeks
Commence quetiapine 25 mg at night and review in four weeks
Commence donepezil 5 mg daily and arrange cognitive assessment
Arrange urgent computed tomography of the brain and admit
Explain the condition, improve lighting and review in four weeks

subtopic_detail: Sequencing drug withdrawal before adding an antipsychotic in Parkinson disease psychosis
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar reviewing a 74-year-old man with Parkinson disease of eight years duration in the movement disorder clinic. His wife says that for six weeks he has been seeing cats and small children in the hallway in the evenings, and that last week he began accusing her of hiding money from him.

He takes levodopa with carbidopa four times daily and ropinirole, which was added six months ago for end of dose wearing off. His conscious state is clear and steady through the day, his attention is intact and his memory and conversation are unchanged from six months ago. He has no urinary symptoms, no cough and no constipation.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 74 beats per minute, blood pressure 128/72 mmHg lying and 112/66 mmHg standing, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, calcium, liver function tests, thyroid stimulating hormone, urinalysis and chest radiograph all within normal limits
data_table.Cognitive assessment: Montreal Cognitive Assessment 25 out of 30, unchanged from six months ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first step?

options.text: Reduce and cease ropinirole while continuing levodopa with carbidopa
Commence risperidone 0.5 mg at night and continue current therapy
Commence olanzapine 2.5 mg at night and continue current therapy
Commence haloperidol 0.5 mg as required and review in one week
Increase the levodopa with carbidopa dose and review in one week

subtopic_detail: Antidepressant selection where a cytochrome interaction would reduce the efficacy of cancer therapy
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 52-year-old woman eight months into tamoxifen 20 mg daily for an oestrogen receptor positive breast cancer. For the past three months she has had low mood most of the day, has stopped seeing friends, wakes at four each morning and has lost interest in work she used to enjoy.

She also describes drenching hot flushes about ten times a day that disturb her sleep. She has no suicidal thoughts, no past psychiatric history and no history of mania. She takes no other regular medication and her ECG shows a corrected QT interval of 418 ms.

data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, liver function tests and thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits

lead_in: Which antidepressant is the most appropriate choice?

options.text: Commence paroxetine 20 mg daily and review in four weeks
Commence fluoxetine 20 mg daily and review in four weeks
Commence bupropion 150 mg daily and review in four weeks
Commence venlafaxine 75 mg daily and review in four weeks
Commence duloxetine 60 mg daily and review in four weeks

subtopic_detail: Managing lithium toxicity precipitated by a newly added antihypertensive
stem:
You are the emergency registrar seeing a 58-year-old man with bipolar affective disorder who has taken lithium carbonate 900 mg at night for nine years with concentrations consistently between 0.6 and 0.8 mmol/L. His wife says that for four days he has been vomiting, his hands have been shaking badly enough to spill his drink, and he has been walking as if he were drunk.

His general practitioner started a tablet for blood pressure three weeks ago. He is alert and orientated with slurred speech, a coarse tremor of both hands and a broad based unsteady gait. There is no fever, no rigidity, no clonus and no seizure activity.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 92 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Serum lithium 1.9 mmol/L (0.6-0.8), creatinine 132 micromol/L (60-110), estimated glomerular filtration rate 48 mL/min/1.73m2, sodium 133 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 3.3 mmol/L (3.5-5.2)
data_table.Medications: Lithium carbonate 900 mg at night, indapamide 2.5 mg daily started three weeks ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Arrange urgent haemodialysis and cease all regular medication
Cease lithium and indapamide and give intravenous sodium chloride
Halve the lithium dose and recheck the concentration in one week
Give activated charcoal 50 g and observe on the ward overnight
Continue lithium at a reduced dose and cease indapamide only

subtopic_detail: Oral supplementation requirements when initiating a long acting injectable antipsychotic
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar in a community mental health team seeing a 26-year-old man with schizophrenia who has been well on oral aripiprazole 15 mg daily for four months after a relapse that followed several weeks of missed tablets. He works shift work and tells you he forgets his morning dose whenever his roster changes.

He has agreed to a monthly injection of the same drug and has never received a long-acting injectable before. He has no extrapyramidal signs, his weight and metabolic screen are stable, and his last relapse resolved fully on oral treatment.

data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, liver function tests, fasting glucose, lipids and prolactin within normal limits
data_table.Electrocardiogram: Sinus rhythm with a corrected QT interval of 402 ms

lead_in: How should the first injection be managed?

options.text: Give the injection and cease oral aripiprazole on the same day
Give the injection and continue oral aripiprazole for three days
Give the injection and continue oral aripiprazole for fourteen days
Give the injection and repeat a second loading dose after one week
Give the injection and start oral olanzapine cover for fourteen days

subtopic_detail: Distinguishing a movement side effect from worsening psychosis in an inpatient
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 23-year-old man admitted three weeks ago with a first episode of psychosis and started on olanzapine 15 mg at night. The voices that frightened him on admission have almost gone and he no longer believes his flatmates are recording him.

Over the past five days he has been pacing the corridor for hours and cannot stay seated through a meal. He tells you his legs feel like they have to keep moving and that this is worse than the voices ever were. There is no rigidity, no tremor, no fever and no diaphoresis, and the nursing staff have asked whether the dose should be increased.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 124/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 118 U/L (40-320), full blood count, electrolytes, liver function tests and thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Constant shifting of weight from foot to foot when standing and rocking when seated, with normal tone and no cogwheeling

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Increase olanzapine to 20 mg daily to target residual psychosis
Commence benzatropine 2 mg twice daily and review in one week
Commence lorazepam 1 mg three times daily and review in a week
Commence sodium valproate 500 mg twice daily for the agitation
Reduce the olanzapine dose and commence propranolol 10 mg daily

subtopic_detail: Recognising a surgical emergency behind a common clozapine adverse effect
stem:
You are the emergency registrar seeing a 38-year-old man with treatment resistant schizophrenia who has taken clozapine 450 mg daily for two years with a stable mental state. He tells you he has not opened his bowels for five days and that his belly has become tight and swollen.

He brought up dark green fluid twice this morning and has not been able to keep water down since. His abdomen is distended and tympanic with no guarding and no bowel sounds audible over two minutes. He takes an occasional docusate tablet that his mother buys for him and no other regular medication.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 108 beats per minute, blood pressure 116/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 37.3 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 13.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), neutrophils 9.2 x10^9/L (2.0-7.5), potassium 3.3 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), creatinine 108 micromol/L (60-110), lactate 2.4 mmol/L (less than 2.0)
data_table.Examination: Distended tympanic abdomen with no bowel sounds and an empty rectum on digital examination

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Prescribe macrogol daily and review the bowel chart in 48 hours
Continue clozapine and add docusate with senna each evening
Reduce the clozapine dose and start a stimulant laxative today
Withhold clozapine and arrange an urgent abdominal radiograph
Arrange an outpatient colonoscopy within the next two weeks

subtopic_detail: Antidepressant associated inappropriate antidiuresis in an older adult
stem:
