You are the general practitioner reviewing a 79-year-old woman who started sertraline 50 mg daily four weeks ago for a moderate depressive episode. Her daughter says she has become sleepy in the afternoons, is unsteady getting out of her chair, and twice this week could not remember the day.

Her mood and appetite had begun to improve before this change. Her mucous membranes are moist, her jugular venous pressure is visible 2 cm above the sternal angle and there is no peripheral oedema or postural drop. She takes no diuretic and her serum sodium was 139 mmol/L before the antidepressant was started.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 72 beats per minute, blood pressure 132/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 15 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 124 mmol/L (135-145), serum osmolality 258 mmol/kg (275-295), urine osmolality 480 mmol/kg, urine sodium 62 mmol/L, potassium 4.1 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), creatinine 68 micromol/L (45-90)
data_table.Additional tests: Thyroid stimulating hormone and 9 am cortisol within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Continue sertraline and restrict oral fluid to 1000 mL daily
Switch to citalopram and recheck the serum sodium in one week
Commence tolvaptan and continue the current antidepressant
Infuse hypertonic 3 per cent sodium chloride 100 mL over 10 minutes
Cease sertraline and restrict oral fluid with sodium recheck

subtopic_detail: Choosing first line management for behavioural symptoms where antipsychotic sensitivity is expected
stem:
You are the general practitioner asked to review a 78-year-old man in residential aged care whose cognition has declined over three years. Staff describe days when he converses normally and days when he stares and cannot be roused into conversation, and he regularly tells them there are children standing in the corner of his room.

His wife says he shouts and kicks in his sleep and has fallen out of bed twice. He has a stooped posture and slow movements without a tremor. For the past two weeks he has been shouting and pushing staff away during evening personal care, and no trigger has been identified.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 70 beats per minute, blood pressure 126/74 mmHg lying, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, calcium, liver function tests, thyroid stimulating hormone, urinalysis and chest radiograph within normal limits
data_table.Medications: Perindopril 4 mg daily and colecalciferol 1000 units daily, with no changes in six months

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Commence risperidone 0.5 mg twice daily and review in one week
Implement a behaviour support plan and review pain and constipation
Commence haloperidol 0.5 mg as required for episodes of agitation
Commence olanzapine 2.5 mg each night and review again in one week
Commence diazepam 2 mg twice daily and review again in one week

subtopic_detail: Managing an elevated mood state caused by a drug that cannot simply be stopped
stem:
You are the medical registrar called to the respiratory ward about a 58-year-old man on day five of prednisolone 50 mg daily for an exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Nursing staff say he has not slept for two nights, talks over everyone, and telephoned his sister at three in the morning about buying a caravan to drive around the country.

He is irritable when interrupted but knows where he is, follows a three step command and can recite the months backwards. He sees and hears nothing unusual. He has no psychiatric history and no family history of mood disorder, and he is still wheezy with an oxygen requirement of 2 litres per minute.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 142/84 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, SpO2 93 per cent on 2 litres per minute, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, calcium, liver function tests, thyroid stimulating hormone and urinalysis within normal limits, blood glucose 9.2 mmol/L (3.0-7.7 fasting)
data_table.Substance history: No alcohol for six years, no illicit substance use, urine drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reduce prednisolone to the lowest effective dose and add olanzapine
Commence lithium and continue prednisolone at the current dose
Commence sodium valproate and continue prednisolone unchanged
Continue prednisolone and prescribe temazepam for the insomnia
Cease prednisolone abruptly and commence sertraline for the mood

subtopic_detail: Selecting pharmacotherapy where one antidepressant class is specifically contraindicated
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 24-year-old woman who has been binge eating and then making herself vomit about four times a week for two years. She has been seeing a psychologist fortnightly for three months and finds the sessions useful but says the urges are still overwhelming.

For the past two months she has also had persistently low mood, poor concentration and early morning waking. Her body mass index is 22 kg per square metre and her blood pressure shows no postural drop. She has never had a seizure, takes no regular medication and asks whether a tablet could help.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 68 beats per minute, blood pressure 112/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Potassium 3.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), bicarbonate 30 mmol/L (22-32), magnesium 0.78 mmol/L (0.70-1.10), full blood count and liver function tests within normal limits
data_table.Electrocardiogram: Sinus rhythm with a corrected QT interval of 424 ms

lead_in: Which medication is the most appropriate addition?

options.text: Commence bupropion 150 mg daily alongside psychological therapy
Commence topiramate 50 mg daily alongside psychological therapy
Commence fluoxetine 60 mg daily alongside psychological therapy
Commence mirtazapine 30 mg daily alongside psychological therapy
Commence venlafaxine 75 mg daily alongside psychological therapy

subtopic_detail: Serotonin toxicity precipitated by an antibiotic with monoamine oxidase inhibiting activity
stem:
You are the medical registrar called to the surgical ward about a 45-year-old woman who has taken sertraline 100 mg daily for three years. She was started on linezolid three days ago for a resistant enterococcal wound infection after other options were excluded on susceptibility testing.

She has become agitated and confused over the past eight hours and is drenched in sweat. She has brisk reflexes that are more pronounced in the legs than the arms, sustained clonus at both ankles, and dilated pupils. Her limbs move freely with normal tone, and her creatine kinase is not raised.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 124 beats per minute, blood pressure 158/92 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, SpO2 96 per cent on room air, temperature 38.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 190 U/L (40-320), white cell count 11.2 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), creatinine 84 micromol/L (45-90), sodium 138 mmol/L (135-145), venous lactate 2.1 mmol/L (less than 2.0)
data_table.Examination: Sustained inducible ankle clonus bilaterally, hyperreflexia greater in the lower limbs, mydriasis, normal limb tone

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Cease sertraline only and continue linezolid with close observation
Cease both drugs and give intravenous benzodiazepine with cooling
Commence dantrolene and continue both drugs with cardiac monitoring
Commence bromocriptine and continue both drugs with cardiac monitoring
Give intramuscular haloperidol for the agitation and observe closely

subtopic_detail: Cardiovascular prerequisites before initiating stimulant therapy in an adult
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 34-year-old electrician whose specialist assessment has confirmed attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, supported by primary school reports and a collateral history from his mother. He has never been treated and wants to start medication because he is making costly errors at work.

His blood pressure has been 158/98 mmHg and 154/96 mmHg at two visits four weeks apart, and he has never taken an antihypertensive. His body mass index is 31 kg per square metre. He has no chest pain, no exertional breathlessness and no syncope, and there is no family history of sudden cardiac death before the age of 40.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 78 beats per minute, blood pressure 156/97 mmHg today, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Electrolytes, creatinine, fasting glucose and thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, urine albumin to creatinine ratio 1.8 mg/mmol (less than 2.5)
data_table.Electrocardiogram: Sinus rhythm with normal axis, no left ventricular hypertrophy and a corrected QT interval of 406 ms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Treat the hypertension first and reassess before starting a stimulant
Commence methylphenidate now and monitor the blood pressure each month
Commence dexamfetamine at a low dose and monitor the blood pressure
Commence atomoxetine now and monitor the blood pressure each month
Refer for echocardiography before commencing any stimulant medication

subtopic_detail: Structuring a benzodiazepine taper after failed abrupt cessation attempts
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 62-year-old woman who has taken oxazepam 30 mg three times daily for six years, started for insomnia after a bereavement and continued ever since. She now wants to come off it because she feels foggy during the day and had a fall last month.

She has tried stopping twice on her own. On the first attempt she stopped over three days and had two nights of tremor, sweating and rebound insomnia before restarting. On the second she stopped abruptly and had a witnessed generalised seizure on day three. Her liver function tests and albumin are within normal limits and she drinks no alcohol.

data_table.Examination: Alert and orientated, no tremor at rest, gait steady with normal tandem walking
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes and liver function tests within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Halve the oxazepam dose today and cease it completely in one week
Continue the oxazepam and add temazepam at night for the insomnia
Substitute quetiapine 25 mg at night and cease the oxazepam today
Convert to an equivalent diazepam dose and reduce gradually each fortnight
Cease the oxazepam entirely now and cover withdrawal with as required diazepam

subtopic_detail: Distinguishing a body focused repetitive behaviour from alopecia areata and choosing behavioural therapy over an antidepressant
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 19-year-old university student who has noticed patches of hair loss on her scalp over the past year. She says it is worst during examination periods and that she often finds herself doing it while reading, without noticing until a handful comes away.

She describes a build up of tension beforehand and a sense of relief afterwards, and she is ashamed enough to have started wearing a beanie indoors. She has no intrusive thoughts about contamination, order or harm, and no rituals she feels compelled to complete in a set sequence. On examination the affected areas contain broken hairs of many different lengths with normal underlying skin, no scale, no scarring and no tapering hairs at the margins.

data_table.Examination: Two irregular patches on the right frontoparietal scalp, hairs of varying lengths within the patches, no erythema, no scale, no scarring, eyebrows and eyelashes intact
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, ferritin and thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Start topical minoxidil and review the scalp again in three months
Refer for habit reversal behavioural therapy as initial treatment
Start fluoxetine 20 mg daily and review her again in six weeks
Start olanzapine 2.5 mg at night and review her in four weeks
Refer to dermatology for scalp biopsy before any other treatment

subtopic_detail: First line management of gambling disorder presenting through insomnia and low mood
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 34-year-old man who booked in for sleeping tablets. He has been awake most nights for two months, has lost interest in the football he used to play, and says he feels flat but denies any thoughts of self-harm.

When you ask what keeps him awake, he tells you his wife found a sports betting app on his phone last week and that he has taken out a second personal loan without telling her. He has tried to stop several times and lasted at most a fortnight. He drinks two beers a week and uses no other substances. He wants help and has brought his loan statements with him.

data_table.Examination: Reactive affect, no psychomotor retardation, no psychotic features, no suicidal ideation on direct questioning
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, liver function tests and thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits

lead_in: What would you first recommend?

options.text: Start naltrexone 50 mg daily and review his craving in four weeks
Advise a self imposed casino and betting app ban with review in three months
Refer for inpatient withdrawal management and review after discharge
Refer for gambling focused psychological therapy and financial counselling
Start sertraline 50 mg daily and review his mood again in four weeks

subtopic_detail: Separating illness anxiety from somatic symptom disorder and stopping the reassurance cycle
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 41-year-old man for the eleventh time in two years. His uncle died of motor neurone disease and since then he has been convinced he has the same illness.

He reports occasional twitching in his calves after running but says the twitching itself does not bother him; what keeps him up is what it means. He inspects his tongue in the mirror several times a day, films his hands to compare them week to week, and asks at every visit for another set of tests. Two nerve conduction studies and needle electromyography 14 months apart were normal, as were four neurological examinations including yours today. He works full time and has never sought a certificate, a benefit or a compensation claim.

data_table.Examination: Normal bulk and power throughout, no tongue fasciculation, reflexes symmetrical and normal, plantar responses flexor
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 96 U/L (30-150), thyroid stimulating hormone 1.8 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), nerve conduction studies and electromyography reported as normal on two occasions

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Repeat nerve conduction studies to provide definitive reassurance
Start regular reassurance appointments with weekly examination
Refer to neurology for a third opinion and muscle biopsy review
Start quetiapine 50 mg at night and review him in six weeks
Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy targeting health anxiety

subtopic_detail: Treating a recurrent winter pattern depressive illness with bright light therapy
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 38-year-old woman who moved from Cairns to Hobart four years ago for work. For the past three winters she has become flat, slept 11 hours a night and still felt unrefreshed, craved bread and biscuits and gained around 5 kg each year.

Each year she has been back to her usual self by October without treatment, and she describes those summer months as entirely normal rather than elevated, with no reduced need for sleep and no overspending. Her energy is the symptom that bothers her most; she has no thoughts of self-harm. This year she has come in during May asking to prevent the pattern rather than wait it out. Her thyroid function is normal and her vitamin D is 68 nmol/L.

data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone 2.2 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), 25 hydroxyvitamin D 68 nmol/L (50-150), haemoglobin 134 g/L (115-165), ferritin 62 mcg/L (20-200)
data_table.Examination: Reactive affect, no psychomotor change, no psychotic features

lead_in: What would you first recommend?

options.text: Melatonin 2 mg at bedtime through the winter months each year
Lithium carbonate with three monthly concentration monitoring
Modafinil each morning through the winter months of each year
Vitamin D 1000 units daily through the winter months each year
Bright light therapy each morning through the winter months

subtopic_detail: Recognising cataplexy behind a referral for depression with hypersomnia
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 23-year-old apprentice referred by his mother because she thinks he is depressed. He sleeps ten hours at night, still falls asleep in the training room most afternoons, and has been written up twice for it.

He tells you that when something really strikes him as funny his knees give way and his jaw goes slack for a few seconds, and that he stays completely aware throughout and can hear everyone around him. Twice on waking he has been unable to move for a minute or so, and he sometimes sees a figure at the end of the bed as he is dropping off. He describes his mood as fed up rather than sad, still plays five a side on weekends and enjoys it, and has no thoughts of self-harm.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 24 kg/m2, normal cranial nerve and limb neurological examination, no neck circumference increase and no tonsillar hypertrophy
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, ferritin, thyroid stimulating hormone and glycated haemoglobin within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Advise sleep hygiene measures and review him again in three months
Arrange polysomnography followed by a multiple sleep latency test
Start sertraline 50 mg daily and review his mood in four weeks
Arrange an electroencephalogram and refer to the epilepsy service
Start modafinil 200 mg each morning and review him in four weeks

subtopic_detail: Responding to complex sleep behaviour on a sedative hypnotic rather than substituting another agent
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 58-year-old woman who has taken zolpidem 10 mg at night for eight months, originally prescribed after her mother died.

Her husband tells you he has twice found her standing at the kitchen bench at three in the morning making and eating toast, answering him in a flat voice and not remembering any of it in the morning. Last week she found biscuit wrappers on the bedroom floor and a half typed message on her phone sent to a work colleague at 2:40 am that she has no memory of writing. She drinks no alcohol and takes no other sedating medication. She sleeps about six hours a night and says the tablet is the only thing that gets her off to sleep.

data_table.Examination: Alert and orientated, normal neurological examination, body mass index 26 kg/m2
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, liver function tests and thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Cease the zolpidem and refer for cognitive behavioural therapy
Halve the zolpidem dose and review her again in four weeks
Switch to temazepam 10 mg at night and review in four weeks
Add melatonin 2 mg at night and continue the current zolpidem
Arrange overnight polysomnography before changing any treatment

subtopic_detail: Separating consistent situational failure to speak from autism and from a language disorder
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 6-year-old girl referred by her school. She has not spoken a single word at school in the 18 months since she started, communicating with her teacher by nodding, pointing and handing over written notes.

At home she chatters constantly to her parents and her older brother, tells long detailed stories about her day and argues about bedtime. Her mother has recorded her at home and plays you a clip in which her speech is fluent, grammatical and age appropriate. She plays imaginative games with her cousins, takes turns, shares jokes and makes easy eye contact at home. She has no restricted interests, no repetitive movements and no insistence on routines. An audiology assessment last month was normal.

data_table.Examination: Interacts with the examiner by nodding and pointing, makes brief eye contact, no dysmorphic features, normal neurological examination
data_table.Investigations: Audiology assessment normal, growth and development otherwise age appropriate

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Refer for autism diagnostic assessment before any intervention
Start fluoxetine 10 mg daily and review her again in six weeks
Arrange formal speech pathology language assessment and review
Advise the school to allow written answers and review in a year
Refer for graded exposure therapy with a school based plan

subtopic_detail: Managing anxiety based school refusal presenting as recurrent morning abdominal symptoms
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 9-year-old boy brought by his mother with six weeks of stomach aches and vomiting on school mornings. He wakes at six, complains of pain, retches once or twice into the sink, and by ten o'clock at home he is playing and asking for lunch.

There are no symptoms on Saturdays or Sundays, and he was entirely well through the two week term break in July. He has been at school four days in the past three weeks. He tells you he worries that something will happen to his mother while he is out of the house, and he has been getting into his parents' bed most nights since his grandfather died in May. His weight is tracking along the 50th centile, he has no night waking with pain, no blood in the motions and no mouth ulcers.

data_table.Examination: Soft abdomen, no tenderness, no masses, no perianal disease, growth along the 50th centile for weight and height
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, C reactive protein, coeliac serology with total immunoglobulin A and faecal calprotectin all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: A graded return to school plan developed with the school and parents
Start fluoxetine 10 mg daily and review him again in six weeks
Home schooling arrangement until the abdominal symptoms settle
Abdominal ultrasound and coeliac serology before any other management step
Refer to paediatric gastroenterology for further investigation

subtopic_detail: Choosing behavioural therapy ahead of antipsychotic medication for impairing tics
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing an 11-year-old boy whose parents are worried about movements that started when he was eight. He blinks hard, jerks his head to the left and shrugs one shoulder, and for the past 18 months he has also cleared his throat repeatedly and made a short barking sound.

He tells you he gets a build up of feeling in his neck beforehand, like an itch he has to scratch, and that he can hold the movements in for a minute or two at the cost of the feeling getting worse until he lets go. The movements settle when he is absorbed in building models and are worst when he is tired or being watched. Between movements he is fully alert with no confusion and no loss of awareness. His handwriting has deteriorated because of the head jerks and two boys have started imitating him in the playground.

data_table.Examination: Multiple motor and vocal tics observed during the consultation, briefly suppressible on request, normal tone, power, coordination and gait
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, liver function and thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Start clonidine at night and review his tics again in six weeks
Arrange an electroencephalogram before any treatment is started
Advise that no treatment is needed and review him in six months
Refer for a comprehensive behavioural intervention for his tics
Start risperidone 0.5 mg at night and review him in four weeks

subtopic_detail: Requiring prospective symptom charting before treating a suspected premenstrual mood disorder
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 29-year-old woman who says that for five years she has become irritable, tearful and unable to concentrate in the week before her period, and that she once slammed a door hard enough to crack the frame.

She tells you the symptoms lift within two or three days of her period arriving and that she feels entirely herself for the fortnight after that. She has never written any of this down and is describing it from memory. She is not using hormonal contraception and does not wish to conceive in the next year. Her partner has told her the pattern is obvious to him but he has not tracked it either.

data_table.Examination: Reactive affect on the day of review, which is day 8 of her cycle, no psychomotor change and no psychotic features
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, ferritin, thyroid stimulating hormone and beta human chorionic gonadotrophin within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start sertraline 50 mg daily and review her again in two cycles
Start a combined oral contraceptive and review her in two cycles
Measure serum progesterone and oestradiol on day 21 of the cycle
Refer for gonadotrophin releasing hormone agonist therapy trial
Prospective daily symptom rating across two consecutive cycles

subtopic_detail: Separating a chronic subsyndromal bipolar spectrum illness from affective instability of personality
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar assessing a 26-year-old graphic designer referred with mood swings that have gone on since she was 22. She describes stretches of four or five days at a time when she needs only five hours sleep, works through the night on side projects and talks over people, followed by stretches of a week or so when she is flat, oversleeps and cancels plans.

She has never had a period of elevated mood lasting four full days with the impairment or the number of symptoms her previous psychiatrist described as needed for a formal episode, and she has never been admitted or psychotic. The shifts come on over a day or two and are not obviously set off by arguments or rejections. She has had the same partner for five years and the same three close friends since school, has never self harmed, and does not describe chronic emptiness or fears of abandonment. In four years she has never been free of symptoms for as long as two months.

data_table.Examination: Euthymic on the day of review, normal speech rate, no psychotic features, no suicidal ideation
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, liver function tests and thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Advise watchful waiting with review of her mood in six months
Commence a mood stabiliser with psychoeducation and mood charting
Commence sertraline 50 mg daily with review again in four weeks
Refer for dialectical behaviour therapy with weekly skills group
Commence a stimulant trial after formal attention testing is done

subtopic_detail: Washout interval before a monoamine oxidase inhibitor after a long half life antidepressant
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar in an outpatient clinic reviewing a 47-year-old man with a depressive illness that has not responded to two adequate trials. He completed 12 weeks of sertraline at 200 mg and then eight months of venlafaxine at 225 mg without meaningful improvement.

He was changed to fluoxetine 40 mg daily six months ago and took his last dose three days ago in anticipation of today's appointment. The consultant plans to start moclobemide. He takes no other medication, no over the counter preparations and no herbal products, and he has no cardiac or hepatic disease. His most recent electrolytes and liver function tests were within normal limits.

data_table.Examination: No clonus, no hyperreflexia, no tremor, no diaphoresis, normal tone
data_table.Investigations: Electrolytes, liver function tests and full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan for starting the new agent?

options.text: Start it after a 48 hour gap with close outpatient review
Cross taper the two agents over the coming fortnight instead
Wait five weeks after the last fluoxetine dose before starting it
Wait two full weeks after the last fluoxetine dose before starting it
Start it now because the agent is a reversible inhibitor

subtopic_detail: Distinguishing persistent detachment with intact reality testing from focal seizures and from panic
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar assessing a 24-year-old woman who describes episodes in which she feels as though she is watching herself from a few feet behind her own head, and the room looks flat, like a stage set.

The episodes come on over minutes and last from several hours to most of a day. Throughout them she knows the feeling is not real and can carry on a conversation, drive and work, and afterwards she can recount everything that happened. She has no lip smacking or hand fumbling, no rising sensation in her stomach, no unusual smells and no period of confusion at the end. There is no chest tightness, palpitations or breathlessness with the episodes. They began during a period of daily cannabis use two years ago and have continued unchanged since she stopped 18 months ago.

data_table.Examination: Normal cranial nerve, motor and sensory examination, orientated in time place and person, insight fully preserved
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, liver function tests, thyroid stimulating hormone and urine drug screen within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the brain before treatment
Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy targeting the symptoms
Arrange prolonged video electroencephalogram monitoring first
Start propranolol before predictable stressors and review later
Start olanzapine 5 mg at night and review her again in six weeks

subtopic_detail: Separating persistent bereavement related distress from a depressive episode
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar seeing a 62-year-old woman referred by her general practitioner sixteen months after her husband died from bowel cancer. She says she aches for him every day, keeps his voicemail message on her phone and plays it most nights, and cannot bring herself to walk past the cafe where they used to meet.

She tells you she does not know who she is any more without him and feels that part of her died with him. She still meets her sister weekly, laughs at her grandchildren, cooks properly and has continued her volunteer shifts at the op shop. She denies feeling worthless, denies wanting to die, and her appetite and concentration are unchanged. She sleeps about five hours and wakes thinking of him.

data_table.Examination: Reactive affect with tearfulness when speaking of her husband, no psychomotor retardation, cognition intact
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes and thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Major depressive disorder of moderate severity
Post-traumatic stress disorder following the death
Prolonged grief disorder with identity disruption
Adjustment disorder with depressed mood
Uncomplicated bereavement within the expected range

subtopic_detail: Choosing a household intervention over dose escalation after repeated early relapse
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar in an early psychosis service reviewing a 21-year-old apprentice fourteen months after his first episode of psychosis. He has been readmitted twice in that time, each admission following a fortnight of escalating arguments at home.

His father tells you in front of him that the boy is lazy, could snap out of it if he tried, and needs watching every minute. His mother has given up her shifts to supervise him and phones him hourly when she is out. A depot antipsychotic has been given on schedule with dispensing records confirming every dose, and his plasma level last week was in the expected range. He uses no alcohol or other drugs and urine drug screening has been negative on each admission. Between admissions he has no delusions or hallucinations, sleeps normally and is looking for work.

data_table.Examination: Euthymic, no thought disorder, no perceptual abnormality, no extrapyramidal signs on examination
data_table.Investigations: Antipsychotic plasma concentration within expected range, urine drug screen negative, full blood count and metabolic panel within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next intervention?

options.text: Increase the depot antipsychotic dose at the next scheduled administration
Add an antidepressant to cover the emotional distress before each relapse
Refer for individual cognitive behavioural therapy for psychotic symptoms
Arrange supported accommodation so that he moves out of the family home
Offer structured family intervention with psychoeducation for the household

subtopic_detail: Choosing the NSW instrument that records treatment preferences for a future episode
stem: In a NSW community clinic you see a 34-year-old teacher with bipolar disorder, well for eleven months on lithium. She has had three manic episodes, two ending in involuntary admission. Olanzapine caused such severe inner restlessness that she paced all night. She would accept another antipsychotic, and wants her sister rather than her father contacted. She reasons through each preference today.

data_table.Examination: Euthymic, no pressure of speech, insight into illness intact
data_table.Investigations: Serum lithium 0.72 mmol/L, thyroid and renal function normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate action at this consultation?

options.text: Arrange an enduring power of attorney so her sister manages her affairs
Explain that a future treating team will decide her treatment regardless
Record the olanzapine reaction in her file as an adverse drug reaction
Support an advance care directive and a designated carer nomination today
Apply for a community treatment order now to prevent a further admission

subtopic_detail: Repetitive theft of items of no use or value in a woman with intact cognition
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar asked to assess a 47-year-old accountant referred by the court after her third shoplifting charge in two years. She earns a good income and had more than enough money in her purse on each occasion.

She describes a tightening tension that builds over an hour or two in the shop, a rush of relief at the moment she puts the item into her bag, and then hours of shame. The items were a hairbrush, a packet of batteries and a child's colouring book, none of which she needed. She has given them away or thrown them out unopened. She has never been in trouble otherwise, has held the same job for nineteen years, and says the whole thing horrifies her. Her sleep, appetite and energy are unchanged and she has had no periods of reduced need for sleep or increased spending.

data_table.Examination: Euthymic with appropriate shame, no pressure of speech, no grandiosity, Montreal Cognitive Assessment 29 out of 30
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, liver function and thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Manic episode with disinhibited and impulsive behaviour
Antisocial personality disorder with a pattern of unlawful conduct
Behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia presenting with theft
Kleptomania with the characteristic tension and relief cycle
Obsessive compulsive disorder with a compulsion expressed as stealing

subtopic_detail: Separating defiant oppositional behaviour from a conduct disorder in a school aged child
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a community child health clinic seeing a 9-year-old boy brought by his mother after a note from his teacher. For about ten months he has argued with every adult instruction, refused to do what he is asked, and needled his younger sister until she cries, then insisted she started it.

His mother says he is touchy, loses his temper several times a week when he is asked to stop what he is doing, and holds a grudge for days. He has never hurt another child or an animal, and nothing at home or at school has been broken, stolen or set alight. Between confrontations he is cheerful, plays well with two friends and is calm at his swimming club. He reads at his year level and his teacher reports he sits and finishes his written work without prompting.

data_table.Examination: Engages well in conversation, reciprocal eye contact and shared enjoyment, no repetitive behaviours, no motor tics
data_table.Investigations: Hearing screen and vision screen normal, developmental history unremarkable

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder of the combined presentation
Conduct disorder with aggression towards people and property
Oppositional defiant disorder of angry and vindictive pattern
Disruptive mood dysregulation disorder with severe temper outbursts
Autism spectrum disorder presenting as rigidity and demand refusal

subtopic_detail: Responding to a request for further cosmetic surgery driven by appearance preoccupation
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar seeing a 24-year-old man referred by a plastic surgeon who declined to operate. He asks you to write a supporting letter for a second rhinoplasty.

He describes his nose as twisted and says people glance at it on the train. He checks it in reflective surfaces for around four hours a day, photographs it under different lights, and has stopped going to his warehouse shifts because of it. His first rhinoplasty two years ago left him more distressed than before. Two surgeons and his general practitioner have told him the nose looks normal, and he says he can accept that they see it differently but he knows what he sees. He has no hallucinations, no ideas of reference beyond his appearance, and no thought interference.

data_table.Examination: Nasal contour symmetrical with a well healed scar, mood reactive, no perceptual abnormality, no formal thought disorder
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen negative, full blood count and thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Provide the supporting letter and refer him to a second plastic surgeon
Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy and start a serotonin reuptake inhibitor
Commence an atypical antipsychotic given the fixity of the appearance belief
Refer for long term psychodynamic psychotherapy without medication
Prescribe a short course of diazepam to reduce his distress before deciding

subtopic_detail: Distinguishing accumulation driven by difficulty discarding from neglect driven squalor
stem:
You are the medical registrar on a hospital in the home round visiting a 68-year-old retired librarian after the fire brigade raised a welfare concern. Newspapers, books, empty jars and folded plastic bags are stacked from floor to ceiling through the hallway and both bedrooms, leaving a narrow path to a single chair and the kitchen bench.

She washes daily, her clothes are clean, there is no rotting food and no animal or human waste in the house. She explains that each item might be needed, that the jars are perfectly good, and becomes visibly distressed when you ask what would happen if a box went out with the rubbish. She has been buying newspapers she does not read for about fifteen years and the accumulation has grown steadily. She has no handwashing rituals, no checking rituals and no intrusive thoughts that she tries to neutralise.

data_table.Examination: Montreal Cognitive Assessment 28 out of 30, self care intact, mood reactive with no anhedonia, insight partial
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, thyroid function and vitamin B12 within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Obsessive compulsive disorder with contamination related saving
Obsessive compulsive personality disorder with rigidity about possessions
Severe domestic squalor from self neglect with cognitive decline
Major depressive disorder with amotivation and household neglect
Hoarding disorder with excessive acquisition of unneeded items

subtopic_detail: Pathway to gender affirming hormone treatment for a competent adolescent in Australia
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in an adolescent clinic seeing a 15-year-old who was recorded female at birth, attends with both parents, and asks you to start testosterone. He has consistently described himself as male since the age of nine, uses a male name at school, and says the distress about his chest and periods has worsened each year.

Both parents support him and say the request has been consistent for years. He is in year 10, attends school daily and has close friends. Breast development is complete and he has been menstruating for three years. He describes his reasoning clearly, understands that some effects of testosterone are permanent while others are not, and asks about fertility preservation without prompting. He denies self-harm and has no current suicidal thoughts.

data_table.Examination: Tanner stage 5 breast and pubic hair development, height on the 60th centile, blood pressure within normal limits
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, liver function, renal function and thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer to a multidisciplinary gender service for assessment of readiness and competence
Apply to the Family Court for authorisation before any hormone treatment begins
Commence a gonadotrophin releasing hormone analogue to suppress further puberty
Commence testosterone today with a written treatment agreement and monitoring
Advise that no medical treatment can be considered until he turns eighteen

subtopic_detail: Conducting a first mental health assessment when the accompanying relative is interpreting
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 42-year-old man who arrived in Australia two years ago and holds a bridging visa. He has come about eight months of daily headaches and broken sleep, and his 16-year-old son has come to translate for him.

Through his son he says only that his head hurts and that he is tired. When you ask about his mood, he looks at the floor and the son answers that his father is fine and just needs tablets. Physical examination including neurological examination is normal and there are no red flag features for the headache. He shakes his head when the son asks whether anything happened before he came to Australia, but you notice his hands begin to tremble.

data_table.Examination: Neurological examination normal, no papilloedema, no neck stiffness, blood pressure within normal limits
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, thyroid function and iron studies within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue the consultation with his son translating and explore his mood directly
Engage an accredited interpreter by telephone and continue the assessment today
Refer directly to a specialist torture and trauma service without further assessment
Prescribe mirtazapine for the insomnia and review him again in four weeks
Ask him to return with a written translation of his symptoms at the next visit

subtopic_detail: Acting on fabricated illness in a child when only one observer reports the events
stem:
You are the consultation liaison psychiatry registrar asked to see the mother of a 3-year-old girl on the paediatric ward. This is her seventh admission in fourteen months for reported episodes in which she stops breathing and goes blue.

Every episode has been witnessed by her mother alone, including two that were reported as occurring in the bathroom during previous admissions. Prolonged video electroencephalography over four days recorded no events and no epileptiform activity, and cardiac, metabolic and airway investigations have all been normal. Nursing staff document that the girl is playful and eats well, and that she has had no episodes across three nights when her mother was not on the ward. Her mother trained as an enrolled nurse, has researched the condition extensively, and has requested transfer to a fourth hospital.

data_table.Examination: Child alert, playful, growth on the 50th centile for weight and height, no bruising and no injuries
data_table.Investigations: Four day video electroencephalography with no recorded events, echocardiogram normal, metabolic screen normal, full blood count and electrolytes within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Discharge home with a monitor and outpatient paediatric review in two weeks
Arrange covert video surveillance of the mother in the ward cubicle
Notify child protection services and convene a multidisciplinary case meeting
Interview the mother alone and put the inconsistencies in the history to her
Repeat the neurological workup with extended ambulatory monitoring at home

subtopic_detail: First line treatment choice for established post traumatic stress disorder
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar seeing a 29-year-old paramedic nine months after a highway crash in which the driver she was treating died. She reports vivid intrusive images of the scene several times a day, wakes at three most mornings after the same dream, and has driven a forty minute detour to avoid that stretch of road every shift since.

She startles when a colleague drops equipment and has stopped attending the station debrief because the talk brings it back. Her mood lifts at home with her partner and she has not lost interest in her hobbies. She drinks two standard drinks a week, uses no other substances, and has no delusions or hallucinations. She has taken no medication and asks what will actually help.

data_table.Examination: Alert and engaged, hypervigilant to noise in the corridor, no psychomotor retardation, no anhedonia
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, liver function and thyroid function within normal limits, urine drug screen negative

lead_in: What treatment would you recommend first?

options.text: A single session structured psychological debriefing about the crash
Trauma-focused psychological therapy delivered over eight to twelve sessions
Sertraline titrated to an effective dose with review at four weeks
Diazepam at night for the sleep disturbance and morning waking
Non directive supportive counselling with her workplace employee service

subtopic_detail: Impaired control over gaming with functional collapse in a final year school student
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar seeing a 17-year-old brought by his father after failing three year 12 subjects. For about eighteen months he has played an online game for eight to ten hours a day, mostly overnight, and has told his parents he was studying when he was playing.

He quit the soccer team he had played in since he was eight and no longer sees the friends he played with. He has twice tried to cut back to two hours a day and lasted a few days each time. When his father took the console away last month he shouted, punched a door and did not sleep. He describes himself as absorbed and content while playing and flat and restless when he cannot. He drinks no alcohol, uses no other substances, and his weight and appetite are unchanged.

data_table.Examination: Reactive affect that brightens when discussing the game, no psychomotor retardation, no thought disorder, no self-harm
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, iron studies and thyroid function within normal limits, urine drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Major depressive disorder with withdrawal and loss of interest
Social anxiety disorder with avoidance of peers through online activity
Adjustment disorder in response to academic pressure in year 12
Gaming disorder with impaired control and functional deterioration
Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder presenting as academic failure

subtopic_detail: Deep unconsciousness at a dance party with bradycardia and no response to an opioid antagonist
stem: A 22-year-old man is brought in 40 minutes after swallowing a capful of clear liquid at a warehouse party. He is deeply unconscious, localising to a trapezius squeeze. Intranasal naloxone 800 micrograms produced no change. A jaw thrust and lateral position keep his airway clear and he ventilates spontaneously.

data_table.Examination: Glasgow coma scale 7, pupils 4 mm and reactive, glucose 6.4 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Continue airway positioning and close monitoring
Give further intravenous naloxone until he wakes
Administer intravenous flumazenil and reassess
Insert a nasogastric tube and give activated charcoal
Perform rapid sequence intubation for his coma

subtopic_detail: Seizure at a music festival after a stimulant and large volumes of water with a serum sodium of 118
stem:
You are the emergency registrar called to a 19-year-old woman who had a two minute generalised seizure in the department. Her friends say she took two tablets sold as ecstasy about six hours ago and has been drinking water steadily all evening because she was worried about overheating.

She vomited twice before the seizure and had complained of a severe headache. She is now drowsy but rousable and has not seized again. Her temperature is normal, her skin is dry, and there is no rigidity, clonus or trismus. She takes no regular medication and has no history of epilepsy. Her serum sodium is 118 mmol/L, her serum osmolality is 248 mOsm/kg, her urine osmolality is 620 mOsm/kg and her urine sodium is 58 mmol/L. Her creatine kinase is 210 U/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 96 per minute, blood pressure 116/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 118 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 3.6 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), serum osmolality 248 mOsm/kg (275-295), urine osmolality 620 mOsm/kg, urine sodium 58 mmol/L, creatine kinase 210 U/L (less than 200), capillary glucose 5.8 mmol/L (3.5-7.8)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

options.text: Restrict her fluid intake to 800 mL daily and recheck her serum sodium in six hours time
Give a bolus of hypertonic 3 per cent saline and reassess her symptoms and sodium afterwards
Infuse two litres of 0.9 per cent sodium chloride over four hours and monitor her urine output
Administer intravenous mannitol to reduce cerebral oedema and arrange urgent computed tomography
Commence dantrolene and active cooling for presumed serotonergic hyperthermia from the tablets

subtopic_detail: Third relapse of psychotic depression within months of two successful acute electroconvulsive therapy courses
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 68-year-old woman in the outpatient clinic. Over eighteen months she has had two episodes of severe depression with nihilistic delusions, each of which responded fully to a course of electroconvulsive therapy after failing to improve on medication.

After the second course she was maintained on venlafaxine at a therapeutic dose with lithium augmentation, and a dispensing record confirms she has collected every prescription. Her lithium level a fortnight ago was 0.72 mmol/L and her thyroid function and renal function are normal. Over the past three weeks she has again stopped eating, is sleeping two hours a night and has begun saying her bowels have rotted away. She scores 26 on a depression rating scale. Her cognition between episodes has returned to her baseline and she lives independently with her husband.

data_table.Examination: Psychomotor retardation, poor oral intake, nihilistic delusions concerning her abdomen, no thoughts of self-harm elicited but limited engagement
data_table.Investigations: Lithium 0.72 mmol/L (0.6-0.8 maintenance), thyroid stimulating hormone 2.1 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), estimated glomerular filtration rate greater than 60 mL/min/1.73m2, full blood examination and electrolytes normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate long term treatment plan once this episode is treated?

options.text: Switch her antidepressant to a tricyclic agent and continue outpatient review every four weeks
Increase the lithium dose to achieve a level at the upper end of the therapeutic range for her
Arrange maintenance electroconvulsive therapy at spaced intervals alongside her current medication
Refer her for cognitive behavioural therapy delivered weekly as the mainstay of relapse prevention
Add a second generation antipsychotic and reduce the frequency of her clinic reviews accordingly

subtopic_detail: Rapid weight gain fourteen weeks into olanzapine treatment that has finally controlled a first episode psychosis
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 24-year-old man in the early psychosis clinic. His first episode involved persecutory delusions and command hallucinations that persisted through an adequate trial of risperidone, stopped for intolerable akathisia, and then aripiprazole, stopped for lack of benefit.

He has been on olanzapine 15 mg at night for fourteen weeks and is now free of hallucinations, back at his apprenticeship and keen to stay on the medication that finally worked. His weight has risen from 74 to 83 kg over that period and his waist circumference is 104 cm. He eats takeaway most nights and has stopped playing football. He is not diabetic and has no family history of diabetes. His fasting glucose is 5.9 mmol/L, triglycerides 2.6 mmol/L and high density lipoprotein cholesterol 0.85 mmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 82 per minute, blood pressure 132/84 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Weight 83 kg, waist circumference 104 cm, fasting glucose 5.9 mmol/L (3.0-5.4), glycated haemoglobin 5.6 per cent (less than 6.0), triglycerides 2.6 mmol/L (less than 1.7), high density lipoprotein cholesterol 0.85 mmol/L (greater than 1.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of his metabolic changes?

options.text: Switch him to a different antipsychotic with a lower metabolic burden and taper the olanzapine
Halve the olanzapine dose so that the metabolic effect falls while some antipsychotic cover remains
Continue the olanzapine, add metformin and refer him to a structured diet and exercise program
Give dietary advice at each review and repeat his metabolic screen again in twelve months' time
Add topiramate as a weight loss agent and monitor his cognition and renal function during treatment

subtopic_detail: Starting medication in a newly diagnosed adult who drives a heavy vehicle for a living
stem:
You are the psychiatrist seeing a 29-year-old woman whose assessment, including collateral from her mother and school reports, has confirmed attention deficit hyperactivity disorder with childhood onset. She has never been treated.

She drives a rigid truck for a delivery company and has had two at fault low speed collisions in the past year, both while distracted. She smoked cannabis most weekends until two years ago and has not used it since. She has no chest pain, no exertional syncope and no palpitations, and there is no family history of sudden cardiac death or cardiomyopathy. Her mood is stable and she is not pregnant and uses an implant for contraception. Her physical examination including cardiovascular examination is normal and her thyroid function is normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 76 per minute, blood pressure 138/86 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Normal cardiovascular examination with no murmur, weight 68 kg, height 166 cm
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone 1.6 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), full blood examination and electrolytes within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment plan?

options.text: Order an electrocardiogram and echocardiogram before any medication because of her occupational driving
Prescribe atomoxetine as first line because her history of cannabis use makes a stimulant unsuitable
Offer structured psychological therapy alone and reserve any medication for a later review point
Record baseline pulse, blood pressure and weight, then start a long-acting stimulant with review in four weeks
Begin an immediate release dexamfetamine preparation dosed three times daily to allow flexible timing

subtopic_detail: Dizziness and sensory disturbance four days after abruptly stopping a serotonin noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 34-year-old woman who stopped taking venlafaxine 150 mg four days ago. She had been well for nine months after a single depressive episode and decided to stop when her repeat prescription ran out while she was away.

Since the second day she has felt light headed whenever she turns her head, has had brief sensations she describes as a zap through her scalp when she moves her eyes, and has felt nauseated and unusually irritable. Her sleep is broken by vivid dreams. She still enjoys her hobbies, has been at work every day, denies any low mood or loss of interest, and her appetite and concentration are unchanged. There are no thoughts of self-harm. Her neurological examination is normal and her blood pressure shows no postural drop.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 78 per minute, sitting blood pressure 118/74 mmHg with no postural drop, respiratory rate 14 per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Normal cranial nerve, cerebellar and gait examination, no nystagmus, mood reactive with normal range of affect

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Diagnose an early relapse and increase her venlafaxine above the dose she was previously taking
Prescribe a short course of a benzodiazepine to cover the symptoms until they settle by themselves
Switch her to fluoxetine and then stop that agent after a fortnight without any further tapering
Reassure her the symptoms will fade within a week and review her again if they have not resolved
Restart venlafaxine at her previous dose and reduce it gradually over several weeks with review

subtopic_detail: Sodium valproate maintenance in a woman of reproductive age who is not using reliable contraception
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar conducting an annual review of a 26-year-old woman with bipolar affective disorder. She has had two manic episodes, the last three years ago, and has been well on sodium valproate 1000 mg daily since then.

She works full time, has a new partner of six months, and says she is not trying to conceive but is using condoms inconsistently and would continue a pregnancy if one occurred. She has never been counselled about the medication and pregnancy. Her mother took the same drug for epilepsy without problems, which she mentions as reassurance. Her mood is euthymic, she has no psychotic symptoms and her sleep is regular. Her weight is stable, her full blood examination and liver function are normal, and her serum valproate concentration is within the usual maintenance range.

data_table.Examination: Euthymic, no psychomotor change, no psychotic features, weight stable at 64 kg
data_table.Investigations: Full blood examination normal, liver function normal, serum valproate within the maintenance range, beta human chorionic gonadotropin negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Counsel her on the fetal risks, arrange reliable contraception and plan a switch to another mood stabiliser
Continue the valproate unchanged and add high dose folic acid to reduce the risk to a future pregnancy
Continue the current dose and repeat her serum concentration and liver function every six months
Cease the valproate at today's visit and review her in the clinic in four weeks to assess her mood
Change her directly to lithium at a standard starting dose and defer discussion of pregnancy planning

subtopic_detail: Tachycardia with a rising troponin during the third week of a clozapine titration
stem: A 27-year-old man on day nineteen of a clozapine titration, now 250 mg daily, has three days of fatigue and breathlessness on the ward stairs with a tachycardia that does not settle.

data_table.Investigations: Eosinophils 0.9 x10^9/L (0.0-0.5), C reactive protein 96 mg/L, was 4, troponin I 180 ng/L (<16)
data_table.Imaging: Chest radiograph clear, ejection fraction 48 per cent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Continue clozapine and add a beta blocker
Cease clozapine and refer urgently to cardiology
Halve the clozapine dose and repeat the troponin
Attribute this to benign titration tachycardia
Start antibiotics for presumed pneumonia

subtopic_detail: Confusion and coarse tremor in a long term lithium user whose serum level is within the therapeutic range
stem:
You are the medical registrar assessing a 72-year-old woman brought in by her son. She has taken lithium for twenty years for bipolar affective disorder and has never had a manic relapse.

For three days she has been unsteady, has slurred her words and has been muddled about the day of the week, and this morning she could not manage her own kitchen. She had four days of vomiting and diarrhoea last week after a family gathering and has been drinking little. Her general practitioner started perindopril for hypertension five weeks ago. On examination she has a coarse irregular tremor of both hands, myoclonic jerks in her legs, and an unsteady wide gait. There is no fever, no rigidity, no clonus and no rash, and her neck is supple.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 92 per minute, blood pressure 108/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 per minute, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Serum lithium 0.94 mmol/L (0.6-0.8 maintenance), creatinine 132 micromol/L (45-90, baseline 78), sodium 133 mmol/L (135-145), estimated glomerular filtration rate 38 mL/min/1.73m2, thyroid stimulating hormone 3.2 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), creatine kinase 140 U/L (less than 200)
data_table.Examination: Coarse irregular tremor, leg myoclonus, wide based ataxic gait, no rigidity or clonus, no neck stiffness

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Continue lithium at the usual dose because the serum concentration is not in the toxic range
Prescribe benzatropine for the tremor and arrange outpatient review of her lithium level next week
Withhold lithium, rehydrate with intravenous sodium chloride and monitor levels and renal function
Arrange immediate haemodialysis on the basis of her neurological signs and impaired renal function
Treat her for neuroleptic malignant syndrome with dantrolene and supportive cooling measures

subtopic_detail: Frequent prolonged attacks with normal video telemetry captured during a typical event
stem:
You are the neuropsychiatry registrar reviewing a 26-year-old woman referred after four admissions this year. She has three to five attacks a week in which she falls, shakes and is unresponsive for eight to twelve minutes.

During a typical attack captured on video telemetry this week, her eyes were tightly closed with resistance to opening, her head moved from side to side, the shaking waxed and waned in amplitude, and she was talking within thirty seconds of it stopping. The electroencephalogram showed normal awake rhythms throughout the event and afterwards. A venous lactate taken fifteen minutes after the attack was normal. She has taken levetiracetam and lamotrigine at therapeutic doses without any change in frequency. She discloses a history of childhood sexual abuse and has never been offered psychological treatment.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 84 per minute, blood pressure 116/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Video electroencephalogram during a typical event shows normal awake rhythms with no ictal correlate, venous lactate 1.2 mmol/L (0.5-2.2) at 15 minutes post event, magnetic resonance imaging of brain normal, levetiracetam and lamotrigine within therapeutic ranges

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Add a third antiepileptic drug and titrate it to the maximum tolerated dose over eight weeks
Instruct the emergency department to give intravenous levetiracetam whenever an attack lasts over five minutes
Repeat ambulatory electroencephalography over a week before accepting the telemetry findings as valid
Explain the diagnosis to her carefully and refer for psychological therapy while withdrawing the antiepileptics
Refer her to an epilepsy surgery program for evaluation of a possible frontal lobe seizure focus

subtopic_detail: Detailed recurrent visual hallucinations with fluctuating attention and mild parkinsonism in an older man
stem: A 76-year-old man has twelve months of forgetfulness. His daughter describes days when he converses normally and days when he stares blankly for hours. Several times a week he sees small children in the lounge room and describes their clothing. For years he has shouted and thrashed during sleep.

data_table.Examination: Mild bradykinesia and rigidity, no tremor; mini mental state examination 23 of 30

lead_in: How should his hallucinations be managed?

options.text: Prescribe regular haloperidol at a low dose
Start low dose risperidone titrated to effect
Commence olanzapine at night for sleep too
Use quetiapine as the safest antipsychotic here
Modify the home environment and start rivastigmine

subtopic_detail: Agitation and racing thoughts emerging five weeks after an antidepressant was added for bipolar depression
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar seeing a 31-year-old woman with bipolar II disorder, diagnosed after two clear hypomanic episodes and multiple depressive episodes. Her general practitioner started sertraline five weeks ago for a depressive episode and increased it a fortnight ago. She takes no mood stabiliser.

She says her mood is as low as ever and she cries daily, but she now cannot sit still, her thoughts race so fast she cannot hold a conversation, and she has slept three hours a night for a week without feeling tired. She is irritable with her family and has spent two evenings cleaning the house until dawn. She denies grandiosity, has no psychotic symptoms and has no thoughts of self-harm. She uses no alcohol or other drugs, and her thyroid function and full blood examination are normal.

data_table.Examination: Restless with psychomotor agitation, pressured speech at times, mood described as low with an irritable and reactive affect, no psychotic features, insight retained
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone 1.9 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), full blood examination and electrolytes within normal limits, urine drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her treatment?

options.text: Cease the sertraline and start quetiapine, with close review of her mood and sleep
Increase the sertraline dose further because her depressive symptoms have not yet responded
Add lamotrigine and continue the sertraline while the lamotrigine is slowly titrated upwards
Add lithium at a standard dose while maintaining her current antidepressant treatment unchanged
Prescribe a hypnotic for her insomnia and reassess her symptoms in the clinic in four weeks

subtopic_detail: Four months of memory complaints with prominent distress and early morning waking after a bereavement
stem:
You are the geriatrician assessing a 72-year-old retired accountant referred with memory loss. His wife died five months ago and his daughter dates the change to the weeks that followed.

He reports his memory in detail and with obvious distress, saying he is a burden and that his mind has gone. During cognitive testing he answers do not know to most questions without attempting them, yet later recalls the name of the ward clerk and the route he took to the clinic. He wakes at four each morning and has lost 6 kg without dieting. He has stopped attending bowls and no longer reads. His gait, tone and reflexes are normal, there are no hallucinations, and his mini mental state examination is 25 out of 30 with variable effort across items.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 68 per minute, blood pressure 134/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Psychomotor retardation, restricted affect, no focal neurological signs, normal gait and tone
data_table.Investigations: Full blood examination, electrolytes, calcium, thyroid function, vitamin B12 and folate within normal limits, magnetic resonance imaging of brain shows mild generalised atrophy appropriate for age with no hippocampal predominance

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start donepezil now and repeat cognitive testing again in six months to assess his trajectory
Treat the depressive episode and repeat formal cognitive assessment once his mood has responded
Refer him for fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography to define the pattern of hypometabolism
Attribute his presentation to normal grief and arrange bereavement counselling with review in three months
Commence a low dose antipsychotic to address his belief that he is a burden on his family

subtopic_detail: Involuntary lip and tongue movements emerging in the fourth year of antipsychotic treatment in a woman also taking an anticholinergic
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 62-year-old woman with schizophrenia in a community clinic. She has taken risperidone 4 mg daily for four years, and benzatropine 2 mg daily was added in the first month for stiffness and a tremor which settled and has not returned.

Her daughter has noticed over the past four months that her mother is constantly chewing on nothing and that her tongue pushes against the inside of her cheek. On examination there are repetitive lip smacking and tongue rolling movements with occasional finger movements, which stop briefly when you ask her to open her mouth and hold still and which her daughter says are absent while she is asleep. She has no rigidity, her arm swing is symmetrical, and she sits comfortably without shifting or pacing. Her psychotic symptoms have been in remission for three years and she is distressed that people stare at her at the shops.

data_table.Examination: Repetitive lip smacking and tongue rolling with choreiform finger movements, briefly suppressible on request, no cogwheel rigidity, symmetrical arm swing, no truncal restlessness
data_table.Medications: Risperidone 4 mg orally daily for four years, benzatropine 2 mg orally daily for four years
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, urea electrolytes and creatinine, liver function tests, thyroid function and calcium all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Increase the benzatropine dose to control the abnormal facial movements
Add propranolol 10 mg three times daily and review her again in two weeks
Increase the risperidone dose to suppress the movements more completely
Order a brain MRI and refer to neurology before changing any medication
Cease the benzatropine and arrange review of her antipsychotic regimen

subtopic_detail: Two years of escalating rule breaking and aggression in a fourteen year old who describes it flatly and shows no remorse
stem: A 14-year-old boy is referred after a second school suspension. Over two years he has had repeated fights, twice forced entry into a neighbour's shed, stayed out overnight, and last month deliberately injured a neighbour's cat. He describes this flatly and shows no remorse. No abuse or neglect is identified.

data_table.Examination: Flat, unconcerned affect; mood, sleep and appetite normal
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen negative; cognitive testing in the average range

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Start risperidone to reduce his aggression
Refer the family for a structured parenting program
Refer him for weekly insight oriented psychotherapy
Start fluoxetine and review in four weeks
Refer him to a residential wilderness program

subtopic_detail: Repeated hair pulling with visible scalp loss in a woman who describes tension before and relief afterwards, without any intrusive thought
stem: A 23-year-old student has pulled hair from her scalp since she was fifteen. She pulls in the evening while watching television, with a build up of tension that eases as each hair comes out. She denies any intrusive thought or fear preceding it. She has tried repeatedly to stop and now avoids swimming.

data_table.Examination: Broken hairs of varying lengths within the patch, no scaling or scarring

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Start fluoxetine and titrate over six weeks
Refer for a scalp biopsy before any treatment
Advise her to keep her hands busy instead
Refer for habit reversal training with a therapist
Start low dose risperidone for the behaviour

subtopic_detail: Constant pacing ten days into antipsychotic treatment in a young man whose psychotic symptoms are simultaneously improving
stem: A 24-year-old man admitted ten days ago with first episode psychosis had aripiprazole increased from 10 to 20 mg four days ago. Since yesterday he paces continuously and cannot sit for meals, with restlessness in his legs eased only by walking. His psychotic symptoms have improved.

data_table.Examination: Normal tone, temperature 36.9 degrees C, creatine kinase 118 U/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reduce the aripiprazole and add propranolol 10 mg three times daily
Add benzatropine 1 mg twice daily for the extrapyramidal effect
Increase the aripiprazole, as this is psychotic agitation
Add diazepam 5 mg twice daily and change nothing else
Cease the aripiprazole and give intramuscular haloperidol

subtopic_detail: Amenorrhoea and milk discharge in the second year of antipsychotic treatment with a prolactin level in the range that overlaps drug effect and tumour
stem: A 27-year-old woman has taken risperidone 3 mg daily for fourteen months after a single episode of psychosis. Her periods stopped eight months ago and for three months she has had bilateral milky nipple discharge.

data_table.Examination: Bilateral milky discharge; normal visual fields; no headache
data_table.Investigations: Prolactin 1780 and 1850 mIU/L on two mornings (less than 500); pregnancy test negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Add cabergoline 0.5 mg weekly and continue risperidone
Order an MRI of the pituitary before any change
Switch her to aripiprazole and repeat the prolactin
Add a combined oral contraceptive pill to restore periods
Stop all antipsychotic treatment and monitor the prolactin

subtopic_detail: Accumulated possessions blocking a woman's home after a fire safety inspection, without any rituals or intrusive thoughts
stem: A 58-year-old woman is referred after a fire safety inspection found only a narrow path through her house. Newspapers and clothing fill her kitchen, bath and bedroom; she has slept in a chair for two years. Discarding feels like losing part of herself. She reports no intrusive thoughts and no rituals.

data_table.Mental state: Montreal Cognitive Assessment 28 out of 30, no delusions

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Arrange a professional house clear out with the council
Start high-dose fluvoxamine as the primary treatment now
Start risperidone for her beliefs about the possessions
Apply to the guardianship tribunal for a welfare order
Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy for discarding and acquiring

subtopic_detail: A student referred with presumed depression whose knees buckle when he laughs and whose mood is fully reactive
stem: A 22-year-old student referred with presumed depression has been overwhelmingly sleepy for eighteen months and falls asleep in lectures. His naps are short and refreshing. Laughing hard makes his knees give way and his jaw go slack for half a minute while he stays fully aware.

data_table.Sleep history: Eight hours undisturbed sleep, no snoring
data_table.Investigations: Patient Health Questionnaire 9 score 5 of 27

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start sertraline 50 mg daily and review in four weeks
Start modafinil 200 mg each morning for his sleepiness
Arrange home oximetry for obstructive sleep apnoea
Advise a regular sleep schedule and review later
Refer for polysomnography and a multiple sleep latency test

subtopic_detail: Seven months of early morning waking in a woman whose sleep diary shows nine and a half hours in bed for five and a half hours of sleep
stem: A 47-year-old accountant has had seven months of waking at three each morning and lying awake for ninety minutes or more. She is tired and irritable by day but does not doze off. Temazepam helped three months ago and she asks for more.

data_table.Sleep diary: Average 9.5 hours in bed for 5.5 hours of sleep
data_table.Investigations: Patient Health Questionnaire 9 score 4, no snoring

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Prescribe temazepam 10 mg nightly for three months
Start quetiapine 25 mg nightly for its sedating effect
Start mirtazapine 15 mg nightly and review in a month
Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia
Advise sleep hygiene measures alone and review later

subtopic_detail: Repeated admissions for events witnessed only by one parent across three hospitals, with every investigation normal
stem: A four-year-old boy has had eleven admissions across three hospitals for reported episodes of stopping breathing and shaking. Despite a gastrostomy inserted elsewhere for feeding difficulty, he is on the 50th centile and eats well on the ward. Every reported episode has occurred while his mother, a former enrolled nurse, was alone with him.

data_table.Investigations: Five days of video electroencephalogram captured no event, other investigations normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Discuss your concerns with the mother today
Arrange covert video surveillance of the cubicle
Notify the state child protection service today
Refer the mother for psychiatric assessment
Arrange a further video electroencephalogram
