subtopic_detail: Fourteen months of preoccupation with a neurological diagnosis despite three normal specialist reviews, with almost no bodily symptoms
stem: A 39-year-old accountant has been convinced for fourteen months he has motor neurone disease. He checks his tongue for twitching daily and reads patient forums for two hours nightly. Three neurology reviews, MRI of brain and spine, nerve conduction studies and electromyography were normal; each result settles him for two days.

data_table.Examination: Normal neurological examination, no fasciculation
data_table.Investigations: Patient Health Questionnaire 9 score 6

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Repeat the MRI of his brain and cervical spine
Arrange a fourth neurology opinion at another hospital
Start diazepam as required when the worry peaks
Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy and scheduled review
Advise him to stop searching online, review as needed

subtopic_detail: A doctor consulting you as her own general practitioner who describes starting operating lists still affected by the previous night's drinking
stem: A 44-year-old anaesthetist, your patient for two years, asks for a repeat oxycodone prescription. Prescription monitoring shows oxycodone from two other practices in six weeks. She drinks most of a bottle of spirits most nights and has twice started her operating list still affected. She asks you to tell no one.

data_table.Investigations: Gamma glutamyl transferase 148 U/L (5-35)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate course of action?

options.text: Maintain confidentiality and treat her alcohol use
Refer to the doctors health advisory service
Tell her head of department and leave it to them
Decline to continue as her doctor and refer on
Make a mandatory notification and keep treating her

subtopic_detail: Reduced libido and delayed ejaculation five months into successful treatment in a man whose earlier dose reduction caused relapse
stem: A 34-year-old man on sertraline 100 mg daily for eight months for a first depressive episode has been well for five months. Since the third week he has had reduced libido and delayed orgasm, with normal erections. Reducing to 50 mg six weeks ago brought relapse within a fortnight; 100 mg was restored.

data_table.Investigations: Testosterone and prolactin normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Stop the sertraline, as depression is in remission
Switch to an antidepressant with fewer sexual side effects
Add sildenafil as required and continue the sertraline
Halve the dose again and review in four weeks
Reassure him it will settle and make no change

subtopic_detail: An intoxicated man on an anticoagulant refusing a scan after a head strike, who cannot recall the risks minutes after they are explained
stem: A 46-year-old man on apixaban struck his head 90 minutes ago and demands to go home. Twice told a delayed bleed could be fatal on his anticoagulant, he could not repeat this back five minutes later.

data_table.Examination: Glasgow Coma Scale 15, disoriented to date, occipital haematoma; breath alcohol 0.21 per cent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate course of action?

options.text: Allow him to leave once he signs a discharge against advice
Complete a mental health certificate under the Mental Health Act 2007
Ask his wife to consent as his substitute decision maker
Keep him for the scan under the common law duty of care
Sedate him with intramuscular droperidol and take him to scan

subtopic_detail: Nineteen months after a spouse's death, daily yearning and identity disruption without pervasive anhedonia
stem: A 58-year-old woman is referred nineteen months after her husband died. She still cannot accept that he is gone and plays his voicemail greeting nightly. She has not entered their bedroom or returned to work, and does not know who she is without him. She still enjoys her grandchildren's visits and eats normally.

data_table.Mental state: Patient Health Questionnaire 9 score 11; no intent, but would not mind not waking

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reassure her this is normal grief and review later
Refer her for grief focused psychotherapy
Start sertraline 50 mg daily as first line
Prescribe temazepam at night for a month
Refer her for supportive bereavement counselling

subtopic_detail: Three years of waxing and waning motor and vocal tics in a boy whose mother is asking for medication after teasing at school
stem: An 11-year-old boy has 3 years of eye blinking, head jerking and shoulder shrugging, and 18 months of throat clearing and sniffing. They wax and wane, worsen with stress, and he can briefly suppress them after a premonitory urge. Teasing has begun and he asks to stay home. His mother wants medication today.

data_table.Examination: Tics observed, neurological examination otherwise normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Refer for behavioural therapy for tics
Start low-dose risperidone and review in a month
Start clonidine at night, titrated to response
Reassure the family and take no action
Refer for botulinum toxin to the affected muscles

subtopic_detail: Responding to hazardous drinking detected on routine screening
stem:
A 41-year-old teacher attends your practice for a routine health check. On screening she reports drinking six standard drinks on most Friday and Saturday nights and two on weeknights, totalling around 22 standard drinks weekly. She has done this for about three years since a promotion.

She has never had a withdrawal tremor, morning drinking, blackouts or a seizure, and has never tried to cut down without success. She has not missed work, driven after drinking or had relationship or legal consequences. She is surprised when you total her weekly intake and says she had assumed it was normal for her friendship group. Examination is unremarkable and liver function tests are within normal limits.

data_table.Investigations: Gamma-glutamyl transferase within normal limits, mean corpuscular volume 89 fL (80-100), full blood count within normal limits; body mass index 25 kg/m2

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Deliver structured brief advice with feedback on her intake and agreed drinking goals
Commence naltrexone to reduce her craving and the reinforcing effects of alcohol
Refer to a specialist drug and alcohol service for comprehensive assessment and treatment
Arrange a supervised inpatient withdrawal admission before any reduction is attempted
Reassure her that normal liver function tests indicate her drinking is not causing harm

subtopic_detail: Persistent distress and avoidance after a traumatic birth
stem:
You review a 32-year-old woman five months after the birth of her first child, which involved a prolonged second stage, emergency caesarean under general anaesthesia and a 2 litre haemorrhage. She describes vivid intrusive images of the operating theatre that arrive without warning, and she wakes sweating from dreams of the birth.

She avoids driving past the hospital and has cancelled two appointments there. She cannot watch television programs involving childbirth and becomes distressed when her mother asks about the delivery. She is bonded with her baby, enjoys caring for him and looks forward to their outings. She denies persistent low mood, anhedonia, guilt or suicidal thoughts, and her Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale score is 8.

data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, ferritin and thyroid function within normal limits; Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale score 8 with a score of zero on the self-harm item

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor as first line treatment for her symptoms
Refer for trauma-focused cognitive behavioural therapy with a perinatal informed clinician
Provide a single structured debriefing session reviewing the events of the birth in detail
Reassure her that these reactions are normal after a difficult birth and review in three months
Commence a short course of a benzodiazepine to reduce her arousal and improve her sleep

subtopic_detail: Escalating stimulant requests and inconsistent prescription histories
stem:
A 23-year-old man is a new patient at your practice requesting a repeat prescription for dexamfetamine, saying he was diagnosed with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder interstate and has run out. He has no documentation and cannot name the prescribing specialist.

He asks specifically for immediate release tablets and says slow release preparations do not work for him. He mentions he needs a higher dose than he was on because it wears off by lunchtime, and that he sometimes takes an extra tablet before nights out. The real time prescription monitoring system shows dispensing from four different prescribers across two states in the past three months. He becomes irritable when you say you cannot prescribe today.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96/min, BP 138/84 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Medications: No documented current prescriptions at this practice; prescription monitoring shows dexamfetamine dispensed by four prescribers across two states in three months

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Provide a small bridging supply of immediate release tablets and request records afterwards
Prescribe a long-acting methylphenidate preparation instead as it carries lower misuse potential
Report him to the police given that the prescription monitoring data indicates likely drug diversion
Decline to prescribe today, explain why, and offer review once records and authority are confirmed
Prescribe atomoxetine today as a non-stimulant alternative while awaiting the interstate records

subtopic_detail: Distinguishing a stress related reaction from a depressive episode after a workplace injury
stem:
A 46-year-old plasterer attends your clinic seven weeks after a shoulder injury that has kept him off work. He describes feeling flat, worrying constantly about money and his compensation claim, and sleeping poorly because he ruminates about whether he will work again.

He says he feels much like his old self when his brother visits or when he watches his daughter play netball, and he still enjoys those things. His appetite is unchanged and his weight is stable. He denies feeling worthless, denies guilt beyond frustration at being unable to provide, and denies suicidal thoughts. He has no prior psychiatric history, drinks two beers most evenings as he did before the injury, and his symptoms began about two weeks after the injury.

data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, thyroid function and vitamin B12 within normal limits; Kessler 10 score 24 indicating moderate distress

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Major depressive disorder of moderate severity requiring antidepressant therapy
Generalised anxiety disorder with worry about finances and his occupational future
Persistent depressive disorder that has been unmasked by the stress of the injury
Somatic symptom disorder with excessive preoccupation with his physical condition
Adjustment disorder with mixed anxiety and depressed mood following an identifiable stressor

subtopic_detail: Mood symptoms in the non-birthing parent during the first postnatal year
stem:
A 35-year-old man attends your practice with his partner and their 4-month-old daughter for the baby's immunisations. While you are completing the consultation he mentions, almost in passing, that he has been struggling since the birth.

On further questioning he describes four months of low mood most days, loss of interest in cycling and seeing friends, waking at 4 am unable to return to sleep, and irritability that has led to arguments with his partner. He has been drinking more than usual and has withdrawn from the baby, saying he feels he is no use to her. He denies suicidal thoughts. His partner was screened for postnatal depression at six weeks and scored in the normal range, and she says she is coping well.

data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, iron studies, thyroid function and HbA1c within normal limits; alcohol intake increased from 6 to 20 standard drinks weekly since the birth

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reassure him that adjusting to a new baby is difficult and review at the six month immunisations
Advise him that treatment services are directed to mothers and refer his partner for screening
Advise reducing his alcohol intake first and reassess his mood in eight weeks if it persists
Assess his risk and symptom severity, then arrange psychological therapy with alcohol advice
Refer him to a parenting support group to build confidence in caring for his daughter

subtopic_detail: Long term hypnotic use identified during a medication review
stem:
A 66-year-old woman attends your practice for a medication review. She has taken zolpidem 10 mg nightly for four years, started after a bereavement, and now says it barely works but she cannot sleep at all without it. She has tried stopping twice and each time had two nights of almost no sleep and restarted.

She has had two falls in the past year, both when getting up to the toilet overnight, and her daughter has noticed she is more forgetful. Her mood is reactive and she denies low mood, anhedonia or suicidal thoughts. She drinks no alcohol. Physical examination, cognitive screening and thyroid function are unremarkable, and she has no symptoms of sleep apnoea or restless legs.

data_table.Medications: Zolpidem 10 mg nightly for four years; atorvastatin; no antidepressant, no opioid and no other sedating medicine

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Substitute temazepam nightly at an equivalent dose to provide more reliable sedation
Advise abrupt cessation tonight and provide a sleep hygiene handout with review in one month
Continue the current dose indefinitely and add a falls prevention referral for her mobility
Negotiate a gradual dose reduction and refer for cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia
Add low dose amitriptyline at night to allow the current hypnotic to be stopped immediately

subtopic_detail: Abdominal symptoms in a patient established on clozapine
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 38-year-old man with treatment resistant schizophrenia who has taken clozapine 450 mg daily for three years with good symptom control. He tells you he has not opened his bowels for nine days and has vomited twice today.

His abdomen is distended and tympanic with sluggish bowel sounds and generalised discomfort but no guarding. He mentions he stopped taking his laxative several months ago because he disliked the taste. He has no fever, no cough and no urinary symptoms. His last full blood count two weeks ago showed a neutrophil count within the normal range, and he has had no missed doses.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 104/min, BP 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 9.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), neutrophils 5.4 x10^9/L (2.0-7.5), C-reactive protein 22 mg/L (less than 5), lactate 1.6 mmol/L (0.5-2.0), potassium 3.6 mmol/L (3.5-5.2)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Withhold clozapine and arrange urgent full blood count to exclude neutropenia
Arrange urgent echocardiography and troponin testing to assess for myocarditis
Prescribe a stimulant laxative and reassess his bowel function in 48 hours on the ward
Prescribe an antiemetic and increase his oral fluid intake with a review the following morning
Arrange urgent abdominal imaging and surgical review for suspected bowel obstruction

subtopic_detail: Acute behavioural and mood change after commencing high dose corticosteroid
stem:
You are the consultation liaison psychiatry registrar asked to review a 54-year-old woman on the respiratory ward. She was admitted six days ago with a severe asthma exacerbation and started on prednisolone 50 mg daily. Over the past three days she has slept only two to three hours nightly, talks rapidly and has been ordering expensive items online.

Nursing staff report she is irritable when interrupted and has been telling other patients she has been chosen to reform the hospital. She has no personal or family history of mood disorder and has never had a similar episode. She takes salbutamol and a preventer inhaler, and is on no antibiotics. She is fully oriented with no fluctuation in attention and no visual hallucinations.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92/min, BP 136/82 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 139 mmol/L (135-145), calcium corrected 2.36 mmol/L (2.15-2.60), thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, C-reactive protein 14 mg/L (less than 5), urine drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence lithium and arrange level monitoring for a first presentation of bipolar disorder
Discuss reducing the corticosteroid dose with the treating team and start an antipsychotic
Cease the corticosteroid abruptly today and observe her mental state over the next 24 hours
Commence an antidepressant given the disturbed sleep and marked change in her behaviour
Treat as hyperactive delirium with regular haloperidol and full delirium precautions

subtopic_detail: Weighing antipsychotic risk against harm in dementia related agitation
stem:
You are the visiting medical officer at a residential aged care facility asked to review an 84-year-old man with moderate Alzheimer disease. Over three weeks he has become increasingly agitated in the late afternoon, calling out and pushing staff away during personal care, and last week he struck a carer.

Staff have tried moving him to a quieter area without benefit. He has been checked for constipation, urinary retention and infection, all of which were absent, and a hearing aid battery was replaced two weeks ago. His pain is difficult to assess but he has severe knee osteoarthritis and is on no regular analgesia. He is not distressed at other times of day, his attention is stable and there is no acute cognitive fluctuation.

data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, calcium, thyroid function and C-reactive protein within normal limits; midstream urine culture shows no growth; no new medicines in the past three months

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence regular risperidone at a low dose with review of benefit at 12 weeks
Commence regular scheduled paracetamol and reassess the behaviour after two weeks
Commence a benzodiazepine at night to reduce his arousal and improve his sleep pattern
Commence a cholinesterase inhibitor to improve cognition and thereby reduce his agitation
Commence an antidepressant given that late day distress may indicate an underlying depression

subtopic_detail: Persistent sleepiness and low mood in a rotating shift worker
stem:
A 29-year-old process operator attends your practice reporting eight months of exhaustion, difficulty concentrating and irritability. He works a rotating roster of four night shifts, then four days off, then four day shifts, and has done so since starting the job.

He says he sleeps only three to four hours after night shifts because of daylight and household noise, and sleeps well for eight hours on his days off, waking refreshed. He enjoys his weekends with friends and denies anhedonia, guilt, hopelessness and suicidal thoughts, and says he feels normal by his third day off. He drinks four cups of coffee during each night shift. He does not snore and his partner has noticed no pauses in his breathing.

data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, iron studies, thyroid function and HbA1c all within normal limits; body mass index 24 kg/m2; sleep diary confirms 3 to 4 hours of daytime sleep on night shift blocks and 8 hours on days off

lead_in: What is the most likely explanation for his symptoms?

options.text: Shift work disorder from misalignment between his roster and his circadian rhythm
Major depressive disorder presenting predominantly with fatigue and poor concentration
Obstructive sleep apnoea causing fragmented sleep and consequent daytime impairment
Chronic insomnia disorder maintained by conditioned arousal and poor sleep habits
Caffeine use disorder producing rebound fatigue and irritability between shift blocks

subtopic_detail: New low mood in the menopausal transition with vasomotor symptoms
stem:
A 49-year-old woman attends your clinic with five months of low mood, poor concentration and loss of interest in activities she previously enjoyed. Her periods have become irregular over the past year, with two gaps of more than 60 days.

She has 10 to 12 hot flushes daily and wakes drenched most nights, which she says is the worst part. She has never had a depressive episode before and has no history of postnatal depression or premenstrual mood change. She denies suicidal thoughts, has no alcohol or drug use, and thyroid function and full blood count are within normal limits. She has no personal or family history of breast cancer, no migraine with aura and no history of venous thromboembolism.

data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, full blood count within normal limits, ferritin 68 micrograms/L (30-300), HbA1c within normal limits; body mass index 26 kg/m2

lead_in: What would you first recommend?

options.text: Commence a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor as first line treatment for the mood symptoms
Measure follicle stimulating hormone and oestradiol to confirm the menopausal transition first
Commence menopausal hormone therapy and review both mood and vasomotor symptoms at six weeks
Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy alone and review her mood symptoms in eight weeks
Recommend a phytoestrogen supplement and lifestyle modification with review in three months

subtopic_detail: recurrent hair pulling with visible patchy loss and mounting tension before pulling in an adolescent
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 15-year-old girl brought by her mother after the school nurse noticed patchy hair loss. The girl acknowledges, once her mother steps out, that she pulls hair from her scalp while doing homework and watching television.

She describes a build-up of tension before pulling and relief afterwards, followed by shame. She has tried to stop several times and has not managed more than a few days. She does not swallow the hair and has no abdominal pain. On examination there are irregular patches of thinned hair over the right frontoparietal scalp with hairs of varying lengths and no scaling, no scarring, no erythema and no broken hairs elsewhere. She denies low mood, has friends, is doing well academically, and there is no self-harm, no restrictive eating and no substance use. Thyroid function and iron studies requested by the nurse are within normal limits.

data_table.Examination: Irregular patches of thinned scalp hair with hairs of varying length, no scaling, scarring or erythema, eyebrows and eyelashes intact
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid function and iron studies within normal limits
data_table.Mental state: Euthymic, engaged, no suicidal ideation, no restrictive eating, no substance use

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment?

options.text: Start N-acetylcysteine at a standard adult dose and review the pulling in twelve weeks
Begin self monitoring of pulling episodes and refer for habit reversal training now
Start fluoxetine 20 mg daily and review the response after six weeks of treatment
Prescribe topical minoxidil solution to the affected scalp and review the regrowth in three months
Arrange a scalp biopsy to distinguish scarring from non-scarring causes of the hair loss

subtopic_detail: deliberate under-dosing of insulin for weight control with recurrent ketoacidosis and normal body weight
stem: A 19-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes since age nine is admitted with her fourth episode of diabetic ketoacidosis in eight months. She skips her long-acting insulin because she gains weight when her glucose is controlled, and checks her body repeatedly in the mirror.

data_table.Investigations: Glycated haemoglobin 11.8 per cent, risen from 7.4
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 21.5 kg/m2, weight stable

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Refer for joint eating disorder and diabetes care
Increase her long-acting insulin with clinic review
Start sertraline and review her mood in four weeks
Apply mental health legislation for involuntary care
Discharge with diabetes educator follow up and a sick day plan

subtopic_detail: request to assess whether a man with early dementia can validly instruct a solicitor to change his will
stem: A solicitor asks whether a 79-year-old man with mild Alzheimer disease can change his will to favour the daughter who cares for him. He knows what a will does, names his three children and his approximate assets, gives a coherent reason, and accepts the others may be upset. No coercion is evident.

data_table.Cognition: Mini-Mental State Examination 23 out of 30 six months ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate response to the solicitor?

options.text: Advise that dementia itself invalidates his will
Report that he shows the abilities required
Recommend that his caring daughter decide instead
Suggest repeat cognitive testing before any opinion
Decline because capacity is for the courts alone

subtopic_detail: intense dread of giving birth in a first pregnancy with avoidance of antenatal care and no prior birth trauma
stem:
You are the psychiatrist in a perinatal clinic. A 28-year-old woman at 22 weeks in her first pregnancy is referred by her midwife because she has missed three appointments and becomes distressed whenever labour is mentioned.

She describes intrusive images of dying in childbirth, nightmares about being torn, and panic with palpitations and sweating when she passes the birth suite. She has been avoiding antenatal classes and the hospital tour, and says she has considered not attending for the birth at all. She wanted this pregnancy and is looking forward to the baby. She has no history of sexual assault, no previous birth, no previous trauma and no history of depression or an anxiety disorder, and she is not misusing substances. Her Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale score is 11 with a zero response on the self-harm item, and she sleeps poorly only on nights when she has been thinking about labour.

data_table.Symptoms: Intrusive images of dying in childbirth, nightmares, panic on approaching the birth suite, avoidance of classes and appointments
data_table.Screening: Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale 11 with zero on the self-harm item
data_table.History: First pregnancy, no prior trauma or assault, no previous psychiatric history, wanted pregnancy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Prescribe diazepam to be taken before antenatal visits and again during early labour
Advise that she request a planned caesarean section so that labour can be avoided altogether
Offer structured psychological therapy for childbirth fear with a birth planning session
Start sertraline given the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale score and review in six weeks
Reassure her that anxiety about a first birth is normal and arrange midwife review at 34 weeks

subtopic_detail: vivid formed visual hallucinations with full insight in an older adult with advanced macular degeneration
stem:
You are the doctor at a residential aged care facility. Staff ask you to review an 84-year-old woman who has been describing children in period costume standing at the end of her bed and patterned brickwork spreading across the wall.

She tells you calmly that she knows they are not really there, that they appear most in the late afternoon and last several minutes, and that she finds them curious rather than frightening. She has advanced age related macular degeneration with vision of 6/60 in both eyes after a recent further decline. She hears nothing unusual, has no delusions and no persecutory ideas, and she is oriented to place and person and gives a clear account of her day. There is no fluctuating attention, no tremor, no rigidity, no falls, no recent change in medication and no urinary symptoms, and her observations and screening bloods are unremarkable.

data_table.Examination: No tremor or rigidity, no postural instability, attention sustained through the interview, oriented to place and person
data_table.Vision: Visual acuity 6/60 bilaterally with advanced age related macular degeneration and recent further decline
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, renal function, calcium, thyroid function and urinalysis all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start risperidone 0.25 mg at night and review the frequency of the hallucinations in two weeks
Arrange a computed tomography scan of the brain to exclude an occipital infarct or tumour
Treat for delirium with a septic screen, medication review and regular orientation by staff
Explain the visual origin of the images, review her vision, and monitor with staff education
Commence a cholinesterase inhibitor for probable dementia with Lewy bodies and monitor closely

subtopic_detail: depressive episodes recurring each winter with hypersomnia and carbohydrate craving that remit fully in spring
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 34-year-old woman who moved from Darwin to Hobart four years ago. Each year since, from late May, she has become flat, sleeps 10 to 11 hours and still feels unrefreshed, craves bread and sweet foods, gains about 5 kg, and withdraws from her netball team.

By early October she is back to her usual self, energetic and social, with the weight coming off without effort, and she stays well right through summer. This has now happened four winters in a row and has never happened at any other time of year. She works indoors in an office with no window. She denies elevated mood, reduced need for sleep or overspending at any time, and there is no alcohol or other substance misuse. Her thyroid function, full blood count, iron studies and vitamin D are all within normal limits, and she is currently five weeks into this year's episode with no suicidal ideation.

data_table.Symptom pattern: Four consecutive winters of low mood with hypersomnia, carbohydrate craving and 5 kg weight gain, full remission each spring
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid function, full blood count, iron studies and vitamin D within normal limits
data_table.Mental state: Low mood with reactivity preserved, no suicidal ideation, no history of elevated mood

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment for this episode?

options.text: Start lithium as a mood stabiliser given the regular recurrence of her mood episodes
Prescribe high dose oral vitamin D through winter and review her mood in eight weeks
Begin bright light therapy each morning with structured behavioural activation alongside it
Refer for electroconvulsive therapy because the episodes have recurred for four consecutive years
Advise watchful waiting until October, since her episodes have always resolved spontaneously

subtopic_detail: patient request for a psychedelic assisted treatment after reading about its regulatory approval
stem:
You are the psychiatrist seeing a 46-year-old man with a 14 month depressive episode. He asks to be started on psilocybin assisted therapy, having read that it is now legally available in Australia for treatment resistant depression, and says he does not want to try another tablet.

His current episode has been treated with sertraline titrated to 200 mg daily for 10 weeks with partial response, then a switch to venlafaxine 225 mg daily for 9 weeks with no further improvement. He has had 12 sessions of cognitive behavioural therapy. He has never had psychosis or mania, has no family history of bipolar disorder, drinks two standard drinks a week, and takes no other medication. He remains able to work part time and denies suicidal ideation. He asks you directly whether you can prescribe it for him at this appointment or whether he should buy it privately from an overseas supplier.

data_table.Treatment history: Sertraline 200 mg daily for 10 weeks with partial response, venlafaxine 225 mg daily for 9 weeks with no improvement, 12 sessions of cognitive behavioural therapy
data_table.Risk: No suicidal ideation, no psychosis or mania, no family history of bipolar disorder
data_table.Substance use: Two standard drinks per week, no other substances

lead_in: What is the most appropriate response to his request?

options.text: Prescribe psilocybin yourself today, since it is now approved for this indication in Australia
Tell him that the treatment is unavailable in Australia and that overseas purchase is his only route
Agree to supervise a session if he obtains the substance himself and brings it to the clinic
Explain the authorised prescriber pathway and offer an evidence-based next step meanwhile
Decline the discussion and restate that only a third antidepressant trial is acceptable now

subtopic_detail: loss of control over online gaming with withdrawal from school and sport over twelve months
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 15-year-old boy brought by his father, who is worried about the amount of time he spends gaming. Over the past 12 months his gaming has risen to eight or nine hours daily, mostly between 7 pm and 3 am.

He has quit the soccer team, stopped seeing friends in person, and his school attendance has fallen to about half the timetable, with grades dropping from mostly B to mostly D. He becomes verbally aggressive when the internet is switched off and has repeatedly promised to cut down and failed within days. He denies low mood when he is gaming but says everything else feels pointless, and he has no suicidal ideation on direct questioning. He eats irregularly, has lost 3 kg, is not using alcohol or other substances, and there is no history of trauma or bullying that either he or his father can identify.

data_table.Pattern: Eight to nine hours daily gaming mostly overnight for twelve months, repeated failed attempts to reduce, irritability when access is removed
data_table.Function: School attendance halved with falling grades, sport and in-person friendships abandoned, 3 kg weight loss
data_table.Mental state: No suicidal ideation, no substance use, denies low mood while gaming

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Assess for depression and other comorbidity, then refer for family based psychological therapy
Advise the father to remove the console and the router permanently from the house tonight
Start an antidepressant now, since withdrawal from activities indicates a depressive episode
Reassure the father that heavy gaming is normal at this age and recommend a screen time contract
Refer him to a residential drug and alcohol rehabilitation program for behavioural addiction

subtopic_detail: belief that a spouse has been replaced by an identical impostor in a man with fluctuating cognition
stem: A 76-year-old man has insisted for three months that his wife is an identical looking substitute, twice asking her to leave at night. His attention fluctuates from day to day, he has seen small animals for over a year, and he acts out dreams. He is slower and stooped with a mild left resting tremor.

data_table.Investigations: Screening bloods normal, no anticholinergic medication

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of the misidentification?

options.text: Start haloperidol 0.5 mg nightly for the belief
Admit urgently for a delirium screen and fluids
Advise his wife to show him wedding photographs
Begin a cholinesterase inhibitor with a carer safety plan
Commence levodopa for the parkinsonian features

subtopic_detail: colleague smelling of alcohol before a ward round after repeated concerns raised by nursing staff
stem: Your consultant smells strongly of alcohol before the morning ward round, has a tremor and slurs words. He is due to lead a round on 18 inpatients, three detained with leave pending. No other consultant is on the ward.

data_table.Corroboration: Two nurses report the same twice last week
data_table.Response to approach: Denies drinking, irritable, declines to step back

lead_in: What should you do?

options.text: Say nothing now and raise it privately after the round
Escalate to the on call senior to cover the round, then notify
Ask the nurses to document and file an incident report
Lead the round yourself and keep it between you
Arrange a blood alcohol level and act on the result

subtopic_detail: early script requests and a negative urine screen in a young adult prescribed stimulant medication
stem:
You are the psychiatrist reviewing a 23-year-old man diagnosed with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder 18 months ago and prescribed dexamfetamine. He has requested early replacement scripts three times in five months, citing a lost bottle, a spilled bottle and a bag stolen at a music festival.

He reports that the medication works well and that he has no side effects. His flatmate telephoned the clinic last month to ask whether the tablets could be bought. A urine drug screen collected at the last visit, two days after he said he had taken his morning dose, detected no amphetamine. His weight is stable, his blood pressure is normal, and he is in his third year of an engineering degree with passing grades. He appears well, is not agitated, and there are no signs of intoxication or withdrawal, no injection marks and no reported alcohol or other substance use.

data_table.Prescribing history: Three early replacement script requests in five months with differing explanations
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen negative for amphetamine two days after a reported dose, weight stable
data_table.Collateral: Flatmate telephoned the clinic asking whether the tablets could be purchased

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Issue the replacement script and arrange a pharmacy owed-medication record for future losses
Report him to police for suspected supply and cease all prescribing without further discussion
Double the dose, on the basis that the negative screen indicates inadequate absorption of the drug
Check the real time prescription monitoring system, discuss the findings openly, and revise the plan
Switch immediately to atomoxetine without discussing the screen result or the script requests

subtopic_detail: severe irritability and despair confined to the week before menstruation with complete resolution by day three
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 33-year-old woman who describes becoming, in her words, a different person for about six days before each period. She is irritable to the point of shouting at her children, feels hopeless, cannot concentrate at work, and has cancelled social plans repeatedly.

By the third day of bleeding she feels entirely well again and stays well for the rest of the month. She has kept a daily symptom chart for three consecutive cycles at her previous doctor's suggestion, and it shows the symptoms confined to the luteal phase with symptom-free scores from day three through to day 18 in every cycle. Her thyroid function and full blood count are normal. She has never had a depressive episode outside this pattern, drinks alcohol rarely, does not use contraception and does not plan a pregnancy this year, and there is no suicidal ideation now or during the symptomatic phase.

data_table.Symptom chart: Three consecutive cycles charted with symptoms confined to the six days before menstruation and complete resolution by day three of bleeding
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid function and full blood count within normal limits
data_table.History: No depressive episodes outside the luteal phase, no suicidal ideation, no pregnancy planned this year

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment?

options.text: Prescribe calcium and vitamin B6 supplementation and review the charts after three cycles
Refer for a gonadotropin releasing hormone agonist with added back hormonal therapy
Start a serotonergic antidepressant given either continuously or in the luteal phase only
Begin lithium at a low dose, treating this as a rapid cycling presentation of a bipolar disorder
Advise aerobic exercise and sleep hygiene alone, with review only if the symptoms worsen further

subtopic_detail: escalating self directed dose increases of a gabapentinoid with euphoria and early script exhaustion
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 31-year-old man who was prescribed pregabalin 150 mg twice daily for neuropathic pain after a work injury nine months ago. He asks for an early script for the third month running.

He tells you that he has been taking up to 1200 mg a day because the usual dose stopped helping, and that at the higher doses he feels relaxed and euphoric for a few hours. He has bought extra capsules from a friend twice. He drinks four to six standard drinks on most evenings, which he says helps the effect last. He is not injecting anything, has no opioid prescription, and denies stimulant use. His original pain has largely settled and his back examination today is normal, with no new neurological signs. He says he feels sweaty and anxious if he goes a day without taking any.

data_table.Medication use: Prescribed 300 mg daily, taking up to 1200 mg daily, purchasing additional capsules, early script requests three months running
data_table.Other substance use: Four to six standard drinks most evenings, no opioids, no injecting drug use
data_table.Examination: Back examination normal with no new neurological signs, original neuropathic pain largely resolved

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Plan a structured taper with staged dispensing, and address the alcohol use at the same time
Stop the pregabalin immediately today and provide a letter explaining the decision to him
Increase the prescribed dose to 600 mg twice daily so that he stops buying from other sources
Switch him to a slow release opioid to manage the pain and avoid a withdrawal reaction
Refer to a pain clinic and continue the current prescription unchanged until he is seen there

subtopic_detail: Smoking cessation pharmacotherapy in a patient stabilised on clozapine
stem: A 47-year-old man with schizophrenia has been stable on clozapine 400 mg nightly for five years; his level was 480 microg/L (target 350-600). He has smoked 25 cigarettes daily for 30 years and wants to quit.

data_table.Investigations: Full blood count normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacotherapy plan?

options.text: Nortriptyline 25 mg nightly titrated to 75 mg, with clozapine continued unchanged
Bupropion 150 mg twice daily for twelve weeks, with clozapine continued unchanged
Varenicline for twelve weeks, monitoring clozapine levels and reducing clozapine 25 percent at quit date
Combination nicotine replacement with patch and lozenges, with clozapine unchanged
Abrupt cessation with peer support only, avoiding all cessation pharmacotherapy

subtopic_detail: Adult ADHD diagnosis and stimulant initiation in the context of anxiety and driving
stem: A 28-year-old software developer has lifelong inattention, disorganisation and lateness, worse since starting full-time work. School reports from age 8 document the same. He has moderate generalised anxiety disorder (GAD-7 12) predating the worsening.

data_table.Assessment: DIVA-5 meets combined presentation; electrocardiogram QTc 410 ms; urine drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacological treatment plan?

options.text: Atomoxetine 40 mg daily, avoiding stimulants because of his anxiety and driving
Immediate release methylphenidate 5 mg twice daily, with cognitive behavioural therapy
Diazepam 5 mg twice daily, deferring ADHD treatment until the anxiety settles
Bupropion extended release 150 mg daily, titrated to 300 mg daily
Three-month trial of mindfulness-based cognitive therapy before any pharmacotherapy

subtopic_detail: Catatonia recognition and lorazepam challenge in a mixed presentation
stem: A 38-year-old woman on olanzapine 20 mg nightly for schizoaffective disorder was found mute and immobile two days ago. She does not speak or follow commands. An arm raised above her head stays there a minute, with grimacing and echolalia.

data_table.Investigations: Brain imaging, cerebrospinal fluid and electrolytes normal; creatine kinase 220 U/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Increase olanzapine to 30 mg nightly, adding haloperidol 5 mg as needed
Amantadine 100 mg twice daily as first line pharmacological therapy
Emergency electroconvulsive therapy without a benzodiazepine trial
Lorazepam 2 mg intramuscularly, reassessed at 30 minutes, then 6 to 24 mg daily
Intravenous midazolam 5 mg as the challenge, repeated every 30 minutes

subtopic_detail: Serotonin syndrome versus neuroleptic malignant syndrome differentiation
stem: A 42-year-old woman has 8 hours of tremor, agitation and confusion. She takes sertraline 200 mg daily, started tranylcypromine 9 days ago and took tramadol 50 mg 12 hours ago.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 138 /min, blood pressure 178/98 mmHg, temperature 39.4 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Sustained ankle clonus, hyperreflexia, mydriasis, hyperactive bowel sounds, tone increased not rigid
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 380 U/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Phenytoin 20 mg/kg with whole body ice pack cooling to 37 degrees C
Bromocriptine 2.5 mg eight-hourly with dantrolene, continuing sertraline
Intramuscular haloperidol 5 mg, with sertraline held 24 hours only
Stop serotonergic drugs, give fluids and benzodiazepines, then cyproheptadine 12 mg
Oral olanzapine 20 mg and transfer to a psychiatric unit overnight

subtopic_detail: Alcohol withdrawal with high seizure risk and CIWA-vs-fixed regimen choice
stem: A 54-year-old man drinks 40 standard drinks daily, last drink 30 hours ago. He has had a witnessed tonic-clonic seizure. Symptom-triggered dosing failed at a detoxification two years ago, progressing to delirium tremens.

data_table.Investigations: Sodium 133 mmol/L, magnesium 0.62 mmol/L (0.7-1.1)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Symptom-triggered diazepam on the ward, electrolyte replacement and haloperidol
Phenytoin 20 mg/kg, fluid restriction and as needed oral oxazepam 30 mg
Fixed diazepam 20 mg orally two-hourly until CIWA-Ar below 10, in high dependency
Intramuscular olanzapine 10 mg, then 10 mg daily through withdrawal
Acamprosate and naltrexone now, with hourly CIWA-Ar on the ward

subtopic_detail: Gamma-hydroxybutyrate withdrawal with autonomic instability and delirium
stem: A ventilated 26-year-old man is agitated, diaphoretic and confused over 12 hours. His partner discloses 14 months of 1,4-butanediol use every 2 hours, last dose 22 hours ago.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 138 /min, blood pressure 195/108 mmHg, temperature 39.1 degrees C
data_table.Sedation: Diazepam 30 mg plus lorazepam 4 mg intravenously, transient effect only
data_table.Investigations: CT brain and septic screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Propofol and dexmedetomidine infusions with no further benzodiazepine
Stop benzodiazepines and give haloperidol 10 mg with olanzapine 10 mg
High dose midazolam infusion plus phenobarbital loading 5 mg/kg
Intravenous flumazenil 0.2 mg, repeated to reverse accumulated benzodiazepines
Baclofen 20 mg via nasogastric tube eight-hourly as sole treatment

subtopic_detail: Second-generation antipsychotic metabolic monitoring
stem:
You are the community mental health registrar seeing a 28-year-old man who was commenced on olanzapine 15 mg nightly six months ago after a first-episode psychosis. He has been adherent, has had no relapse, and is enrolled in an early psychosis service. He now describes low energy, snoring witnessed by his partner, and a 9 kg weight gain since commencement.

His pre-treatment weight was 78 kg (BMI 24); his weight today is 87 kg (BMI 27). His fasting bloods this week show glucose 6.4 mmol/L, total cholesterol 6.1 mmol/L with LDL 4.0 mmol/L and triglycerides 2.6 mmol/L, and HbA1c 44 mmol/mol.

He describes his mental state as stable with residual mild negative symptoms; he lives with his partner and has re-started a plumbing apprenticeship.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82 /min, blood pressure 138/86 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.7 degC
data_table.Examination: BMI 27, waist circumference 102 cm, no thyroid enlargement
data_table.Investigations: Fasting glucose 6.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.5), HbA1c 44 mmol/mol (<42 non-diabetic), total cholesterol 6.1 mmol/L, LDL 4.0 mmol/L, HDL 0.9 mmol/L, triglycerides 2.6 mmol/L, ALT 42 U/L, TSH 1.6 mIU/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Continue olanzapine unchanged, refer to a community dietitian, and set a review appointment for six months' time
Discuss switching to aripiprazole or a lower-metabolic-risk antipsychotic and start metformin plus lifestyle program
Add a low dose of an atypical antipsychotic like risperidone to allow olanzapine dose reduction over three months
Prescribe a moderate-intensity statin now to treat dyslipidaemia and continue olanzapine at the current dose
Cease olanzapine abruptly and monitor for return of psychotic symptoms with weekly community mental health review

subtopic_detail: Alcohol withdrawal seizure prophylaxis in general medical ward
stem:
You are the medical registrar admitting a 44-year-old man to the general medical ward after presenting to the emergency department with 12 hours of coarse tremor, sweating, nausea and one episode of vomiting. He is a mechanic with a long-standing pattern of drinking eight standard drinks daily; his last drink was 18 hours ago when he 'decided to stop' after his wife left. He has had two previous withdrawal seizures during unmedicated abstinence attempts but has never had delirium tremens.

He is agitated but oriented. His current Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol - revised score is 18. Vital signs are stable. Bedside blood glucose is 5.8 mmol/L. He denies suicidal ideation and does not report visual or auditory hallucinations.

He has no known liver disease, no benzodiazepine dependence, and no chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108 /min, blood pressure 148/92 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 37.1 degC
data_table.Examination: Coarse tremor bilaterally, diaphoretic, oriented, no asterixis, no jaundice, no focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: Glucose 5.8 mmol/L, ALT 58 U/L, GGT 145 U/L, INR 1.1, platelets 168 x10^9/L, thiamine yet to be given

lead_in: What is the single best next step?

options.text: Give oral thiamine 100 mg daily and observe without benzodiazepine because he is oriented at the moment
Give oral chlordiazepoxide 25 mg every 6 hours on a fixed schedule for 5 days regardless of symptom pattern
Commence oral diazepam 20 mg every 2 hours titrated to CIWA-Ar plus parenteral thiamine 300 mg IV first dose
Commence phenytoin 15 mg/kg intravenous load and lorazepam 1 mg intramuscularly as seizure prophylaxis today
Start clonidine 150 microgram three times daily to control autonomic features without any benzodiazepine

subtopic_detail: Lithium initiation pre-treatment workup
stem:
You are the community mental health registrar reviewing a 32-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder recovering from her third manic episode. She has been managed with olanzapine and lorazepam during admission and is now stable on olanzapine 10 mg nightly. She wants to change to a longer-term mood stabiliser and is not pregnant, not planning pregnancy in the next 12 months, and uses a copper intrauterine device. She has no diagnosed cardiac or thyroid disease.

She is otherwise well with no NSAID or ACE inhibitor use. She works as an accountant with regular access to routine bloods. Her BMI is 24 and her blood pressure is 118/72.

After discussion of options, she prefers lithium given the family history of bipolar disorder that responded well to lithium.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78 /min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degC
data_table.Examination: BMI 24, no goitre, no oedema, cardiovascular examination unremarkable
data_table.Investigations: TSH 2.1 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), free T4 within normal limits, creatinine 68 micromol/L, eGFR >90 mL/min, sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.2 mmol/L, corrected calcium 2.32 mmol/L, urine hCG negative

lead_in: Which of the following investigations is the single most important to complete before commencing lithium?

options.text: Baseline 12-lead electrocardiogram to exclude conduction abnormalities before starting lithium therapy
Baseline liver function tests including ALT, AST, ALP, GGT, bilirubin and albumin before commencement
Fasting glucose plus lipid profile including total cholesterol, LDL, HDL and triglycerides before commencement
Pregnancy test plus baseline UEC, thyroid function and calcium documenting adherence to reliable contraception
Anti-thyroid antibodies including anti-TPO and anti-thyroglobulin to identify latent autoimmune thyroid disease

subtopic_detail: Catatonia in acute psychiatric setting
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar called to the acute psychiatric inpatient unit to review a 24-year-old man with schizoaffective disorder who has become progressively unwell over 24 hours. He was admitted a week ago for a psychotic relapse and started on risperidone 3 mg twice daily. Over the last day he has stopped eating and speaking and is now mute, staring past the interviewer.

On examination he holds his right arm in a raised position when you gently lift it, maintaining the posture for over a minute after you withdraw your hand. He resists passive movement with equal counter-force ('gegenhalten') and grimaces intermittently. There is no tremor and no lead-pipe rigidity.

His observations show mild tachycardia; he is afebrile.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108 /min, blood pressure 128/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 37.0 degC
data_table.Examination: Waxy flexibility, gegenhalten, mutism, staring, negativism (turning away from food), Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale score 16
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 220 U/L (<200), sodium 138 mmol/L (135-145), calcium and magnesium within normal limits, urine drug screen negative, blood cultures pending

lead_in: What is the single best next step?

options.text: Continue risperidone, add haloperidol 5 mg intramuscularly, and reassess response within the next hour
Refer immediately for electroconvulsive therapy without a lorazepam trial or diagnostic challenge
Start dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg intravenously for suspected neuroleptic malignant syndrome with rigidity
Trial olanzapine 10 mg intramuscularly and escalate second-generation antipsychotic sedation dosing
Give a test dose of lorazepam 1 to 2 mg intramuscularly and reassess response over 10 to 15 minutes

subtopic_detail: Valproate in women of reproductive age
stem:
You are the community mental health registrar seeing a 26-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder who has had two hospital admissions for mania. She has failed adequate trials of lithium and olanzapine (poor efficacy and metabolic weight gain respectively). Her psychiatrist is considering valproate as the next mood stabiliser. She is sexually active with her male partner, uses condoms only, and has not made pregnancy plans.

She has no personal history of neural tube defects and no family history of open spina bifida. Baseline liver function and platelet count are normal. She has been counselled that condom-only use has around a 15% typical-use annual failure rate.

She would prefer to try valproate but wants to explore what safety framework applies.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 74 /min, blood pressure 116/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degC
data_table.Examination: BMI 26, no goitre, no oedema, cardiovascular examination unremarkable
data_table.Investigations: ALT 22 U/L, platelets 268 x10^9/L, INR 1.0, urine hCG negative

lead_in: What is the single best next step?

options.text: Establish highly effective LARC contraception plus signed annual acknowledgement, then commence valproate
Start sodium valproate 500 mg twice daily immediately, with a plan to review contraception at three months
Add carbamazepine as a mood stabiliser instead of valproate, since carbamazepine is safer in early pregnancy
Recommend lamotrigine 25 mg daily titrated up over six weeks with no additional contraceptive advice given
Continue current management with olanzapine indefinitely because valproate is contraindicated in her situation

subtopic_detail: SSRI discontinuation vs depression relapse
stem:
You are the general practitioner registrar seeing a 38-year-old woman five days after she stopped her paroxetine 20 mg daily. She had been on paroxetine for 14 months for a moderate major depressive episode that fully remitted after six weeks; she stopped the medication herself on advice from a friend who felt she had 'been on it long enough'. Her last dose was five days ago.

Since then she describes new brief lightning-like sensations down her arms and legs on turning her head ('electric shocks'), vivid dreams, mild nausea, dizziness on standing, and a low-grade flu-like sensation. Her partner reports she is a bit irritable but not tearful or withdrawn. She is sleeping.

Her mood examination reveals a normal-range mood, appropriate reactivity, no anhedonia, no suicidal ideation, and no hopelessness.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76 /min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg (no significant postural drop), respiratory rate 14 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degC
data_table.Examination: Alert, normal affective range, no psychomotor slowing, no anhedonia, no suicidality, no hopelessness

lead_in: What is the single best next step?

options.text: Diagnose major depressive relapse and increase the paroxetine dose to 30 mg daily with review in two weeks
Restart paroxetine 20 mg daily and plan a slow taper over 8 to 12 weeks with a fluoxetine bridge if needed
Prescribe a benzodiazepine short-term for the anxiety-like symptoms and reassess response in two weeks' time
Add lithium as an augmentation agent for treatment-resistant depression despite prior full remission on paroxetine
Advise ongoing abstinence and predict resolution within 5 days regardless of severity or symptom duration

subtopic_detail: Acute mania first line pharmacotherapy
stem: A 24-year-old man with bipolar I disorder has four days of reduced sleep, pressured speech and grandiose plans. He self-ceased quetiapine 300 mg nightly six weeks ago and has never taken lithium.

data_table.Investigations: Electrolytes, liver and thyroid function normal; electrocardiogram normal; urine drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line pharmacological treatment?

options.text: Diazepam 10 mg orally four-hourly as the sole pharmacotherapy
Sertraline 50 mg daily titrated to 100 mg over two weeks
Lithium carbonate 500 mg at night, targeting a level of 0.8 to 1.0
Lamotrigine 25 mg daily titrated to 200 mg over six weeks
Fluoxetine 20 mg daily as monotherapy with review at two weeks

subtopic_detail: OCD SSRI titration
stem: A 28-year-old woman with obsessive compulsive disorder washes her hands four to six hours daily, with cracked painful skin. She has taken sertraline 100 mg daily for six weeks, up-titrated from 50 mg, with weekly exposure and response prevention for two months. Urge intensity is mildly less but washing is unchanged, with no side effects.

data_table.Examination: Excoriated hands, no tremor

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next pharmacological step?

options.text: Titrate sertraline up to 200 mg daily
Add risperidone 1 mg daily as an adjunct
Switch to a benzodiazepine for the anxiety
Switch to venlafaxine 75 mg daily
Refer for transcranial magnetic stimulation

subtopic_detail: Clozapine agranulocytosis monitoring
stem:
You are the community psychiatry registrar reviewing a 35-year-old man on clozapine for treatment resistant schizophrenia. He has been stable for three years with much reduced positive symptoms after trials of risperidone and olanzapine did not achieve remission. He attends his monthly clozapine clinic today for his four weekly review and blood collection.

His full blood count today returns with a neutrophil count of 1.3 x10^9/L (2.0-7.5), down from 2.6 four weeks ago. His platelets and haemoglobin are within normal limits. He is clinically well without fever, sore throat or infective symptoms. He has been fully adherent with medication and denies smoking cessation, new medications, or substance use.

He lives independently, is engaged in supported employment and reports his best psychosocial functioning in a decade. He is very keen to remain on clozapine and asks what happens next.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84 /min, blood pressure 122/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degC
data_table.Examination: Alert, no oral thrush, no pharyngeal erythema, chest clear, no lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Neutrophils 1.3 x10^9/L (was 2.6), white cells 4.2 x10^9/L (4-11), haemoglobin 145 g/L, platelets 240 x10^9/L, CRP <5 mg/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Continue clozapine at the current dose and repeat the full blood count twice weekly until stable
Stop clozapine immediately and admit for urgent GCSF and daily haematology inpatient review this week
Reduce clozapine dose by 50% and continue four weekly full blood count monitoring in the community
Switch to olanzapine 20 mg daily now and cease clozapine monitoring bloods from this appointment onwards
Add lithium 500 mg daily as neutrophil count booster and continue current four weekly monitoring at clinic

subtopic_detail: Lorazepam challenge test
stem: A 42-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder stopped lithium six months ago. She is on day 3 of a medical admission for dehydration after refusing to eat, drink or speak. She lies motionless, does not respond to voice, holds her arm where it is placed and echoes single words.

data_table.Investigations: Bloods, electrolytes, calcium, thyroid function and CT brain normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Give oral diazepam 10 mg three times daily and review
Start intramuscular olanzapine 5 mg and observe
Restart lithium 500 mg at night for prophylaxis
Arrange lumbar puncture before any acute treatment
Give lorazepam 2 mg intravenously, reassess at 15 minutes

subtopic_detail: Acute behavioural disturbance rapid tranquillisation
stem: A 32-year-old man is shouting, pacing and punching a wall in the emergency department, accusing staff of poisoning him. He has schizoaffective disorder and stopped his depot two months ago. He refuses oral medication, has no intravenous access, and de-escalation over 20 minutes has failed. He is detained under the NSW Mental Health Act 2007.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line pharmacological management?

options.text: Intramuscular promethazine 50 mg alone by the team
Intramuscular haloperidol 10 mg with lorazepam 2 mg
Oral olanzapine wafer 10 mg after de-escalation
Intramuscular ketamine 4 mg/kg with monitoring
Intramuscular droperidol 10 mg with midazolam 5 mg

subtopic_detail: Tricyclic overdose immediate management
stem: A 26-year-old woman arrives one hour after taking 40 tablets of amitriptyline 50 mg. She had one witnessed 60 second seizure in the ambulance and is now drowsy with GCS 12, dry flushed skin and dilated pupils.

data_table.ECG: QRS 148 ms (baseline 84 ms), R wave in aVR 4 mm
data_table.Investigations: Venous pH 7.28, bicarbonate 18 mmol/L, potassium 3.6 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Intravenous amiodarone 300 mg for the wide QRS
Intravenous flumazenil 0.2 mg then naloxone 0.4 mg
Intravenous phenytoin 15 mg/kg for seizure prophylaxis
Activated charcoal 50 g by nasogastric tube alone
Intravenous sodium bicarbonate 100 mmol against QRS width

subtopic_detail: Fitness to drive when starting stimulant treatment
stem:
You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 28-year-old woman with a recent diagnosis of adult attention deficit hyperactivity disorder by a psychiatrist. She has moderate to severe symptoms with impaired concentration at work as a data analyst and difficulty organising study for a professional exam. She has an unrestricted private driver licence and drives 30 minutes to work daily. She is due to start methylphenidate extended release under a shared care arrangement with the psychiatrist. She has no seizure history, no cardiac disease and normal blood pressure at 118/74 mmHg.

She asks whether she can continue to drive during the initiation period. She has not had any recent motor vehicle crash and holds no commercial licence.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76 /min, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degC
data_table.Examination: Alert, no tremor, no thought disorder, unremarkable cardiovascular examination
data_table.Investigations: Baseline electrocardiogram sinus rhythm 74 /min, thyroid function normal, urine drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice about driving under the AU Assessing Fitness to Drive standard?

options.text: Continue driving her private vehicle while ADHD is treated and stable, with duty to self report medication adverse effects
Surrender her private licence for a minimum of 6 months from the day of diagnosis regardless of any treatment response
Barred from private driving until she has completed a 6 monthly cognitive testing battery with a neuropsychologist
Switch to a commercial licence pathway and follow more frequent review criteria before returning to any driving
Because methylphenidate is a schedule 8 stimulant she must not drive at any time on it regardless of stability

subtopic_detail: Smoking cessation pharmacotherapy choice in a patient with depression
stem:
You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 45-year-old man who has been smoking 20 cigarettes daily for 25 years. He wants to quit and has tried nicotine patches alone twice for 4 weeks each with relapse in the second week both times. He has moderate depression currently controlled on sertraline 100 mg daily with a Kessler 10 score of 18. There is no history of self-harm, psychotic symptoms or bipolar disorder. He has no seizure history. He is not on any other medication. Cardiovascular examination is normal. He has no gastrointestinal disease and no renal impairment.

He asks whether varenicline is safe for someone with depression, having heard mixed information from friends. He is motivated to try a different medication approach this time.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78 /min, blood pressure 128/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.7 degC
data_table.Examination: Alert, euthymic today, no thought disorder, no psychomotor slowing
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, liver function tests and urea and electrolytes within normal limits; carbon monoxide breath 22 parts per million

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line pharmacotherapy option now?

options.text: Nicotine patch 21 mg daily alone for a third attempt with a slower taper this time over an extended 12 week period
Varenicline titrated over 1 week and continued for 12 weeks, with counselling on mood and sleep monitoring throughout
Bupropion 150 mg daily added to sertraline for a combined effect on mood and craving over the coming quit attempt
Nortriptyline titrated up to 75 mg daily as an off label option for smoking cessation over the coming quit attempt
Electronic cigarette (nicotine vaping product) prescribed under the current AU scheduling framework as a first line option

subtopic_detail: Long term monitoring on lithium
stem:
You are the community psychiatry registrar reviewing a 42-year-old woman with bipolar affective disorder type I. She has been stable on lithium carbonate 900 mg nocte for 3 years, most recently steady state trough level 0.7 mmol/L on 12 hour post dose sample. Her mood is euthymic today. She is asymptomatic. She reports no polyuria, no weight change, no cognitive dulling and no tremor.

Her last comprehensive monitoring bloods were taken 12 months ago. She has never had renal, thyroid or parathyroid disease. She takes no other prescribed medication. She lives independently and works in a public library. She asks what routine monitoring she should have now given the yearly review is due.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76 /min, blood pressure 116/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degC
data_table.Examination: Alert, euthymic, no fine tremor, no thyroid enlargement, no periorbital oedema
data_table.Investigations: Trough lithium 0.7 mmol/L 3 months ago; other bloods 12 months ago all normal

lead_in: Which monitoring panel best matches Therapeutic Guidelines Psychotropic recommendations for stable long term lithium therapy?

options.text: Lithium level every 6 months and full blood count every 6 months only, no other bloods routinely required in stable therapy
Electrocardiogram every 6 months and weight only, no bloods needed at these routine reviews in stable long term therapy
Lithium level, urea and electrolytes with estimated glomerular filtration rate, thyroid stimulating hormone and calcium every 6 to 12 months
Vitamin D and iron studies annually with a lithium level every 3 months, thyroid stimulating hormone every 2 years only
Fasting lipid panel and haemoglobin A1c every 6 months only because lithium is known to be associated with weight gain

subtopic_detail: Tricyclic antidepressant overdose electrocardiogram threshold for sodium bicarbonate
stem:
You are the emergency medicine registrar receiving a 34-year-old woman by ambulance 90 minutes after a witnessed ingestion of a partner's amitriptyline. Her partner estimates 60 tablets of 25 mg were missing. She is now agitated, tachycardic, mildly hypotensive and has had one brief tonic clonic seizure at the scene lasting under 1 minute that terminated spontaneously. Ambulance gave 5 mg intravenous midazolam and 1 L 0.9 percent saline. She is protecting her airway.

Cardiac monitor shows a wide complex regular rhythm at 118 /min. A 12 lead electrocardiogram has been performed. Point-of-care glucose 6.2 mmol/L. She has been under continuous cardiac monitoring since arrival. There is no other co ingestion reported. Charcoal has not been given because of the delayed presentation.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118 /min, blood pressure 96/60 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.9 degC
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but arousable, dilated pupils reactive at 5 mm, dry mucous membranes, no clonus, no focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: 12 lead electrocardiogram: sinus tachycardia at 118 /min, terminal 40 ms axis R in aVR 5 mm, QRS 152 ms, QTc 480 ms; venous pH 7.32 lactate 3.0 mmol/L

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate intervention now?

options.text: Intravenous flumazenil 0.2 mg because midazolam given by ambulance may be contributing to her drowsiness on arrival
Intravenous physostigmine 2 mg because dilated pupils and dry mouth suggest a peripheral anticholinergic toxidrome now
Intravenous amiodarone 300 mg for the broad complex tachycardia now visible on the cardiac monitor at present
Intravenous magnesium sulfate 2 g bolus and observation only, with no other pharmacological intervention required now
Intravenous sodium bicarbonate 8.4 percent 1 to 2 mmol/kg bolus over a few minutes then further boluses to QRS narrowing

subtopic_detail: Discriminating substance induced psychosis from a primary psychotic disorder
stem: A 22-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after bizarre behaviour. He is agitated, believes his housemates have been replaced by imposters and hears third person voices. His mother reports increasing daily high potency cannabis use over 3 months. He has no psychiatric history.

data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen positive for cannabinoids only; CT brain normal
data_table.Progress: Still paranoid after 6 hours of observation

lead_in: Which feature best discriminates cannabis induced from primary psychosis?

options.text: Persistence beyond 1 month of confirmed abstinence
Paranoid delusions confirm a primary psychotic disorder
Third person hallucinations exclude a substance induced cause
A positive cannabinoid screen confirms a drug induced cause
No family history excludes a primary psychotic disorder

subtopic_detail: First line psychological therapy for post traumatic stress disorder
stem:
You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 36-year-old former soldier who returned from deployment 2 years ago. He describes intrusive memories of a specific vehicle borne improvised explosive device incident, distressing nightmares 3 to 4 times per week, hypervigilance when driving, and avoidance of crowded shopping centres. He drinks 6 to 8 standard drinks daily to sleep and has not worked for 6 months. He denies current suicidal intent but has ongoing passive thoughts of not wanting to be alive. He is not psychotic. He has never had structured psychological therapy. He has been on sertraline 100 mg for 6 months with only partial improvement in mood.

He is engaged and asks what specific psychological therapy would be most helpful. He has private health insurance and can access accredited psychologists.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82 /min, blood pressure 122/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.7 degC
data_table.Examination: Alert, dysphoric, no thought disorder, no psychomotor slowing, no cognitive impairment
data_table.Investigations: Kessler 10 score 32, PTSD Checklist for DSM-5 score 62; full blood count, liver function tests and urea and electrolytes within normal limits

lead_in: Which psychological therapy has the strongest first line evidence for post-traumatic stress disorder in AU adult veterans?

options.text: Supportive psychotherapy weekly for 12 sessions delivered by a general counsellor with mental health experience
Trauma-focused cognitive behavioural therapy or eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing as first line therapy
Psychodynamic psychotherapy weekly for 12 months delivered by an accredited psychodynamic psychotherapist locally
Group interpersonal therapy alone delivered by an accredited practitioner for the recommended 12 week program
Mindfulness based stress reduction as sole therapy delivered by an accredited practitioner for the 8 week program

subtopic_detail: Antipsychotic selection for severe behavioural disturbance in dementia with Lewy bodies
stem: A 78-year-old man on a rivastigmine patch has 8 months of cognitive fluctuation, well formed visual hallucinations of animals, dream enactment and mild bradykinesia. His urinary tract infection has been treated; the hallucinations preceded it by 2 months. He is agitated overnight, throwing furniture, despite non-pharmacological measures. Haloperidol 0.5 mg previously caused severe worsening of his Parkinsonism.

data_table.Examination: Bradykinesia, cogwheel rigidity, left arm rest tremor

lead_in: Which pharmacological approach is most appropriate now?

options.text: Quetiapine 12.5 to 25 mg orally with monitoring
Haloperidol 2.5 mg intramuscularly for tranquillisation
Risperidone 0.5 mg orally as initial antipsychotic
Olanzapine 5 mg orally wafer for rapid onset
Diazepam 5 mg orally eight-hourly as monotherapy

subtopic_detail: Discriminating somatic symptom disorder from illness anxiety disorder in a general practice setting
stem: A 42-year-old woman has attended your general practice more than 30 times in 3 years with headache, abdominal pain, joint pain and finger tingling, with repeatedly normal investigation. She is distressed by the symptoms themselves rather than preoccupied with any particular illness, spends most of the day thinking about her health, and has cut her work hours.

data_table.Investigations: Extensive investigation including brain magnetic resonance imaging, endoscopy and nerve conduction studies all normal

lead_in: Which diagnosis best describes her presentation?

options.text: Functional neurological disorder, given the tingling
Illness anxiety disorder, given her health focus
Somatic symptom disorder, given the symptom burden
Malingering, given the normal investigations
Factitious disorder, given the repeated attendances

subtopic_detail: Persistent depressive disorder differentiation from major depressive disorder in general practice
stem: A 34-year-old man has felt low for most of the day for at least 4 years, with no 2 week period free of symptoms. He has low energy, poor self esteem, poor concentration and mild insomnia, but still works. He has never had a manic or hypomanic episode.

data_table.Investigations: Screening bloods and thyroid function normal; Patient Health Questionnaire 9 score 14

lead_in: Which diagnosis best fits his presentation?

options.text: Adjustment disorder with depressed mood following a workplace stressor
Major depressive disorder, single episode of moderate severity
Cyclothymic disorder with chronic subsyndromal mood variability
Persistent depressive disorder, formerly known as dysthymia
Depressive personality traits representing a stable character pattern

subtopic_detail: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome recognition after olanzapine dose increase in schizophrenia
stem: A 34-year-old man with schizophrenia had olanzapine increased from 10 to 20 mg 8 days ago. He presents with 24 hours of fever, muscle stiffness and confusion.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 138 /min, blood pressure 168/104 mmHg, temperature 39.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Lead-pipe rigidity, no clonus, Glasgow Coma Score 12
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 8400 U/L, creatinine 145 micromol/L

lead_in: Which combination is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Cease olanzapine, intravenous fluids, active cooling, dantrolene if severe
Increase olanzapine to 30 mg with intravenous lorazepam 2 mg
Cease olanzapine and give cyproheptadine 12 mg orally now
Continue olanzapine, give paracetamol 1 g and observe closely
Give intramuscular haloperidol 5 mg for rapid tranquillisation

subtopic_detail: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor induced hyponatraemia in an elderly outpatient
stem: A 78-year-old woman started sertraline 50 mg daily for depression 3 weeks ago. She reports 5 days of headache, nausea and unsteadiness, with no seizure or altered conscious state. She takes hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily.

data_table.Examination: Euvolaemic, no oedema
