data_table.Investigations: Sodium 122 mmol/L (baseline 138), urine osmolality 480 mOsm/kg, urine sodium 68 mmol/L, thyroid function and morning cortisol normal

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate management now?

options.text: Hypertonic saline 3 percent 150 mL over 20 minutes
Add tolvaptan 15 mg daily, continuing both drugs
Cease both drugs, restrict fluid to 800 mL/day, admit
Intravenous 0.9 percent saline and increase water to 2 L/day
Repeat the sodium in one week, changing nothing now

subtopic_detail: Parenteral thiamine dosing for Wernicke encephalopathy prevention in alcohol dependent admission
stem: A 52-year-old man is admitted for alcohol withdrawal. He drinks 30 standard drinks daily with a poor diet and 6 kg weight loss. He has no confusion, ophthalmoplegia or ataxia.

data_table.Investigations: Glucose 5.2 mmol/L

lead_in: Which thiamine regimen is most appropriate for Wernicke prophylaxis?

options.text: Oral thiamine 100 mg twice daily with a daily multivitamin capsule
Intramuscular thiamine 100 mg for 3 days, then oral 100 mg daily
Intramuscular multivitamin injection weekly for 4 weeks without extra thiamine
Intravenous glucose 50 percent 50 mL, then intravenous thiamine 100 mg
Intravenous thiamine 300 mg three times daily for 3 to 5 days, then oral 300 mg daily

subtopic_detail: Management of moderate postnatal depression with intrusive thoughts of self harm at 6 weeks postpartum
stem: A 30-year-old primipara attends her 6 week postnatal check. She describes 4 weeks of low mood, poor sleep independent of the baby, and thoughts that her family would be better off without her. She denies any plan. She is breast feeding and has a supportive partner.

data_table.Mental state: Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale 18 with question 10 scored 2; no infanticidal ideation or psychosis

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Prescribe temazepam alone and defer any antidepressant
Reassure her this is baby blues and rescore in 4 weeks
Admit involuntarily under the Mental Health Act
Stop breast feeding and start fluoxetine 20 mg daily
Start sertraline 50 mg daily, safety plan, refer urgently

subtopic_detail: Emergency management of moderate lithium toxicity in a chronic user with intercurrent dehydration
stem: A 62-year-old woman on lithium 750 mg nocte for 20 years presents with 2 days of tremor, dysarthria and unsteadiness. She has had 3 days of vomiting and diarrhoea, takes diclofenac for back pain and ramipril.

data_table.Neurology: Coarse tremor, dysarthria, mild confusion, brisk reflexes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Withhold lithium, stop diclofenac and ramipril, give saline, consider dialysis
Continue lithium and give activated charcoal 50 g four-hourly
Give sodium bicarbonate to alkalinise urine, continuing lithium
Give oral polystyrene sulfonate 15 g twice daily, continuing lithium
Give haloperidol and lorazepam, and reduce lithium to 500 mg

subtopic_detail: First line pharmacotherapy choice for newly diagnosed attention deficit hyperactivity disorder in an adolescent
stem: A 13-year-old boy meets criteria for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder on parent and school Vanderbilt scales, with impairment at home and school. Six months of a behavioural program and academic accommodations have not helped. He has mild episodic tics.

data_table.Cardiac: Normal 12 lead electrocardiogram, no family history of sudden cardiac death
data_table.Growth and observations: 60th centile height and weight, blood pressure 110/68 mmHg

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Immediate release methylphenidate 5 mg three times daily
Extended release methylphenidate 20 mg daily, titrated to response
Atomoxetine 40 mg daily as a non stimulant first line
Clonidine 25 micrograms twice daily, deferring stimulants
Fluoxetine 20 mg daily for underlying anxiety symptoms

subtopic_detail: First step management of behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia without imminent risk in residential care
stem: An 84-year-old woman with Alzheimer disease in residential aged care has become agitated each afternoon for 4 weeks, wandering and calling out. She has not been aggressive and sleeps 3 hours a night. Her medications are unchanged for 6 months.

data_table.Observations: Afebrile, urinalysis negative, no constipation, no focal neurological signs

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first management step?

options.text: Start temazepam 10 mg nightly for the wandering
Start risperidone 0.25 mg orally twice daily
Start a structured non-pharmacological plan
Increase her donepezil 5 mg to 10 mg daily
Refer for brain computed tomography to exclude stroke

subtopic_detail: Action on new neutropenia during weekly monitoring in an established clozapine patient with schizophrenia
stem: A 34-year-old man with treatment resistant schizophrenia has taken clozapine 400 mg nocte for 3 years. His routine weekly neutrophil count today is 1.2 x10^9/L, having been 3.8 x10^9/L last week. He is asymptomatic and afebrile, and had a viral upper respiratory infection 5 days ago.

data_table.Laboratory: White cell count 3.0 x10^9/L, haemoglobin and platelets normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Continue clozapine and start prophylactic amoxicillin with clavulanic acid
Cease clozapine today, admit for isolation and start filgrastim
Reduce clozapine to 200 mg and switch to olanzapine 20 mg
Continue clozapine and wait for next week's routine count
Continue clozapine with twice weekly counts and review within 48 hours

subtopic_detail: First line therapy for post traumatic stress disorder 6 months after a single traumatic event
stem: A 42-year-old woman is reviewed 6 months after a motor vehicle collision. She has nightmares four times a week, avoids driving on major roads, is hyperaroused and has not returned to work. She has no suicidal ideation and takes no medication.

data_table.Assessment: Post-traumatic stress disorder, chronic, single event
data_table.Access: Trauma trained psychologist available within 4 weeks

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment?

options.text: Trauma-focused cognitive behavioural therapy for 8 to 12 sessions
Sertraline 50 mg daily instead of psychological therapy
Diazepam as required with prazosin at night for nightmares
Single session psychological debriefing before formal therapy
Mirtazapine 30 mg at night for sleep as monotherapy

subtopic_detail: Refeeding management of a severely underweight adolescent with anorexia nervosa admitted for medical stabilisation
stem: A 15-year-old girl with anorexia nervosa is admitted. She weighs 34 kg (body mass index 13.6), has eaten under 500 kcal daily for 3 weeks and lost 6 kg.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 42 /min, blood pressure 108/68 lying and 88/56 mmHg standing, temperature 35.6 degrees C
data_table.Laboratory: Phosphate 0.85 mmol/L (0.75-1.5), magnesium 0.7, potassium 3.4, glucose 3.1 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial refeeding plan?

options.text: Start 3000 kcal/day now and check phosphate weekly
Start thiamine 100 mg, correct electrolytes, feed 1400 kcal/day
Withhold feeding 48 hours, infuse 5 percent dextrose
Nasogastric overnight feeding at 40 mL/hour only
Discharge her with weekly outpatient dietitian review

subtopic_detail: First line smoking cessation pharmacotherapy for an adult smoker with well controlled major depression on sertraline
stem: A 44-year-old woman smokes 20 cigarettes daily and wants to quit. She relapsed after 6 weeks on nicotine patches 3 years ago. Her major depression is in remission on sertraline 100 mg daily.

data_table.Dependence: Fagerstrom 6; first cigarette within 5 minutes of waking

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Nicotine patches 21 mg daily alone for 12 weeks without other pharmacotherapy
Varenicline titrated to 1 mg twice daily for 12 weeks, continuing sertraline
Bupropion 150 mg twice daily for 9 weeks, ceasing sertraline beforehand
Referral to an inpatient unit for supervised nicotine withdrawal
Cytisine 1.5 mg titrated over 25 days in place of varenicline

subtopic_detail: First line stimulant choice and prescribing pathway for a newly diagnosed adult with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder
stem: A 28-year-old man is newly diagnosed with combined presentation attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, with childhood symptoms corroborated by his mother. He has no substance use disorder, cardiovascular disease, psychosis or mania.

data_table.Cardiac: Blood pressure 122/74 mmHg, electrocardiogram sinus rhythm, QTc 410 milliseconds

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Atomoxetine 40 mg daily, titrated to 80 mg daily over 4 weeks
Modafinil 200 mg daily, titrated to 400 mg daily over 2 weeks
Lisdexamfetamine 30 mg each morning, titrated by 30 mg weekly to response
Bupropion sustained release 150 mg daily, titrated to 300 mg daily
Risperidone 1 mg at night for impulsivity and hyperactivity

subtopic_detail: Emergency department management of chronic self-harm in a woman with borderline personality disorder attending after a superficial forearm cut without medical severity
stem: A 26-year-old woman with borderline personality disorder cut her forearm 2 hours ago. She has had 12 similar presentations this year and attends weekly dialectical behaviour therapy. She denies suicidal intent but reports an urge to cut again. Her case manager is contactable.

data_table.Wound: 6 cm superficial cut, left volar forearm, neurovascularly intact

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Involuntary admission under the Mental Health Act 2007 (NSW)
Intramuscular olanzapine 5 mg and overnight short stay admission
Suturing under local anaesthetic, then discharge without follow up
Wound dressing, safety plan and next day dialectical behaviour therapy
Referral to community forensic mental health for risk assessment

subtopic_detail: Recognition and lorazepam challenge in a young woman with new onset catatonia superimposed on major depressive disorder
stem: A 24-year-old woman with recurrent major depressive disorder on sertraline 100 mg daily has 5 days of immobility and reduced oral intake. She has had no antipsychotic.

data_table.Bush Francis: Mutism, waxy flexibility, negativism, staring, posturing, prolonged immobility
data_table.Observations: Afebrile, no rigidity, autonomic instability or clonus
data_table.Bloods: Creatine kinase 380 U/L (30-200); brain CT and cerebrospinal fluid normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Intramuscular haloperidol 5 mg, observing for response over 4 hours
Urgent electroconvulsive therapy without a benzodiazepine trial
Intravenous flumazenil 0.2 mg as a diagnostic and therapeutic manoeuvre
Intravenous glucose 5 percent with thiamine 500 mg three times daily
Intravenous lorazepam 2 mg, reassessing Bush Francis score at 15 minutes

subtopic_detail: Sodium bicarbonate indication and dosing for a tricyclic antidepressant overdose with widened QRS on the electrocardiogram
stem: A 32-year-old woman is brought in 90 minutes after taking 40 amitriptyline 25 mg tablets (1000 mg). She is drowsy but rousable, with dilated pupils.

data_table.Electrocardiogram: Sinus tachycardia, QRS 130 milliseconds, terminal R wave in aVR 4 mm

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Intravenous sodium bicarbonate 100 mmol, repeated until the QRS narrows below 100 milliseconds
Intravenous flumazenil 0.2 mg, deferring bicarbonate until reversal is assessed
Activated charcoal 50 g nasogastrically, deferring bicarbonate to a repeat electrocardiogram
Intravenous magnesium sulfate 2 g, deferring bicarbonate until QRS exceeds 160 milliseconds
Intravenous 20 percent lipid emulsion 1.5 mL/kg before considering sodium bicarbonate

subtopic_detail: Baseline investigations, starting dose and target level for lithium initiation in a first episode of bipolar I disorder in a middle aged woman
stem: A 42-year-old woman's first episode of bipolar I mania has settled on olanzapine 15 mg daily. Maintenance lithium is planned at discharge.

data_table.Baseline: Not pregnant; no renal, thyroid or cardiac disease

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initiation plan?

options.text: Lithium 900 mg twice daily immediately without baseline tests, targeting 1.2 to 1.6 mmol/L
Renal, thyroid, calcium, pregnancy test and electrocardiogram, then lithium 250 mg nocte to 0.6 to 0.8 mmol/L
Switch olanzapine to sodium valproate 500 mg twice daily as first line maintenance therapy
Continue olanzapine 15 mg daily as sole maintenance, reviewed in clinic at 6 weeks
Lamotrigine 25 mg daily titrated to 200 mg over 6 weeks, with no baseline investigations

subtopic_detail: Clozapine metabolic and haematological monitoring at 4 weeks
stem: A 38-year-old man with treatment resistant schizophrenia has taken clozapine for 4 weeks, titrated to 300 mg at night, with weekly white cell counts normal. He has gained 3 kg with increased appetite and drowsiness.

data_table.Monitoring: Weight 92 kg from 89 kg, waist 102 cm, baseline metabolic screen normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next monitoring step?

options.text: Cease clozapine and restart risperidone 6 mg daily
Repeat the metabolic bloods today, given the weight gain
Reduce clozapine to 200 mg at night for weight
Repeat fasting lipids, glucose and HbA1c at 3 months
Add ziprasidone 40 mg twice daily as an adjunct

subtopic_detail: Long term lithium monitoring at 6 month review
stem:
You are the community psychiatry registrar. A 47-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder has been on lithium carbonate 900 mg daily for 2 years with good mood stabilisation and no relapses. Her most recent lithium level 3 months ago was 0.72 mmol/L. She takes no other medications, does not smoke, and drinks 3 standard drinks on weekends.

Today she attends for routine monitoring. She feels well with stable mood, no tremor, no polyuria, and no gastrointestinal upset. Her weight is unchanged from baseline. Vital signs are pulse 74, blood pressure 122/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius. Her general physical examination is unremarkable.

Her general practitioner has already arranged today's blood tests: lithium level, urea and electrolytes, creatinine, TSH, and adjusted calcium.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 74, BP 122/76 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.History: Bipolar I; lithium 900 mg daily for 2 years; no relapses; last lithium 0.72 mmol/L three months ago
data_table.Symptoms: Well, no tremor, no polyuria, no GI upset; weight unchanged

lead_in: Which single set of monitoring blood tests is minimally required at this 6 monthly review under Australian guidance?

options.text: Lithium level with urea and electrolytes and creatinine only
Lithium level with 24 hour urine collection for urinary lithium and osmolality
Lithium level with liver function tests and full blood count only
Lithium level and TSH only every 12 months without renal or calcium tests
Lithium level with urea and electrolytes, creatinine, TSH and adjusted calcium

subtopic_detail: Recognition and initial management of catatonia in the acute ward
stem: A 24-year-old woman admitted 5 days ago with a manic relapse has had olanzapine withheld for 48 hours for poor oral intake. For 12 hours she has been mute and immobile, holding any position her limbs are placed in, and resisting passive movement with equal counter-force.

data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 210 U/L (25-190), C reactive protein 4 mg/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Restart olanzapine 10 mg orally today for her mania
Lorazepam 2 mg intramuscularly as a diagnostic challenge
Dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg for neuroleptic malignant syndrome
Sodium valproate 20 mg/kg for non-convulsive status
Haloperidol 5 mg intramuscularly as chemical restraint

subtopic_detail: Amitriptyline overdose with widened QRS in the emergency department
stem: A 32-year-old woman presents 2 hours after taking 40 tablets of amitriptyline 25 mg (1000 mg) with wine. She is drowsy with GCS 12, dry mucous membranes and dilated pupils.

data_table.ECG: Sinus tachycardia, QRS 132 ms (<120), R wave in aVR 5 mm (>3)
data_table.Investigations: Venous pH 7.32, potassium 3.6 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next intervention?

options.text: Sodium bicarbonate 8.4 percent 100 mmol intravenously
Activated charcoal 50 g given by nasogastric tube
Intravenous lipid emulsion 20 percent, 1.5 mL/kg bolus
Flecainide 100 mg intravenously for the wide QRS
Physostigmine 2 mg intravenously for the antimuscarinic signs

subtopic_detail: Smoking cessation pharmacotherapy in a patient with prior seizure
stem: A 44-year-old man smokes 25 cigarettes daily and has smoked for 25 years, with a Fagerstrom score of 7. He has twice relapsed within a month on nicotine gum. He had one alcohol withdrawal seizure 10 years ago and has been abstinent since. He has no psychiatric history and a quit date in 2 weeks.

data_table.Investigations: eGFR 82 mL/min/1.73m2

lead_in: Which first line pharmacotherapy is most appropriate?

options.text: Bupropion 150 mg daily for 3 days then twice daily
Varenicline titrated to 1 mg twice daily for 12 weeks
Nicotine patch 21 mg daily alone for 12 weeks
Nortriptyline 25 mg at night titrated over 4 weeks
Clonidine 25 micrograms twice daily, titrated upwards

subtopic_detail: Valproate in a woman of reproductive age with bipolar
stem:
You are the community psychiatry registrar. A 28-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder has been maintained for 2 years on sodium valproate 1200 mg daily with good mood stabilisation after two failed lithium trials (rash, nausea intolerance). She uses barrier contraception intermittently, has an irregular menstrual cycle, and reports her partner and she are considering starting a family in the next year.

Her last valproate level 4 weeks ago was 520 micromol/L (350-700). She has no current mood symptoms, is not suicidal, and works full time as a school teacher. She has no medical conditions and does not smoke. She has heard from a friend that valproate is unsafe in pregnancy and asks whether she should stop it now.

Her weight is 74 kg, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, and she is up to date with cervical screening.

data_table.Medication history: Sodium valproate 1200 mg daily for 2 years, prior lithium trials failed (rash, nausea)
data_table.Reproductive: Age 28, uses barrier contraception intermittently, irregular cycle, considering pregnancy in next year
data_table.Investigations: Valproate level 520 micromol/L (350-700) four weeks ago; weight 74 kg; BP 118/74 mmHg

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate management step?

options.text: Continue valproate at current dose and add folic acid 500 micrograms daily
Continue valproate and start a 3 month combined oral contraceptive pill without switching
Stop valproate abruptly today with no substitute pharmacotherapy or contraception adjustment
Reduce valproate to 600 mg daily to minimise dose-dependent teratogenicity
Cross taper valproate to lamotrigine and arrange effective contraception until switch complete

subtopic_detail: Panic disorder pharmacotherapy initiation
stem:
You are the GP registrar seeing a 34-year-old accountant with a 4 month history of recurrent unexpected episodes of chest tightness, palpitations, hand tingling, and a sense of impending death that peak within 10 minutes and settle over 30 minutes. He now avoids the train because he had two attacks on the platform, and he telephones his wife to collect him.

He drinks 2 standard drinks on Friday evenings, has never used stimulants or cannabis, and does not use caffeine after midday. TSH, full blood count, electrolytes, ECG, and echocardiogram arranged by the emergency department 3 weeks ago were all within normal limits. He scores 16 on the PHQ-9 with no suicidal ideation and 18 on the GAD-7.

He is otherwise well, on no regular medication, has no family history of bipolar disorder, and is keen to start medication rather than commence psychological therapy at this stage.

data_table.Screening scores: PHQ-9 16 with no suicidal ideation; GAD-7 18
data_table.Prior workup: TSH, full blood count, electrolytes, ECG, echocardiogram all within normal limits
data_table.Substance use: 2 standard drinks weekly; no stimulants, no cannabis, no caffeine after midday

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate initial pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Commence mirtazapine 30 mg orally each evening and continue indefinitely as needed
Commence diazepam 5 mg orally three times daily and continue while panic persists
Commence propranolol 40 mg orally three times daily and continue for symptom control
Commence fluoxetine 20 mg orally daily without any initial low-dose lead-in period
Commence sertraline 25 mg orally daily then increase to 50 mg after one week

subtopic_detail: Antidepressant choice in an exclusively breastfeeding mother
stem:
You are the GP seeing a 29-year-old woman 10 weeks after the birth of her first baby. She is exclusively breastfeeding and describes 3 weeks of low mood, waking at 04:00 with racing thoughts, tearfulness through the day, poor appetite, and guilt about not enjoying the baby. She has no suicidal ideation and no thoughts of harming the baby. The Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale run by the child-health nurse today is 17 with item 10 scored zero.

She has no personal or family history of bipolar disorder, no psychotic symptoms, and no perinatal anxiety earlier in the pregnancy. Thyroid function, ferritin, and B12 are within normal limits. She is not taking any medications and had no antidepressant during pregnancy.

She has been attending fortnightly with the child-health nurse, has family support, and is willing to consider psychological therapy but wants to also start medication because sleep is deteriorating. She wants to continue breastfeeding.

data_table.Screening: EPDS 17 with item 10 scored zero; PHQ-9 not repeated
data_table.Baseline labs: TSH, ferritin, and B12 within normal limits

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate initial pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Advise weaning off breastfeeding before starting any antidepressant
Fluoxetine 20 mg orally each morning continued during breastfeeding
Venlafaxine 75 mg orally each morning continued during breastfeeding
Mirtazapine 30 mg orally each night continued during breastfeeding
Sertraline 50 mg orally each morning continued during breastfeeding

subtopic_detail: Thiamine timing in alcohol withdrawal presenting to ED
stem:
You are the ED RMO seeing a 52-year-old builder brought in by his brother because he has stopped drinking 20 hours ago after 18 years of daily heavy alcohol use averaging 20 standard drinks per day. He is diaphoretic, tremulous, mildly agitated, and confused about the date but knows his name. His CIWA-Ar score is 22.

On arrival his pulse is 118, blood pressure is 168/98 mmHg, respiratory rate is 22, SpO2 is 96 percent on room air, and temperature is 37.6 degrees Celsius. Point-of-care glucose is 3.1 mmol/L (3.5 to 7.7). Weight is 72 kg. He has no history of seizure or delirium tremens in prior withdrawals but has a lifetime pattern of poor nutrition and lost 6 kg in the last two months.

Bloods have been sent and IV access is established. The consultant asks you to co-ordinate the next steps.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118, BP 168/98 mmHg, RR 22, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 37.6 degrees Celsius

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate management step?

options.text: Give IV thiamine 300 mg then IV glucose after the thiamine infusion is running
Give 100 mL of 50 percent glucose IV then oral thiamine 100 mg after glucose
Give oral diazepam 20 mg then reassess the CIWA-Ar score after 60 minutes
Give haloperidol 5 mg IM to control the agitation before any other intervention
Give fixed schedule oral diazepam 10 mg six-hourly without any thiamine cover

subtopic_detail: Refeeding syndrome monitoring in anorexia nervosa admission
stem: A 15-year-old girl with restrictive anorexia nervosa has eaten under 500 kcal daily for 8 weeks, losing 12 kg. Refeeding starts at 1000 kcal daily.

data_table.Investigations: Potassium 3.4 mmol/L, phosphate 0.72 mmol/L (0.8-1.4), glucose 3.6 mmol/L; QTc 470 ms

lead_in: Which refeeding monitoring plan is most appropriate?

options.text: Daily electrolytes, phosphate and glucose for 5 days with intermittent cardiac observations
12-hourly electrolytes, phosphate and glucose for 72 hours with continuous cardiac monitoring
Phosphate every 48 hours, with electrolytes only if she becomes symptomatic
Empirical oral phosphate replacement, deferring routine electrolyte monitoring
Electrocardiogram only if pulse falls below 40 or potassium below 3.0 mmol/L

subtopic_detail: Lithium initiation in acute mania in an adult inpatient
stem: A 32-year-old man, 78 kg, is admitted with 10 days of 2 hours' sleep nightly, pressured speech, grandiose plans and 40,000 dollars of credit card spending. A previous episode responded to lithium.

data_table.Baseline biochemistry: Creatinine 72 micromol/L (60 to 110), eGFR over 90, TSH 2.1 mIU/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial dose regimen for lithium?

options.text: 1500 mg as a loading dose, then 500 mg daily
250 mg at night, with a level at 24 hours
750 mg at night, level at 12 hours after 5 days
250 mg orally three times daily in divided doses
Sodium valproate 500 mg twice daily instead

subtopic_detail: First-line management of PTSD in an adult veteran
stem:
You are the GP registrar seeing a 41-year-old woman who served in the Australian Defence Force and was discharged 4 years ago. Over the last 8 months she has had recurrent intrusive memories of an IED incident, nightmares 5 nights a week, hypervigilance, exaggerated startle response, avoidance of driving on freeways, and a persistent sense of foreshortened future. She does not use alcohol or illicit drugs and has never had psychotic symptoms.

She is up to date on her Open Arms sessions but has attended 4 in the last 6 months only. Her PCL-5 score is 52 and her PHQ-9 is 12 with no active suicidal ideation. She is otherwise well, on no medication, and has no history of bipolar disorder or first-degree family history of mood disorders. Sleep-onset insomnia and impaired concentration are limiting her role as a supply chain analyst.

She is willing to consider both psychological therapy and pharmacotherapy and asks what should be tried first.

data_table.Screening scores: PCL-5 52; PHQ-9 12 with no active suicidal ideation
data_table.Function: Sleep-onset insomnia and impaired concentration limiting employment

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate first-line treatment recommendation?

options.text: Commence sertraline 50 mg orally each morning as monotherapy for 12 weeks
Refer for structured trauma-focused CBT delivered over 8 to 12 weekly sessions
Commence prazosin 1 mg orally each night for nightmares as monotherapy
Commence quetiapine 25 mg orally at night for hyperarousal as monotherapy
Commence diazepam 5 mg orally at night for sleep and startle symptom control

subtopic_detail: SSRI dose escalation strategy in an adult with OCD
stem:
You are the GP registrar seeing a 27-year-old teacher with a 2 year history of contamination obsessions and hand-washing compulsions occupying more than 3 hours daily. He has been on fluoxetine 20 mg orally each morning for 12 weeks with only marginal reduction in his Yale-Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale score from 26 to 22 and no functional improvement.

He attends weekly sessions with a clinical psychologist for exposure and response prevention. He has no history of bipolar disorder, no psychotic symptoms, and no suicidal ideation. Sodium is 140 mmol/L (135 to 145), liver function tests are within normal limits, and ECG shows sinus rhythm with a QTc of 410 ms. He does not use alcohol, illicit drugs, or over-the-counter serotonergic agents.

He is adherent to the current fluoxetine dose, tolerating it without adverse effects, and asks what should happen next.

data_table.Current pharmacotherapy: Fluoxetine 20 mg orally each morning for 12 weeks
data_table.Baseline labs: Sodium 140 (135 to 145); LFTs within normal limits; ECG sinus with QTc 410 ms

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Increase fluoxetine to 60 mg orally each morning and continue current ERP therapy
Switch to sertraline 50 mg orally each morning as SSRI monotherapy for OCD
Add risperidone 1 mg orally each night to current fluoxetine 20 mg regimen
Discontinue fluoxetine and refer for repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation
Discontinue fluoxetine and commence clomipramine 25 mg orally each night instead

subtopic_detail: First-line stimulant selection in newly diagnosed adult ADHD
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar in an adult ADHD clinic reviewing a 26-year-old software developer with newly diagnosed combined presentation ADHD confirmed by a structured DIVA-5 interview, collateral from her mother, and school reports demonstrating longstanding inattention from primary school onwards.

She is otherwise well, on no medication, and has a resting pulse of 76 and a blood pressure of 122/74 mmHg. She has no personal or family history of arrhythmia, cardiomyopathy, structural heart disease, glaucoma, or bipolar disorder. She has no history of substance use disorder and no current comorbid psychiatric diagnosis. Her weight is 62 kg. TSH is within normal limits and ECG shows sinus rhythm with a QTc of 400 ms.

She wants to try medication for the first time and asks what will be started.

data_table.Assessment: DIVA-5 confirms combined presentation ADHD; collateral from mother; primary school reports consistent
data_table.Cardiac screen: Pulse 76; BP 122/74 mmHg; no family history of sudden death or cardiomyopathy; ECG sinus with QTc 400 ms
data_table.Comorbidities: No substance use disorder, no bipolar disorder, TSH within normal limits

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate initial pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Commence bupropion 150 mg orally each morning off-label for adult ADHD
Commence atomoxetine 40 mg orally each morning and review at 4 weeks
Commence lisdexamfetamine 30 mg orally each morning and review at 4 weeks
Commence guanfacine extended release 1 mg orally at night as monotherapy
Defer pharmacotherapy and offer 12 weeks of cognitive behavioural therapy alone

subtopic_detail: First-line management of generalised anxiety disorder in an adult
stem:
You are the GP seeing a 38-year-old primary school teacher with a 14 month history of excessive worry about work performance, her children's safety, and household finances. She describes muscle tension in her shoulders, sleep-onset insomnia, difficulty concentrating on marking, and irritability that has affected her relationship with her partner.

She does not use alcohol, illicit drugs, or nicotine. Her caffeine intake is 1 flat white in the morning. She has no personal or family history of bipolar disorder and no psychotic symptoms. TSH is 1.9 mIU/L (0.4 to 4.0), ferritin is 68 microgram/L (30 to 500), full blood count is within normal limits, and 12 lead ECG shows sinus rhythm with a QTc of 400 ms.

Her GAD-7 score is 16 and her PHQ-9 is 8 with no suicidal ideation. Her symptoms are persistent, present most days for the last 14 months, and cause significant impairment. She has not previously tried medication or psychological therapy and asks what should happen next.

data_table.Screening scores: GAD-7 16; PHQ-9 8 with no suicidal ideation
data_table.Baseline labs: TSH 1.9 (0.4 to 4.0); ferritin 68 microgram/L (30 to 500); FBC within normal limits; ECG sinus QTc 400 ms
data_table.Substance use: 1 flat white daily; no alcohol, tobacco, or illicit drugs

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate initial treatment recommendation?

options.text: Commence diazepam 5 mg orally three times daily for symptom control ongoing
Refer for structured cognitive behavioural therapy over 8 to 12 weekly sessions
Commence pregabalin 75 mg orally twice daily as GAD monotherapy long-term
Commence quetiapine 50 mg orally each night for anxiety and sleep monotherapy
Recommend a repeat GAD-7 score in 6 weeks without any active intervention

subtopic_detail: Chronic insomnia management in an older adult
stem:
You are the GP seeing a 72-year-old retired librarian with an 8 month history of difficulty initiating sleep, taking around 90 minutes to fall asleep on most nights, with 3 to 4 nocturnal awakenings and total sleep time of around 4.5 hours. She feels unrefreshed on waking and fatigued through the day.

She has no history of restless legs, snoring, witnessed apnoeas, or excessive daytime sleepiness on the Epworth Sleepiness Scale (score 6). Her caffeine intake is one flat white at 08:00 only. She does not use alcohol. She takes rosuvastatin 20 mg orally each night and perindopril 4 mg orally each morning. TSH, ferritin, sodium, and eGFR are within normal limits. Her PHQ-9 is 5 and her GAD-7 is 4.

Her bedroom is warm, she watches television in bed until she feels drowsy, and her spouse reports she takes daytime naps of 60 to 90 minutes. She has not tried any behavioural changes or medication for the sleep problem.

data_table.Sleep pattern: Sleep onset latency 90 minutes; 3 to 4 nocturnal awakenings; total sleep time 4.5 hours
data_table.Comorbidities and medications: Rosuvastatin 20 mg nocte; perindopril 4 mg mane; TSH, ferritin, sodium, eGFR within normal limits

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate first-line management?

options.text: Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia over 6 to 8 weekly sessions
Commence temazepam 10 mg orally each night for ongoing use over 12 weeks
Commence zopiclone 7.5 mg orally each night for ongoing use over 12 weeks
Commence mirtazapine 15 mg orally each night for its sedative effect at low dose
Commence prolonged-release melatonin 2 mg orally at night for 13 weeks trial

subtopic_detail: Clozapine rechallenge after benign ethnic neutropenia investigation
stem: A 34-year-old man of West African ancestry with treatment-resistant schizophrenia failed 6 week trials of olanzapine 20 mg and risperidone 6 mg. Clozapine stopped at week 6, three months ago, for neutropenia. He is deteriorating with escalating delusions.

data_table.Haematology: Benign ethnic neutropenia, Duffy-null, predating antipsychotics

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: List him as permanently clozapine-ineligible and continue risperidone
Add lithium 400 mg nightly to raise the neutrophil count
Combine olanzapine 20 mg with amisulpride 400 mg daily
Commence electroconvulsive therapy as the sole treatment
Register on the benign ethnic neutropenia pathway and restart clozapine

subtopic_detail: Augmentation choice for treatment-resistant depression
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar in a community mental health clinic reviewing a 54-year-old warehouse supervisor with major depressive disorder. His current episode is 9 months long and has failed 8 weeks of sertraline 200 mg orally daily then 10 weeks of venlafaxine 300 mg orally daily; his current PHQ-9 is 19 with anhedonia, early morning waking, and 6 kg weight loss.

He has no history of bipolar disorder or psychosis and no active suicidal ideation. He has attended 14 sessions of interpersonal therapy over the last 5 months with only partial benefit. Sodium is 138 mmol/L (135 to 145), creatinine is 84 micromol/L (60 to 110), eGFR is over 90, TSH is 2.0 mIU/L (0.4 to 4.0), and ECG shows sinus rhythm with a QTc of 415 ms. Weight is 82 kg.

He drinks 2 standard drinks weekly, does not use illicit drugs, and asks about the next medication step.

data_table.Symptom severity: PHQ-9 19; 9 month episode; no active suicidal ideation
data_table.Prior trials: Sertraline 200 mg 8 weeks failed; venlafaxine 300 mg 10 weeks failed; 14 sessions IPT partial benefit
data_table.Baseline labs: Sodium 138, creatinine 84 micromol/L, eGFR over 90, TSH 2.0, QTc 415 ms

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Refer for deep brain stimulation of the subgenual cingulate as neurosurgical option
Add fluoxetine 20 mg orally each morning to the current venlafaxine 300 mg regimen
Switch venlafaxine to fluoxetine 40 mg orally each morning as a third SSRI trial
Add clonazepam 0.5 mg orally each night as anxiolytic augmentation to venlafaxine
Continue venlafaxine 300 mg and add lithium 500 mg at night with level in 5 to 7 days

subtopic_detail: Antipsychotic-induced weight gain in a young patient on olanzapine
stem: A 22-year-old man with first-episode psychosis has taken olanzapine 15 mg nightly for 6 months, with full remission. Three months of supervised exercise and dietary change have produced no weight loss.

data_table.Anthropometry: Weight 74 to 92 kg, waist 88 to 104 cm, BP 138/86 mmHg
data_table.Biochemistry: Fasting glucose 4.8 to 6.4 mmol/L, triglycerides 1.2 to 3.8 mmol/L (below 1.7)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step for the metabolic profile?

options.text: Add metformin 500 mg twice daily
Switch olanzapine to aripiprazole 15 mg
Reduce olanzapine to 10 mg nightly
Refer for bariatric surgery assessment
Add orlistat 120 mg three times daily

subtopic_detail: Lithium initiation baseline workup
stem:
You are the community mental health team registrar reviewing a 26-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder who has agreed to commence lithium after two manic episodes in 18 months.

She was well between episodes, has no known other medical conditions, uses combined oral contraceptive pills, and does not use alcohol or recreational substances. She works as a childcare educator, drinks 2 to 3 L of water per day, and drives a car.

Her body mass index is 24 kg/m2. There is no goitre, no tremor, and no oedema on examination. She is normotensive.

She asks what tests she needs before starting lithium and how monitoring will occur once she is on treatment.

data_table.Diagnosis: Bipolar I disorder; two manic episodes in 18 months
data_table.Comorbidities: Nil; no substance use; no chronic medical illness
data_table.Examination: BMI 24 kg/m2; no goitre, tremor or oedema; normotensive

lead_in: Which baseline workup best matches Australian practice before starting lithium?

options.text: Genetic HLA-B*1502 testing, urea and electrolytes, thyroid function, and 12 lead ECG before starting the drug
Urea and electrolytes and thyroid function only, with lithium level checked once monthly after starting
UEC, thyroid function, calcium and PTH, full blood count, ECG, urinalysis, and serum beta hCG at baseline
24 hour urine collection for creatinine clearance, full blood count, and LFTs without electrolytes or thyroid
Baseline HbA1c and lipid panel alone because lithium is associated with metabolic syndrome and weight gain

subtopic_detail: Adult ADHD stimulant initiation and driving
stem:
You are the general adult psychiatry registrar reviewing a 27-year-old man with a new diagnosis of adult ADHD, combined presentation, made after structured assessment including collateral from parents and school reports.

He is fit and well, has no personal or family history of stroke or cardiac disease, and drinks 6 standard drinks per week. He denies stimulant misuse and has never used methamphetamine.

Blood pressure is 128/78, pulse 72 regular, ECG shows sinus rhythm with no QT prolongation. He has a full unrestricted driver licence and works as a solicitor. He asks specifically about starting medication and whether it will affect his driving.

data_table.Diagnosis: Adult ADHD combined presentation; collateral corroborated
data_table.Medical: No cardiac disease; no personal or family history of stroke
data_table.Substance use: 6 standard drinks weekly; denies stimulant misuse; no methamphetamine
data_table.Cardiovascular: BP 128/78; ECG sinus rhythm; no QT prolongation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line pharmacotherapy and driving advice?

options.text: Commence modafinil 100 mg orally daily because it is a Schedule 4 stimulant analogue with a favourable cardiac profile
Commence atomoxetine 40 mg orally daily because non stimulant medication avoids any need for licence notification
Commence sertraline 50 mg orally daily to address inattention through mood improvement rather than direct effect
Commence lisdexamfetamine 30 mg orally each morning, and notify the licensing authority for a conditional licence
Trial cognitive behavioural therapy for ADHD as sole treatment for 12 months before considering any pharmacotherapy

subtopic_detail: EPDS interpretation with active suicidal ideation
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 30-year-old woman for her 6 week postnatal check. She lives with her partner and their first baby, who was born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy and vaginal birth.

She reports she is exhausted and tearful most days but says she is coping. On completion of the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale in the waiting room she scores 16, and item 10 (the self-harm item) is answered as sometimes.

She takes no regular medications and has no personal history of psychiatric illness. Her mother had postnatal depression treated by her general practitioner. She is breastfeeding her baby without difficulty.

data_table.History: Nil past psychiatric history; mother had postnatal depression
data_table.Support: Partner and grandparents involved; baby breastfeeding well; term vaginal birth

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her assessment?

options.text: Advise her to wean the baby from breastfeeding first before any mental health intervention or medication
Commence sertraline 50 mg orally daily immediately because sertraline has the lowest breast milk transfer among SSRIs
Reassure her that scores under 20 are consistent with the baby blues and rescreen with EPDS at 3 months
Refer to the perinatal psychiatry outpatient clinic in 4 weeks' time without any further assessment today
Undertake a structured suicide risk assessment now, including detail of self-harm thoughts, before treatment

subtopic_detail: NMS versus serotonin syndrome discrimination
stem: A 42-year-old man with schizophrenia has been unwell for 3 days. His depot flupenthixol dose was increased two weeks ago and olanzapine 10 mg at night added. He is confused and diaphoretic.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 132/min, BP 168/98 mmHg, temperature 40.1 degrees C
data_table.Neuromuscular: Lead-pipe rigidity in four limbs, reflexes 2+, no clonus, normal pupils
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 12 400 U/L (30-190), creatinine 168 micromol/L

lead_in: What is the diagnosis and first specific intervention?

options.text: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome: cease antipsychotics, cool, intensive care
Serotonin syndrome: cease serotonergic agents, give cyproheptadine 12 mg
Anticholinergic delirium: give intravenous physostigmine 1 mg
Malignant hyperthermia: give intravenous dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg
Acute dystonic reaction: give intramuscular benzatropine 2 mg

subtopic_detail: Clozapine neutropenia management
stem:
You are the community psychiatry registrar reviewing a 38-year-old man with treatment resistant schizophrenia stabilised on clozapine 400 mg orally at night for 3 years. He attends monthly clozapine monitoring bloods without missed reviews.

Today's full blood count reports a neutrophil count of 1.2 x10^9/L (2.0-7.5) with a total white cell count of 3.1 x10^9/L and normal haemoglobin and platelets. His previous monthly counts have been within normal limits. He is otherwise well, has no fever or infective symptoms, and has not travelled overseas recently.

He asks whether he needs to stop his clozapine today.

data_table.Clozapine dose: 400 mg orally at night for 3 years without dose change
data_table.Bloods today: Neutrophils 1.2 x10^9/L (2.0-7.5); WCC 3.1 x10^9/L; haemoglobin and platelets within normal limits
data_table.Symptoms: No fever; no infective symptoms; no recent overseas travel

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step according to the Australian Clozapine Monitoring Protocol?

options.text: Cease clozapine immediately and admit for haematology review because neutrophils below 1.5 x10^9/L represent the red zone
Continue clozapine at the current dose and repeat full blood count twice weekly until neutrophils return above 1.5 x10^9/L
Reduce clozapine dose by 50% and repeat the count in 2 weeks with return to standard monthly monitoring
Continue clozapine at the current dose and continue monthly monitoring because the patient is asymptomatic
Give filgrastim 300 microgram subcutaneous today to raise neutrophils before further blood counts are taken

subtopic_detail: Skin picking with specimens brought to the consultation by an older patient
stem: A 67-year-old woman referred from dermatology has picked at her forearms for eight months. She brings a container of skin flakes and states with complete conviction that mites are burrowing under her skin and laying eggs. Her husband has no symptoms.

data_table.Examination: Excoriations only where she can reach, no burrows, orientation and memory intact
data_table.Investigations: Skin scrapings negative twice

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Persistent delusional disorder with a fixed belief of skin infestation
Excoriation disorder as a body focused repetitive behaviour
Somatic symptom disorder with disproportionate health anxiety
Undiagnosed neurocognitive disorder with a secondary psychosis
Substance induced psychotic disorder with tactile disturbance

subtopic_detail: Recurrent winter depression in a patient who relocated to a high latitude Australian city
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar seeing a 33-year-old woman who moved from Cairns to Hobart four years ago for work. For the past three winters she has developed low mood, profound fatigue, sleeping ten to eleven hours a night, craving carbohydrate and gaining around 5 kg, with full remission each spring.

She has never had an episode outside the winter months and has never had a period of elevated mood, reduced need for sleep or increased goal directed activity. She describes her current episode as moderate, is working with reduced efficiency, and has no suicidal ideation and no psychotic features. Her thyroid function, full blood count, iron studies and vitamin D are normal. She is not pregnant and takes no medication. It is currently late May and she asks what will give her the best chance of getting through this winter.

data_table.Examination: Reactive but subdued affect, psychomotor activity mildly reduced, no psychotic features, cognition intact, no suicidal ideation
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone 2.0 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), haemoglobin 132 g/L (115-155), ferritin 68 micrograms/L (30-200), 25-hydroxyvitamin D 62 nmol/L (greater than 50)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment?

options.text: Referral for cognitive behavioural therapy adapted for seasonal depression as the sole initial intervention
Bright light therapy of adequate intensity used each morning soon after waking through the winter months
High dose colecalciferol supplementation through the winter with repeat measurement of her vitamin D level
A selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor commenced now and continued as maintenance treatment year round
Melatonin taken in the early evening to correct the circadian phase delay underlying the winter symptoms

subtopic_detail: First offence shoplifting in late middle age with personality change reported by family
stem: A 58-year-old school principal is charged with shoplifting after taking goods in full view of supermarket staff. Over two years his wife reports increasing bluntness and rudeness, laughing at others' distress, compulsive sweet eating with 11 kg weight gain, and insistence on the same meal daily.

data_table.Examination: Disinhibited and facetious, no low mood, memory intact, fluency five animals in one minute
data_table.Investigations: Cognitive screen 28/30, bloods and B12 normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Assess for a first manic episode given disinhibition
Provide a court report attributing this to stress
Arrange neuroimaging and neuropsychological assessment
Diagnose kleptomania and refer for cognitive therapy
Start an antidepressant for late onset depression

subtopic_detail: Late onset depression with executive slowing and extensive white matter change on imaging
stem: A 74-year-old man has had a first depressive episode for eighteen months, unchanged after sertraline 200 mg daily and then mirtazapine 45 mg nightly, each for four months. He is slowed rather than sad, needing prompting to start anything. He has hypertension, type 2 diabetes and a previous transient ischaemic attack.

data_table.Magnetic resonance imaging: Confluent white matter hyperintensities with lacunes
data_table.Neuropsychology: Impaired initiation and processing speed, memory preserved

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start a cholinesterase inhibitor for emerging dementia
Refer now for electroconvulsive therapy instead
Add low dose aripiprazole as augmentation
Optimise vascular risk and add behavioural activation
Switch to nortriptyline with drug level monitoring

subtopic_detail: Adolescent unable to wake for school who sleeps normally on holidays and has failed antidepressant treatment
stem: A 16-year-old girl on fluoxetine 20 mg daily for five months for presumed depression is no better. She cannot fall asleep before 3 am however early she goes to bed, and cannot be roused before 11 am for school. On holidays, keeping those hours, she felt well. Melatonin 5 mg at 10 pm for two months has failed.

data_table.Actigraphy: 8 hours sleep on free days, 4.5 on school days

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Increase the fluoxetine to 40 mg each day
Increase the melatonin to 10 mg nightly
Refer for treatment of her school refusal
Prescribe a sedating antihistamine nightly
Move melatonin earlier and add bright morning light

subtopic_detail: Recurrent hair pulling with visible loss and mounting tension before pulling
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar seeing a 19-year-old woman referred by her general practitioner with patchy hair loss on the scalp. She admits she pulls hair out, mostly while studying at night, and has done so for four years.

She describes a building sense of tension before pulling and relief immediately afterwards, and says she often does not register having started. She has begun wearing a beanie indoors and has stopped going to the gym because of the visible bald patches. She has no fixed belief that anything is living in her scalp, no intrusive contamination or checking thoughts, and no rituals. She has never eaten the hair. Her mood is generally reactive and she denies persistent low mood, sleeps adequately and continues at university. Examination shows irregular patches of broken hairs of differing lengths with no scaling, no scarring and no inflammation.

data_table.Examination: Irregular scalp patches with hairs broken at varying lengths, no scale, no erythema, no scarring alopecia, eyebrows and eyelashes intact
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, iron studies and thyroid function all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment?

options.text: Supportive counselling with advice to keep her hands occupied and to reduce her overall study related stress
Habit reversal training delivered as a structured behavioural program with awareness and competing response work
A selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor titrated to the higher dose range used in obsessive compulsive disorder
A low dose antipsychotic prescribed to reduce the compulsive quality of the behaviour she describes
Referral to dermatology for scalp biopsy and topical treatment of the areas of visible hair loss

subtopic_detail: Intense yearning and preoccupation with a deceased spouse more than a year after the death
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar seeing a 61-year-old woman fifteen months after her husband died of pancreatic cancer. Her daughter has brought her because she has left his clothes hanging in the wardrobe, talks to his photograph for hours daily and has not returned to the choir she led for twenty years.

She describes an unrelenting ache to be with him and says she cannot accept that he is gone, replaying the days before his death repeatedly. She feels her own life has no purpose without him but says clearly that she does not want to die and would never harm herself. She has not lost weight, describes her appetite as reasonable, and enjoys her grandchildren's visits while feeling guilty afterwards for having enjoyed them. She sleeps six hours most nights and has no diurnal variation of mood, no psychomotor slowing and no pervasive anhedonia.

data_table.Examination: Tearful when speaking of her husband, reactive affect with grandchildren mentioned, normal psychomotor activity, no perceptual disturbance, cognition intact
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, urea and electrolytes, thyroid function and vitamin B12 all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Prescribe a short course of a benzodiazepine to help her tolerate the distress of sorting his belongings
Arrange neuropsychological assessment given her withdrawal from a long standing leadership role in the choir
Refer for a structured grief focused psychological therapy and arrange regular review of her progress
Start a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor and review the response to treatment after six weeks
Reassure her daughter that this is normal bereavement and that no specific intervention is required now

subtopic_detail: Long standing difficulty initiating and maintaining sleep with daytime consequences
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 44-year-old accountant who has struggled to sleep for two years, taking around ninety minutes to fall asleep and lying awake for an hour or more in the early hours. He asks directly for sleeping tablets, saying a friend takes them.

He goes to bed at 9 pm to give himself the best chance and stays there until 7 am, spending much of that time checking the clock and calculating how much sleep he will get. He drinks one coffee in the morning, no alcohol, and stops screen use an hour before bed. He denies snoring and his partner reports no witnessed pauses or leg movements. His mood is not persistently low, he has no anhedonia, and he denies worry outside the bedroom. His body mass index is 24 kg per square metre and thyroid function and iron studies are normal.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 24 kg per square metre, Mallampati class 2, no goitre, normal mental state examination with euthymic reactive affect
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone 1.5 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), ferritin 110 micrograms/L (30-300), haemoglobin 148 g/L (130-170)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment?

options.text: Low dose amitriptyline taken nightly for its sedating effect with review of tolerance after one month
Prolonged release melatonin taken two hours before bed with advice to maintain his current bedtime routine
Referral for overnight polysomnography to exclude an underlying primary sleep disorder before treatment
Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia including sleep restriction and stimulus control components
A short-acting benzodiazepine receptor agonist prescribed nightly for four weeks with a planned taper

subtopic_detail: Multiple motor and vocal tics with a premonitory urge in an adolescent
stem:
You are the child and adolescent psychiatry registrar seeing a 14-year-old boy whose mother is distressed by his blinking, head jerking and repeated throat clearing. These began at seven, wax and wane, and have never been absent for more than a few weeks at a time.

He describes an uncomfortable building feeling in his neck and throat that is relieved once the movement happens, and he can hold the tics back for a few minutes in class before they come out in a burst afterwards. He is doing well academically, has friends, and is not bothered by the tics himself, though he is embarrassed when they occur during oral presentations. He has no obsessions, no compulsions and no attentional difficulties reported by teachers. His neurological examination is normal and he takes no medication or stimulant.

data_table.Examination: Frequent eye blinking, head jerking and throat clearing observed during interview, suppressible briefly on request, normal tone power reflexes and coordination, no chorea, no dystonia
data_table.Investigations: No investigations performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Start a low dose antipsychotic such as risperidone and titrate according to the frequency of the tics
Advise him to suppress the tics whenever possible in public so that the habit gradually extinguishes itself
Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the brain with copper studies to investigate a secondary cause of tics
Start clonidine at low dose in the evening and increase gradually while monitoring his blood pressure
Psychoeducation for the family and school with referral for a behavioural therapy program for tics

subtopic_detail: Fluctuating inattention and withdrawal after hip surgery mistaken for low mood in an older patient
stem: An 84-year-old woman is day three after hemiarthroplasty. The team asks about an antidepressant because she is withdrawn, tearful and not participating with physiotherapy. Her daughter says she was managing her own finances a fortnight ago. She takes regular oxycodone.

data_table.Examination: Fluctuating attention, cannot recite months backwards, awake overnight, drowsy by day, palpable bladder, no bowel motion since surgery

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start mirtazapine at night and review her mood in two weeks
Arrange brain imaging and cognitive assessment for dementia
Start low dose risperidone to settle the disturbed nights
Start temazepam at night to restore her sleep pattern
Treat the urinary retention and constipation, review the opioid

subtopic_detail: Psychosis that outlasts the mood episode by several weeks in someone with recurrent mania
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 31-year-old woman on an inpatient unit. Over her seven year history she has had three manic episodes and two depressive episodes, each with persecutory delusions and auditory hallucinations that were present only while her mood was disturbed.

During this admission her mania resolved five weeks ago and her mood has been euthymic on objective rating for four weeks, with normal sleep, normal energy and no grandiosity. She nevertheless continues to hear two voices commenting on her actions and remains convinced that staff are relaying information about her to a government agency. Her urine drug screen is negative on three occasions, her thyroid function and inflammatory markers are normal, and magnetic resonance imaging of the brain is unremarkable. She is adherent with her medication and has not taken corticosteroids.

data_table.Examination: Euthymic mood with normal sleep and energy, no pressure of speech, persistent third person auditory hallucinations and persecutory delusions
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen negative on three occasions, thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, C reactive protein less than 5 mg/L, magnetic resonance imaging of the brain unremarkable

lead_in: Which diagnosis best fits her presentation?

options.text: Delusional disorder, persecutory type, given the fixed and circumscribed belief that staff are reporting on her
Bipolar I disorder with psychotic features, given the recurrent manic episodes that have dominated her seven year history
Schizophrenia, given the persistent third person auditory hallucinations and systematised persecutory beliefs
Schizoaffective disorder, bipolar type, given psychosis persisting well beyond the resolution of the mood episode
Substance induced psychotic disorder, given that stimulant use commonly produces persecutory beliefs of this kind

subtopic_detail: Falling phosphate on the third day of nutritional rehabilitation in a severely underweight patient
stem: A 19-year-old woman with anorexia nervosa at a body mass index of 12.8 kg/m2 began nasogastric feeding three days ago. She is mildly breathless with trace ankle oedema. Thiamine was given before feeding and continues daily.

data_table.Investigations: Phosphate 0.52 mmol/L, fallen from 1.12 on admission (0.75-1.50), magnesium 0.62 mmol/L (0.70-1.10), potassium 3.1 mmol/L (3.5-5.2)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Stop the feed until the phosphate has normalised
Replace phosphate orally and increase the feed rate
Replace phosphate and thiamine, increase the feed rate
Replace phosphate, magnesium and potassium, reduce the feed
Replace phosphate, add a loop diuretic, continue feeding

subtopic_detail: Intrusive images of harming the baby that the mother finds abhorrent and acts to avoid
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar called to the maternity ward to see a 29-year-old woman five weeks after the birth of her first baby, referred urgently because she told the child health nurse she keeps imagining dropping the baby down the stairs.

She describes repeated unwanted images of the baby being harmed, which arrive unbidden many times a day and cause her intense distress and shame. She finds them abhorrent and has asked her partner to carry the baby up and down stairs and has stopped bathing the baby alone. She has no delusions, no hallucinations, no thought disorder and no elevated or irritable mood, sleeps when the baby sleeps, and her insight is fully preserved. She has never wanted to harm the baby and is frightened that admitting this will mean the baby is taken from her. She is breastfeeding and there is no substance use.

data_table.Examination: Anxious and tearful, fully oriented, no psychotic phenomena, insight preserved, appropriate attachment behaviour with the baby
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count within normal limits, thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, ferritin 42 micrograms/L (15-200), urine drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Explain the nature of the symptoms, keep mother and baby together, and arrange cognitive behavioural therapy with a serotonergic antidepressant
Make an immediate child protection notification and arrange supervised contact while the risk is formally assessed
Arrange urgent admission to a psychiatric unit without the baby and start an antipsychotic for postpartum psychosis
Advise weaning so that a benzodiazepine can be started for her anxiety, with psychological therapy arranged afterwards
Provide reassurance alone and arrange general practice review in four weeks, treating this as a normal adjustment reaction

subtopic_detail: Sequencing trauma focused work for a resettled refugee living with ongoing family separation
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar seeing a 38-year-old man who arrived in Australia two years ago on a temporary protection visa after imprisonment and torture in his country of origin. He was referred by his general practitioner for headaches, back pain and insomnia for which no physical cause has been found.

Through an interpreter he describes nightmares most nights, being startled by doors closing, and avoiding the news. His wife and two children remain overseas in a camp and he has not been able to speak with them for two months. His visa is due for review in four months and he cannot work. He denies suicidal intent but says life feels pointless when he cannot protect his family. He drinks no alcohol, uses no drugs, and his physical examination and screening bloods are normal.

data_table.Examination: Guarded but engaged through an interpreter, low mood with reactive affect, no psychotic features, no current suicidal intent or plan
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count within normal limits, thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, vitamin D 58 nmol/L (50-150), urine drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial approach?

options.text: Stabilisation with practical advocacy, sleep and pain management and psychoeducation, before starting trauma-focused therapy
Refer him to a generic community mental health service and use a family member as interpreter to speed up assessment
Begin weekly trauma-focused cognitive behavioural therapy with imaginal exposure to the detention experiences immediately
Prescribe a short course of a benzodiazepine for his insomnia and startle response, and review him in four weeks
Start a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor alone and review in six weeks, deferring any psychological therapy

subtopic_detail: Persistent yearning thirteen months after a spouse died with preserved capacity for pleasure
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 68-year-old woman whose husband died of bowel cancer thirteen months ago. She has come in for a routine appointment and, when asked how she is coping, says she thinks about him for most of the day and still keeps his voicemail greeting on her phone so that she can hear his voice.

She has not entered his study since the funeral and has turned down two invitations from her walking group because going without him feels like a betrayal. She sleeps about five hours a night and has lost 3 kg. She still looks forward to her granddaughter's Saturday swimming lessons and enjoys them when she is there, and she does not feel that she has failed anyone or that she is a burden. She has no thoughts of harming herself, although she says she would not mind if she did not wake up one morning.

data_table.Examination: Tearful when speaking about her husband, affect reactive to other topics, no psychomotor retardation, Mini-Mental State Examination 29 out of 30
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone 1.9 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), full blood count and electrolytes within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start sertraline 50 mg daily with weekly phone review and reassess at four weeks
Refer for grief focused cognitive behavioural therapy and reassess at four weeks
Refer for eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing and reassess at four weeks
Advise that this is within the expected range and reassess her at four weeks
Start mirtazapine 15 mg at night with weekly phone review and reassess at four weeks

subtopic_detail: Sleep attacks with knee buckling during laughter in a student referred as treatment resistant low mood
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar seeing a 19-year-old engineering student referred with low mood that has not responded to two antidepressants at adequate dose and duration. He describes being exhausted all day, falling asleep in lectures and once while eating dinner, despite sleeping nine hours overnight.

His mood lifts when he is with friends and he still enjoys gaming and football, and there has been no change in appetite or weight. He mentions, when asked what happens when he laughs hard, that his knees buckle and his jaw sags for about twenty seconds while he stays fully aware of what is going on around him. As he is falling asleep he sometimes sees people in the room who are not there. He drives forty minutes each way to campus.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 68 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 23 kg/m2, no tonsillar hypertrophy, neurological examination normal, Epworth Sleepiness Scale 19 out of 24
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone 2.2 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), ferritin 88 micrograms/L (30-300), full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Switch to a noradrenergic antidepressant and review his energy in four weeks
Start modafinil 100 mg each morning and review his daytime sleepiness in four weeks
Arrange overnight oximetry and refer for consideration of continuous positive airway pressure
Refer for overnight polysomnography followed by a multiple sleep latency test
Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia and a two week sleep diary

subtopic_detail: Hair pulling with a patch of scalp thinning and relief on pulling in a university student
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 20-year-old woman who has noticed a thinning patch at the right crown of her scalp over the past six months. She admits, once asked directly, that she pulls hairs out one at a time while reading and while watching television, mostly in the evenings.

She describes a mounting tension before she pulls and a settling of that tension afterwards, and she has tried to stop several times without success. She does not believe anything is living in her scalp, has no checking, washing or ordering rituals, and does not examine her appearance repeatedly in mirrors. She is embarrassed enough to part her hair differently but has not withdrawn from friends or study.

data_table.Examination: A 4 cm patch of reduced hair density at the right crown containing hairs of many different lengths, no scaling, no erythema, no scarring, no broken hairs elsewhere, eyebrows and eyelashes intact
data_table.Investigations: Ferritin 64 micrograms/L (30-300), thyroid stimulating hormone 1.6 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line management?

options.text: Refer for habit reversal training and review her scalp in eight weeks
Start fluoxetine 20 mg daily and review her scalp in eight weeks
Start N acetylcysteine 1200 mg twice daily and review her scalp in eight weeks
Refer to a dermatologist for scalp biopsy and review the result in eight weeks
Start olanzapine 2.5 mg at night and review her scalp in eight weeks

subtopic_detail: Parents seeking clinical information after an adult son with first episode psychosis refuses consent to share
stem:
You are the registrar in an early psychosis service caring for a 21-year-old man who is three weeks into treatment for a first episode of psychosis. He is a voluntary patient, his persecutory beliefs have receded, and a formal assessment two days ago found him able to understand, retain, weigh and communicate decisions about his care. He has asked the team in writing not to discuss anything about him with his parents, with whom he lives.

His mother telephones you. She does the shopping, prompts him about his tablets each evening and drives him to appointments. She asks what is wrong with him, what the tablets are and what she should be watching for, and adds that she found a syringe in the bathroom bin this morning.

data_table.Examination: Settled in manner, no thought disorder, no current delusional beliefs elicited, no extrapyramidal signs, insight partial
data_table.Investigations: Capacity assessment documented as intact two days ago, urine drug screen at admission positive for cannabis only, full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate response to the mother?

options.text: Decline any contact with her until her son provides written consent to share information
Confirm his diagnosis and medication to her because she is his main practical carer
Listen to her concerns, and give general information about psychosis and carer supports
Ask him again next week and telephone her with an answer once he has decided
Invite her to a family meeting and set out his treatment plan there without asking him

subtopic_detail: Choosing the delivery mode of psychological treatment for moderate depression in a fly in fly out worker
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 41-year-old man who works a two weeks on, one week off roster at an iron ore mine in the Pilbara and flies home to Perth for his week off. For three months he has had low mood most days, poor concentration at work and early waking, with a Patient Health Questionnaire 9 score of 15.

He drinks six standard drinks on two or three nights during his week at home and none on site. He has no thoughts of self-harm, no history of elevated mood, and no psychotic features. He tells you his brother had a bad time coming off an antidepressant and that he does not want tablets. His camp has reliable internet in the donga and a quiet room he can use after shift.

data_table.Examination: Reduced spontaneous speech, restricted affect, no psychomotor retardation, no cognitive deficit on bedside testing
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone 2.4 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), gamma glutamyl transferase 38 units/L (less than 60), full blood count and electrolytes within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Prepare a mental health treatment plan and refer for video delivered cognitive behavioural therapy
Prepare a mental health treatment plan and refer for face to face sessions during his weeks at home
Recommend a self guided internet program and review his symptom score in twelve weeks
Recommend a structured exercise program and review his symptom score in twelve weeks
Negotiate a trial of an antidepressant and review his symptom score in four weeks

subtopic_detail: Persistent sense of watching himself from outside four months after stopping heavy cannabis use
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 23-year-old apprentice who stopped daily cannabis four months ago after a frightening episode of palpitations and breathlessness while smoking. Since that night he has felt, in his words, like he is watching himself in a film and operating his own body by remote control.

Colours look flat to him and familiar rooms seem staged, as though nothing is quite solid. He knows none of this is actually true and finds that reassuring and maddening at the same time. He has had no voices, no beliefs that others are controlling him and no sense that thoughts are being put into his head. He has started refusing shifts on the customer counter because he is afraid someone will see that something is wrong with him.

data_table.Examination: Anxious, fully oriented, no thought disorder, no perceptual abnormality elicited, neurological examination normal
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen negative, thyroid stimulating hormone 1.4 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), full blood count and electrolytes within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start risperidone 1 mg at night and review his perceptual symptoms in four weeks
Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and an electroencephalogram
Start propranolol 20 mg twice daily and review his perceptual symptoms in four weeks
Reassure him that the symptoms are a withdrawal effect and review him in six months
Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy targeting symptom monitoring and avoidance

subtopic_detail: Short day sleep and racing thoughts four weeks into a run of night shifts in an emergency nurse
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 34-year-old emergency department nurse who is four weeks into a block of night shifts. She sleeps about four hours during the day, lies awake feeling wired at four in the morning on shift, snaps at her partner, and has been buying things online at three in the morning that she does not need.

She says her thoughts feel fast and jumbled, but when asked she describes herself as worn out rather than energised and says what she wants most is more sleep. There is no history of elevated mood, no grandiosity, no increase in goal directed activity and no reduction in her perceived need for sleep. On her five days off at the end of the previous block she slept eight hours a night and everything settled within two days. Her bedroom faces east and has thin curtains, and her neighbour is renovating.

data_table.Examination: Tired in appearance, normal rate and rhythm of speech, affect reactive, no flight of ideas, no psychotic features
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone 2.0 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), full blood count and electrolytes within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start lithium and arrange a serum concentration measurement after five days
Start quetiapine 100 mg before her day sleep and review her mood in two weeks
Advise a fixed sleep schedule with timed light exposure and a dark bedroom
Start temazepam 10 mg before her day sleep and review her sleep in two weeks
Refer urgently to the mental health service for assessment of elevated mood

subtopic_detail: Blocked hallways and inability to discard possessions after a fire service safety notice
stem:
You are the general practitioner visiting a 71-year-old widow at home after the fire service attended a smoke complaint and issued a safety notice. Newspapers, containers and clothing are stacked chest high through the house, with a single narrow path between rooms, the kitchen bench and stove are not usable, and she sleeps in an armchair.

She agrees that the fire risk is real and says she is ashamed of the state of the house, but becomes visibly distressed when you pick up an empty ice cream container, explaining that she may need it. She has no beliefs that the items are alive or contaminated and no voices. Her daughter cleared the lounge room two years ago while she was in hospital; the room refilled within four months and they did not speak for a year afterwards. She manages her own banking and medications without error.

data_table.Examination: Well kempt and well nourished, no squalor and no animals, Mini-Mental State Examination 28 out of 30, no delusions elicited, distress on handling of possessions
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone 2.6 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), vitamin B12 420 pmol/L (150-700), full blood count and electrolytes within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Arrange a forced clean out with the council and review her at home in three months
Refer for hoarding specific cognitive behavioural therapy with a case manager
Start fluvoxamine 100 mg daily and review her living conditions in three months
Arrange neuropsychological testing and brain imaging to look for cognitive decline
Apply for a guardianship order to allow decisions about her accommodation

subtopic_detail: Aerosol propellant inhalation in a fifteen year old with a rash around the mouth and falling grades
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 15-year-old boy brought in by his mother, who found a dozen empty deodorant cans under his bed. Over three months his grades have dropped from good to failing and he has stopped going to football.

She describes him coming home some afternoons unsteady on his feet with slurred speech that clears within about an hour, and she has noticed a chemical smell on his clothes. He is guarded but eventually says he does it with two friends behind the shops because it is free and quick. There are no injection marks and no tremor. He denies alcohol and cannabis and his breath alcohol reading today is zero.
