data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78 beats per minute, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Erythematous cracked skin around the mouth and nostrils, conjunctival injection, no needle marks, gait normal today, no cerebellar signs
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen negative, sodium 139 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 4.0 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), alanine aminotransferase 28 units/L (5-35), full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start naltrexone 50 mg daily and refer him to a youth drug and alcohol service
Arrange an urgent blood lead concentration and start chelation if the level is raised
Start nicotine replacement and refer him to a youth drug and alcohol service
Notify child protection services and arrange an involuntary admission today
Refer him to a youth drug and alcohol service and involve his parents in the plan

subtopic_detail: Night time fall at home in a 70 year old taking temazepam every night for eight years
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 70-year-old woman who fell getting up to the toilet two nights ago. She grazed her elbow, there was no fracture and she did not lose consciousness.

She has taken temazepam 20 mg every night for eight years, started during the months after her husband died, and she also takes amlodipine. She tells you the tablet does not really work any more but that she lies awake for hours if she misses it, and she has come in today mainly to make sure the script does not run out. She lives alone, still drives during the day and does her own shopping. She remembers the fall clearly and describes feeling groggy and slow on her feet rather than dizzy or faint.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72 beats per minute, blood pressure 132/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: No postural drop on lying and standing measurement, normal gait and tandem walk, no cerebellar or peripheral neurological signs, visual acuity corrected to 6/9 bilaterally
data_table.Investigations: Electrocardiogram sinus rhythm with normal intervals, vitamin B12 380 pmol/L (150-700), creatinine 74 micromol/L (45-90), full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of her medication?

options.text: Switch her to zopiclone at an equivalent dose and review her sleep in four weeks
Stop the temazepam now and start melatonin, reviewing her sleep in four weeks
Continue the current dose and reassess her falls risk again in twelve months
Reduce the temazepam by a quarter of the dose every two weeks with sleep advice
Convert her to diazepam and reduce that gradually over the next three months

subtopic_detail: Cyclical irritability confined to the ten days before menses with a symptom free follicular phase
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 29-year-old primary school teacher who describes two years of irritability, tearfulness, breast tenderness and bloating that begin about ten days before each period and settle within two days of the bleeding starting.

She has received two formal complaints at work about how she spoke to colleagues, both in the week before a period, and she is frightened of losing her job. A prospective daily symptom record kept over three cycles shows a rating of zero on most days between the end of bleeding and mid cycle, with scores rising steeply from day eighteen. She has migraine with visual aura about twice a month. She uses condoms for contraception and has no intrauterine device in place. She has no thoughts of self-harm.

data_table.Examination: Euthymic and pleasant at this mid follicular visit, affect full range, no psychomotor change, body mass index 24 kg/m2
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone 1.7 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), haemoglobin 128 g/L (115-155), ferritin 42 micrograms/L (30-300)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line pharmacological treatment?

options.text: Sertraline 50 mg taken from day fourteen of the cycle until menstruation starts
A combined oral contraceptive containing drospirenone taken continuously
Micronised progesterone 200 mg nightly during the second half of the cycle
A gonadotrophin releasing hormone agonist with oestrogen and progestogen add back
Evening primrose oil 1000 mg twice daily through the second half of the cycle

subtopic_detail: Agitation with racing thoughts and three hours of sleep three weeks after starting an antidepressant
stem: A 27-year-old woman is reviewed three weeks after starting escitalopram 10 mg daily for depression. She now sleeps three hours a night, feels revved up and miserable, with racing thoughts and new self-harm thoughts. She denies elation. At 22 she had a fortnight of sleeping little and painting all night. Her mother takes lithium.

data_table.Examination: Restless, pressured speech, dysphoric affect
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid function and urine drug screen normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Increase the escitalopram to 20 mg daily
Add diazepam 5 mg twice daily for agitation
Add zolpidem at night and review her sleep
Stop the escitalopram and start quetiapine
Switch to mirtazapine 30 mg at night

subtopic_detail: Punching and shouting in the second half of the night in a veteran assumed to have trauma nightmares
stem: A 64-year-old veteran has shouted, kicked and punched in his sleep for eighteen months, bruising his wife last month. Episodes occur in the early hours; he wakes immediately lucid describing dreams of fighting an intruder, none involving his service. He has two years of constipation and cannot smell whether food has turned.

data_table.Examination: Reduced right arm swing, no resting tremor
data_table.History: Post-traumatic stress disorder treated ten years ago, checklist non-clinical

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start prazosin at night for the nightmares
Refer for polysomnography and make the bedroom safe
Restart trauma-focused psychological therapy
Start quetiapine at night for the behaviour
Arrange an electroencephalogram to exclude seizures

subtopic_detail: New online gambling debt and uncharacteristic sexual behaviour in a man treated for restless legs
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 58-year-old plumber who attends with his wife. She has discovered sixty thousand dollars of debt accumulated through online sports betting over the past eight months, on accounts he opened without telling her.

He has never gambled before, not even on a work sweepstake, and he is tearful and ashamed in the room. She adds that he has been shopping compulsively online and that his sexual demands have changed in a way she finds distressing. He says he has tried to stop several times and cannot. He denies feeling elated or unusually confident, says he sleeps his usual seven hours and needs them, and has taken no new substances. His pramipexole for restless legs was increased six months ago because the symptoms had spread to his arms, and he also takes atorvastatin.

data_table.Examination: Dysphoric and tearful, normal rate of speech, no flight of ideas, no grandiosity, no psychotic features, Montreal Cognitive Assessment 29 out of 30
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone 1.8 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), ferritin 58 micrograms/L (30-300), liver function and electrolytes within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer him to a gambling counselling service and continue his current treatment
Start naltrexone daily and refer him to a gambling counselling service
Start sodium valproate and refer him to a gambling counselling service
Stop the pramipexole abruptly tonight and refer him to a gambling counselling service
Withdraw the pramipexole slowly and refer him to a gambling counselling service

subtopic_detail: Silence at school with loud fluent speech at home in a six year old in her second year of schooling
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 6-year-old girl whose teacher has told her parents she may need an autism assessment. In fourteen months at school she has never spoken a word to a teacher or to another child, communicating by nodding, pointing and writing.

At home she talks constantly, argues with her older brother, invents elaborate games with her cousins and does impressions of her teacher that make the family laugh. Her mother reports that she chats in the car right up to the school gate and then stops. In the consulting room she sits close to her mother, makes eye contact with you, smiles at a joke, and freezes and looks at the floor when you ask her a direct question. She reached all her language milestones on time and has no repetitive behaviours, no restricted interests and no sensory aversions. Her father describes himself as having been painfully shy as a boy.

data_table.Examination: Reciprocal eye contact and shared smiling with her mother and with the examiner, imaginative play observed with the toys, freezing and averted gaze on direct questioning, no dysmorphic features
data_table.Investigations: Audiology assessment normal bilaterally, speech pathology screen of receptive language age appropriate, full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer for a formal autism spectrum assessment and review her after the report
Refer for a speech pathology assessment of expressive language delay
Refer for a behavioural program using graded speaking exposure at school
Start fluoxetine and review her speaking at school in eight weeks
Advise the school to avoid asking her direct questions for a term

subtopic_detail: Abrupt onset of complex tic like movements over two days in a seventeen year old with no childhood history
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar assessing a 17-year-old student whose movements began over two days six weeks ago and have escalated since. She flings both arms outwards, slaps her own sternum, and shouts obscene phrases in an accent that is not her own.

Her mother says the phrases are word for word the ones used by a creator she watches for several hours each night on a video sharing platform. The movements are continuous through the consultation, worsen markedly when the medical students enter, and stop entirely for around a minute when you ask her to copy a two handed tapping rhythm. She reports no warning sensation before a movement and says she cannot hold them back even briefly. She had no tics as a child, and an anxiety disorder was diagnosed a year ago.

data_table.Examination: Complex bilateral flinging movements with self striking, entrainment of the movements to an imposed tapping rhythm, no stereotyped simple motor tics, normal tone power and reflexes, no chorea
data_table.Investigations: Copper studies and caeruloplasmin within normal limits, thyroid stimulating hormone 1.6 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), full blood count and electrolytes within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start aripiprazole and review the frequency of the movements in four weeks
Explain the positive diagnosis and refer for tailored psychological therapy
Start clonidine and review the frequency of the movements in four weeks
Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and review her with the result
Refer for botulinum toxin injection to the most affected muscle groups

subtopic_detail: Nightmares and hypervigilance in a man on a bridging visa awaiting a protection decision with no income
stem:
You are the general practitioner at a community health service seeing a 34-year-old man who arrived by boat six years ago and has been on a bridging visa for three years. A professional interpreter attends in person at his request.

He describes nightmares most nights, waking sweating, intrusive daytime memories of being beaten in custody in his home country, startling at doors closing, and avoiding the news. He has no work rights at present, is sleeping on a friend's couch after being asked to leave his room, and has not seen his wife and daughter for six years. His protection application is awaiting a decision and he says he cannot think past it. He denies thoughts of suicide, has no psychotic symptoms and asks you for sleeping tablets so that he can rest.

data_table.Examination: Guarded and watchful, startles when the door closes, well oriented, no psychotic features, healed scarring over both shins
data_table.Investigations: Vitamin D 38 nmol/L (50-150), haemoglobin 141 g/L (130-175), thyroid stimulating hormone 2.3 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), electrolytes within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start diazepam at night and review his sleep in two weeks with the interpreter
Begin trauma-focused exposure therapy at weekly sessions without further delay
Start mirtazapine at night and review his sleep in two weeks with the interpreter
Defer any mental health treatment until his visa application has been decided
Refer to a specialist torture and trauma service and address housing and income

subtopic_detail: A written advance care directive naming a preferred antipsychotic during a NSW involuntary admission
stem: A 38-year-old carpenter with bipolar disorder is an involuntary patient in NSW. He has not slept for four nights, speaks continuously, spent most of his savings and refuses food, fluids and medication. Eight months ago, while well, he signed an advance care directive declining olanzapine after gaining 18 kg, accepting aripiprazole, and naming his sister as designated carer. Aripiprazole is suitable and available.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118 bpm, BP 142/84 mmHg, temperature 37.2 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 146 mmol/L, creatinine 102 micromol/L, creatine kinase 380 units/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate course of action?

options.text: Treat with the agent he named and notify his designated carer now
Treat with olanzapine, since his directive is not binding while unwell
Apply to the Tribunal for a ruling before giving any antipsychotic medication
Withhold all antipsychotic medication because he is currently refusing treatment
Treat with olanzapine and record your reasons for departing from it

subtopic_detail: A fifth emergency presentation this year with superficial forearm cuts after a relationship ended
stem:
You are the emergency registrar seeing a 24-year-old woman who arrived at eleven at night with parallel superficial cuts to the left forearm made with a craft knife after her partner ended their relationship. None require suturing and there is no tendon or nerve involvement.

This is her fifth presentation in twelve months. She has been attending a dialectical behaviour therapy program for five months and her next skills group is in three days; her therapist's crisis plan is scanned into the record and names an after hours number and two agreed strategies. She is not intoxicated and her observations are normal. Over the ninety minutes since arrival she has become notably calmer, has eaten a sandwich and now says she does not want to die and has no plan. She asks to be admitted so that she will be safe. Her two previous admissions were both complicated by escalating self injury on the ward.

data_table.Examination: Six superficial parallel forearm lacerations with no deep structure involvement, settled and coherent, no depressive psychomotor change, no psychotic features
data_table.Investigations: Breath alcohol zero, paracetamol not detected, full blood count and electrolytes within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate disposition?

options.text: Admit her overnight to the short stay unit and review her with the team tomorrow
Admit her to the psychiatric unit for a period of safety and daily review there
Follow her existing crisis plan and arrange therapist contact within two days
Give a dose of quetiapine and review her again in the department in two hours
Discharge her with advice to attend her next scheduled session in three days

subtopic_detail: Low mood and worthlessness in a woman with metastatic cancer whose prognosis is measured in weeks
stem:
You are the consultation liaison psychiatry registrar asked to see a 61-year-old woman with metastatic pancreatic cancer on the palliative care ward. The treating team estimates her prognosis at four to eight weeks and has asked about depression.

She describes three weeks of low mood present every day and all day, and says nothing lifts it, including a visit from her grandchildren which she previously looked forward to and which she found she could not enjoy at all. She says she has always been the strong one in the family and is now nothing, and that everyone would be better off if it were over. Her attention is intact, she recalls the ward routine accurately and her mental state has not fluctuated across two assessments on different days. Her pain is well controlled on a stable opioid dose and her calcium and sodium are normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88 beats per minute, blood pressure 106/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 96 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Cachectic, alert and fully oriented, months of the year backwards completed without error, no asterixis, affect uniformly flat with no reactivity
data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 2.34 mmol/L (2.10-2.60), sodium 138 mmol/L (135-145), bilirubin 14 micromol/L (less than 20), haemoglobin 102 g/L (115-155)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Start sertraline 50 mg daily and review her mood in four weeks
Start mirtazapine 15 mg at night and review her mood in four weeks
Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy and review her mood in four weeks
Start methylphenidate in the morning and review her mood in three days
Start olanzapine 2.5 mg at night and review her mood in three days

subtopic_detail: Deciding disposition after a first impulsive ingestion when a screening instrument returns a low category
stem:
You are the emergency registrar reviewing a 22-year-old apprentice electrician who swallowed fourteen paracetamol tablets in one go six hours ago, twenty minutes after his partner ended their relationship. He told his flatmate within the hour and they drove him in.

His timed paracetamol concentration sits below the treatment line and his liver enzymes and coagulation profile are normal, so the toxicology registrar has cleared him medically and no antidote is required. He says he did it without thinking, is embarrassed, does not want to die now and has no plan. He has never presented before, takes no medication, does not drink or use drugs, and his two flatmates are in the waiting room and have offered to stay with him. The department's structured screening instrument has returned a score in its lowest category, and the consultant asks you to discharge him on that basis.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 74 beats per minute, blood pressure 122/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Alert and engaged, no psychomotor change, affect reactive, no psychotic features, no self inflicted wounds
data_table.Investigations: Timed paracetamol concentration below the nomogram treatment line, alanine aminotransferase 24 units/L (5-35), international normalised ratio 1.0 (0.8-1.2), electrolytes within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Discharge him with the low risk score documented and advice to see his own doctor
Admit him to the psychiatric unit because any overdose indicates a high level of risk
Repeat the screening instrument in two hours and decide disposition on that score
Discharge him with a referral letter to a private psychologist and no further follow up
Complete a collaborative safety plan with means restriction and follow up in a week

subtopic_detail: Choosing a mood stabiliser for a young woman when the current agent carries teratogenic risk
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 24-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder who has been well for eighteen months on sodium valproate 1000 mg daily, started during an inpatient admission for mania two years ago.

She has a new partner, uses no contraception, and tells you she would like to start a family within the next year or two. She has had one manic episode and two depressive episodes, has never self harmed, and has had no episodes since valproate was started. Her full blood count, liver function and weight are stable, and she takes no other medication. She asks whether she can simply stop the valproate when she decides to try to conceive.

data_table.Examination: Euthymic mood, normal speech and thought form, no psychotic features, no suicidal ideation
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count within normal limits, liver function tests within normal limits, body mass index 26 kg/m2, urine pregnancy test negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Halve the valproate dose now and continue at that level, on the basis that the risk is dose dependent
Continue valproate with high dose folate, and stop the valproate as soon as a pregnancy test becomes positive
Continue valproate with a long-acting reversible contraceptive, and revisit the medication when she actively conceives
Stop valproate now without a replacement, and monitor her mood monthly given eighteen months of stability
Plan a cross taper from valproate to an alternative mood stabiliser now, with reliable contraception during the change

subtopic_detail: Fever and tachycardia in the third week of titration with a normal neutrophil count
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar on an inpatient unit reviewing a 27-year-old man who is on day 19 of clozapine titration for treatment resistant schizophrenia, now taking 250 mg daily.

Over the past two days he has felt feverish and tired, with a temperature of 38.3 degrees Celsius, pulse 124 beats per minute, blood pressure 104/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute and SpO2 97 percent on room air. He has no cough, no dysuria, no diarrhoea and no rash, and his chest is clear. His neutrophil count is 4.8 x10^9/L, C reactive protein 96 mg/L, and troponin is elevated at six times the upper reference limit. An electrocardiogram shows sinus tachycardia with no ST elevation. His psychotic symptoms have improved substantially on this dose.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 124 beats per minute, blood pressure 104/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temperature 38.3 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Chest clear, no murmur, no rash, no focal infective source, mild ankle oedema
data_table.Investigations: Neutrophils 4.8 x10^9/L (2.0-7.5), C reactive protein 96 mg/L (less than 5), troponin six times the upper reference limit, electrocardiogram showing sinus tachycardia, chest radiograph clear

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Continue the clozapine at a reduced dose and repeat the troponin and C reactive protein in forty eight hours
Cease the clozapine immediately and start filgrastim, treating this as a haematological adverse reaction
Cease the clozapine immediately and arrange urgent echocardiography with cardiology review
Continue the clozapine and treat with intravenous antibiotics for a presumed occult bacterial infection
Continue the clozapine and prescribe regular paracetamol, treating this as the benign fever seen during titration

subtopic_detail: Selecting cessation pharmacotherapy for a heavy smoker with stable treated depression
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 47-year-old man who wants to stop smoking. He has smoked 25 cigarettes daily for thirty years and lights his first cigarette within five minutes of waking.

He has recurrent major depressive disorder, well controlled on sertraline 100 mg daily for three years, with no episode in that time and no suicidal ideation ever. He has tried nicotine patches alone twice and relapsed within a fortnight both times. He has no seizure history, no eating disorder, drinks four standard drinks weekly, and his renal function is normal. He asks which medication gives him the best chance and whether any of them are risky given his depression.

data_table.Examination: Euthymic, no psychomotor change, chest clear, no signs of chronic lung disease
data_table.Investigations: Spirometry within normal limits, full blood count within normal limits, creatinine 78 micromol/L (60-110)

lead_in: Which pharmacotherapy would you first recommend?

options.text: Behavioural support alone through a telephone quit service, with pharmacotherapy reserved for a later attempt
Varenicline started a week before his quit date, with behavioural support and review at two and four weeks
Nicotine patch monotherapy at the highest available strength, with behavioural support and review at two weeks
Combination nicotine replacement using a patch with an oral form, with behavioural support and review at two weeks
Bupropion started a week before his quit date, with behavioural support and review at two and four weeks

subtopic_detail: Slowly declining kidney function after more than a decade of maintenance treatment
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 58-year-old man with bipolar I disorder who has taken lithium for fourteen years with excellent mood stability and no admissions in that time.

His estimated glomerular filtration rate has fallen from 78 to 52 mL/min/1.73m2 over the past five years, with the most recent two readings three months apart both at 52 and 54. His twelve hour post dose lithium level is 0.78 mmol/L, urine albumin to creatinine ratio is normal, his blood pressure is 128/76 mmHg, and renal ultrasound shows normal sized kidneys with no obstruction. He passes large volumes of dilute urine and drinks accordingly. He takes no non-steroidal anti inflammatory medication and no diuretic, and he is euthymic with no current symptoms.

data_table.Examination: Euthymic, no tremor, no ataxia, normal reflexes, no oedema
data_table.Investigations: Estimated glomerular filtration rate 52 mL/min/1.73m2 (down from 78 over five years), twelve hour lithium level 0.78 mmol/L (0.6-0.8), urine albumin to creatinine ratio normal, thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, corrected calcium 2.52 mmol/L (2.10-2.60), renal ultrasound normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Stop lithium immediately and substitute sodium valproate, given the fall in kidney function over five years
Continue lithium at a lower target level with nephrology review, and discuss the long term options with him
Add a thiazide diuretic for the polyuria and continue lithium at the current dose and target level
Change the dosing to twice daily at the same total dose, and repeat kidney function in twelve months
Continue lithium unchanged and repeat kidney function annually, since he remains well and the level is in range

subtopic_detail: Pharmacotherapy choice for adult attention difficulties when stimulant diversion is a live concern
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar assessing a 29-year-old man referred with lifelong inattention, disorganisation and restlessness, with clear evidence of impairment from primary school onwards confirmed by school reports and by his mother.

He has used methamphetamine intermittently for three years, most recently four weeks ago, and drinks six standard drinks on two nights a week. He has no psychotic symptoms and no mood disorder. He lives in a shared house where another resident has previously taken his prescribed medication without asking. His blood pressure is 128/80 mmHg, pulse 78 beats per minute, and his electrocardiogram and physical examination are normal. He is engaged with a drug and alcohol service and wants treatment for his attention difficulties.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78 beats per minute, blood pressure 128/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Restless but cooperative, normal speech, no psychotic features, no tremor, normal cardiovascular examination
data_table.Investigations: Electrocardiogram within normal limits, liver function tests within normal limits, urine drug screen negative today, full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: Which pharmacological approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Sertraline titrated over several weeks, with continued engagement in the drug and alcohol service
Atomoxetine titrated over several weeks, with continued engagement in the drug and alcohol service
No pharmacotherapy until he has been abstinent for twelve months, with continued engagement in the service
Modafinil taken each morning, with continued engagement in the drug and alcohol service
Immediate release dexamfetamine three times daily, with continued engagement in the drug and alcohol service

subtopic_detail: Parenteral sedation choice when verbal and oral measures have already failed in the department
stem:
You are the emergency registrar managing a 34-year-old man brought in by ambulance after threatening staff at a bus station. He is pacing, shouting, striking the walls and cannot be engaged in conversation.

De escalation has been attempted for twenty minutes by two experienced nurses and he has refused oral olanzapine wafers. Security is present and physical restraint is in place. His pulse is 126 beats per minute and blood pressure 148/90 mmHg taken during a brief window of cooperation, and his temperature measured tympanically is 37.1 degrees Celsius. He is known to the service with schizophrenia and has not taken his depot for three months. A capillary glucose is 6.2 mmol/L, and no intravenous access has been achieved. There is no history of cardiac disease and no electrocardiogram is available.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 126 beats per minute, blood pressure 148/90 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, SpO2 not obtainable, temperature 37.1 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Agitated and pacing, shouting, striking walls, not engageable, no obvious injury, pupils equal
data_table.Investigations: Capillary glucose 6.2 mmol/L, no intravenous access, no electrocardiogram available, no previous electrocardiogram on file

lead_in: What is the most appropriate parenteral sedation?

options.text: Intramuscular olanzapine with intramuscular lorazepam together, with continuous monitoring after the doses are given
Intramuscular haloperidol with promethazine together, with continuous monitoring after the doses are given
Withhold parenteral sedation until an electrocardiogram can be obtained, continuing physical restraint meanwhile
Intramuscular midazolam as a single dose, with continuous monitoring and a repeat dose if needed after fifteen minutes
Intramuscular droperidol as a single dose, with continuous monitoring and a repeat dose if needed after fifteen minutes

subtopic_detail: Weight gain and impaired glucose handling one year into second generation antipsychotic treatment
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 26-year-old woman one year after her first episode of psychosis, treated with olanzapine 15 mg daily. She has had no psychotic symptoms for eight months and has returned to part time study.

Her weight has risen from 62 kg to 78 kg over the year, her waist circumference is 96 cm, and her fasting glucose is 6.5 mmol/L on two occasions with a glycated haemoglobin of 44 mmol/mol. Fasting triglycerides are 2.6 mmol/L and high density lipoprotein cholesterol is 0.9 mmol/L. Her blood pressure is 124/78 mmHg and her prolactin is normal. She has engaged with a dietitian and an exercise program for four months without weight loss, and she is clear that she does not want to risk another episode of psychosis.

data_table.Examination: Weight 78 kg, waist circumference 96 cm, body mass index 29 kg/m2, no acanthosis nigricans, euthymic with no psychotic features
data_table.Investigations: Fasting glucose 6.5 mmol/L (3.5-5.5) on two occasions, glycated haemoglobin 44 mmol/mol, fasting triglycerides 2.6 mmol/L (less than 1.7), high density lipoprotein cholesterol 0.9 mmol/L (greater than 1.2), prolactin within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue olanzapine and start a statin for the lipid abnormality, with review of glucose in six months
Continue olanzapine unchanged and intensify the dietitian and exercise program with monthly weight review
Discuss switching to an antipsychotic with a lower metabolic risk, with close monitoring for relapse during the change
Halve the olanzapine dose and continue at that level, with review of weight and glucose in three months
Cease the antipsychotic entirely given eight months of remission, with monthly review for early relapse symptoms

subtopic_detail: Broad ventricular complexes after a large ingestion of an older antidepressant
stem:
You are the emergency registrar managing a 41-year-old woman brought in ninety minutes after taking an estimated forty amitriptyline tablets with alcohol, found by her partner with an empty bottle.

She is drowsy but rousable with a Glasgow Coma Scale of 12, her pupils are dilated, her skin is dry and flushed and her bladder is palpable. Her pulse is 128 beats per minute, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 percent on room air and temperature 37.4 degrees Celsius. Her electrocardiogram shows sinus tachycardia with a QRS duration of 132 milliseconds and a prominent R wave in lead aVR. Her venous blood gas shows pH 7.31 and bicarbonate 19 mmol/L, her potassium is 3.6 mmol/L and her capillary glucose is 5.8 mmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128 beats per minute, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temperature 37.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Glasgow Coma Scale 12, dilated pupils, dry flushed skin, palpable bladder, no focal neurological deficit
data_table.Investigations: Electrocardiogram showing QRS 132 milliseconds with a prominent R wave in aVR, venous pH 7.31, bicarbonate 19 mmol/L (22-32), potassium 3.6 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), capillary glucose 5.8 mmol/L, paracetamol level not detected

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

options.text: Oral activated charcoal given via nasogastric tube, repeated hourly while her conscious state is monitored
Intravenous flumazenil given as a slow bolus, repeated until her conscious state and respiratory pattern improve
Intravenous physostigmine given as a slow bolus, repeated to reverse the anticholinergic features she is showing
Intravenous amiodarone given as a loading infusion, repeated if the broad complexes persist on the monitor
Intravenous sodium bicarbonate given as a bolus, repeated until the QRS narrows and the blood pressure improves

subtopic_detail: Lower limb clonus and agitation days after a second serotonergic agent is added for pain
stem: A 52-year-old man two days after laparotomy takes sertraline 150 mg daily and started tramadol for pain. Over twelve hours he has become agitated and sweaty with diarrhoea. He has never taken an antipsychotic.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118/min, BP 152/92 mmHg, temperature 38.4 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Spontaneous ankle clonus, hyperreflexia in the legs, dilated pupils
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 640 units/L (30-200)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Cease the tramadol only, give an antipyretic and observe
Cease both drugs, cool actively and give bromocriptine
Cease both drugs, give benzodiazepines and cooling, then cyproheptadine
Continue both drugs and give antibiotics for presumed sepsis
Cease both drugs, give benzodiazepines and cooling, then dantrolene

subtopic_detail: Duration criterion separating prolonged grief disorder from expected bereavement in an adult
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 58-year-old woman whose husband died of pancreatic cancer 19 months ago. She describes intense daily yearning for him, spends hours each day looking at his photographs and has kept his study exactly as he left it because moving anything feels like a betrayal.

She has stopped seeing the friends they shared because being with couples is unbearable, and says she does not know who she is without him. She sleeps reasonably, eats normally and has maintained her weight. She has no guilt beyond missing him, no anhedonia in activities unrelated to him, no psychomotor slowing and no thoughts of self-harm. She has never had a psychiatric illness.

data_table.Examination: Well groomed, tearful when discussing her husband, reactive affect at other times, no psychomotor retardation, no psychotic features, cognition intact
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, liver function and thyroid function all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reassure her that this is a normal reaction to loss and review her again in six months
Refer for a structured grief focused psychological therapy delivered over several months
Suggest a community bereavement support group as the sole intervention for the next year
Prescribe a short course of a benzodiazepine to help her tolerate the distressing memories
Commence an antidepressant at standard dose and review the response in four weeks

subtopic_detail: Scheduled analgesic trial for agitation in advanced dementia with no verbal pain report
stem:
You are the general practitioner attending a residential aged care facility to review an 84-year-old woman with advanced Alzheimer disease who has become resistive and strikes out during personal care, particularly when staff transfer her or dress her upper body. Her speech is limited to occasional single words.

Staff report the behaviour has built over three weeks and occurs mainly during morning cares rather than at any particular time of day. She has severe knee osteoarthritis and fell onto her right shoulder six weeks ago, after which a radiograph showed no fracture. She takes no regular analgesia. Urinalysis, full blood count, electrolytes, calcium and a chest radiograph performed this week are all unremarkable, and there has been no medication change.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 78/min, blood pressure 132/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.6 C
data_table.Examination: Grimaces and pulls away on passive right shoulder abduction, crepitus in both knees, abdomen soft, no urinary retention on bladder scan, chest clear
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis negative, full blood count, electrolytes, corrected calcium and C-reactive protein within normal limits, chest radiograph clear

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence low dose risperidone and review the behaviour after several weeks of treatment
Commence a low dose antidepressant for presumed depression underlying the behaviour change
Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the right shoulder before making any treatment change
Arrange an as-required oral benzodiazepine for staff to give before morning personal cares
Commence regular scheduled paracetamol and reassess the behaviour after several weeks

subtopic_detail: Baseline cardiovascular assessment required before starting stimulant treatment in an adult
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar in the adult outpatient clinic having completed a diagnostic assessment of a 28-year-old man with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, combined presentation, with a documented history of symptoms from primary school and current impairment at work and at home.

He drinks alcohol twice a week within recommended limits and uses no other substances. He has no history of psychosis, mania or tics. His mother has a pacemaker for complete heart block diagnosed in her sixties and there is no family history of sudden death under 40. He is otherwise well and takes no regular medication. You plan to start a long-acting methylphenidate preparation.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 74/min, blood pressure 124/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 C
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 24 kg/m2, heart sounds dual with no murmur, chest clear, no tremor, no thyroid enlargement

lead_in: What baseline assessment is most important before the first prescription?

options.text: Record pulse, blood pressure, weight and a cardiovascular and family cardiac history
Arrange formal neuropsychological testing to confirm the diagnosis before treatment starts
Arrange urine drug screening and repeat it at every review while treatment continues
Arrange a twelve lead electrocardiogram for every adult before any stimulant is commenced
Arrange transthoracic echocardiography given the family history of conduction system disease

subtopic_detail: Choosing between psychological therapy and medication as initial treatment for uncomplicated adult PTSD
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 34-year-old paramedic who attended a multi-fatality road crash seven months ago. Since then he has had nightly nightmares, intrusive images of the scene when he hears sirens, and he has changed his driving route to avoid the intersection.

He has become irritable with his partner, sleeps four to five hours a night and startles at unexpected noises. He has reduced his shifts and describes feeling permanently on edge. He drinks two standard drinks most evenings, which has not changed. He has no psychotic symptoms, no history of mania and no thoughts of suicide, and he has never had psychiatric treatment.

data_table.Examination: Anxious but engaged, no psychomotor agitation, affect reactive, cognition intact, no psychotic phenomena, insight preserved
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, liver function and thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Advise a period of sick leave with sleep hygiene measures and review him in two months
Commence a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor and review his response in four weeks
Arrange a single session psychological debriefing focused on the details of the incident
Refer for individual trauma-focused cognitive behavioural therapy with a trained therapist
Prescribe prazosin at night as the initial treatment directed at his nightmares and sleep

subtopic_detail: Evaluating new behaviour change in an adult with intellectual disability before attributing it to the disability
stem:
You are the general practitioner asked to see a 32-year-old man with moderate intellectual disability who lives in supported accommodation. Over the past six weeks he has begun hitting the side of his head with his palm and refusing meals he previously enjoyed, and staff describe him as withdrawn from activities he used to seek out.

He communicates with around 40 signs and single words and has never described pain in words. There has been no change in staffing, housemates, routine or medication, and no recent bereavement or family visit change. Staff have requested a referral to a psychiatrist for an antipsychotic because they believe the behaviour is part of his disability.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 88/min, blood pressure 126/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.8 C
data_table.Examination: Reluctant to allow examination of the head and neck, no external ear discharge, no obvious dental abnormality visible on limited inspection, abdomen soft, gait unchanged

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor for a presumed underlying depressive illness
Arrange computed tomography of the brain to exclude an intracranial cause for the behaviour
Undertake a systematic search for a physical cause including dental, ear and gastrointestinal review
Advise staff to implement a behaviour support plan using planned ignoring of the behaviour
Refer to psychiatry for antipsychotic treatment of the self injurious behaviour as requested

subtopic_detail: Reconsidering an existing personality disorder label when an adult woman describes lifelong autistic traits
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 29-year-old woman diagnosed with borderline personality disorder at 21 who has completed two full dialectical behaviour therapy programs with little change. She was referred again after a further period of distress following a workplace restructure.

She describes her overwhelming distress as consistently triggered by unexpected changes to plans, by open plan office noise and by fluorescent lighting rather than by interpersonal rejection. Her relationships have been few but stable, and she denies frantic efforts to avoid abandonment or a chronically unstable sense of self. Her self-harm has always been in response to sensory or change-related overload. She reports rehearsing conversations in advance, and her mother says she lined up her toys in strict order and taught herself to copy other girls' social behaviour at school.

data_table.Examination: Limited eye contact, precise and formal speech, no thought disorder, no psychotic features, mood euthymic today, cognition intact, wears noise cancelling headphones into the consultation
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, liver function and thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Focus treatment on the workplace restructure and refer for supportive counselling and return to work
Refer for a structured multidisciplinary adult autism diagnostic assessment with developmental history
Refer her for a third course of dialectical behaviour therapy with a different treating team
Commence a mood stabiliser to reduce affective instability while continuing her current therapy
Administer a self report autism screening questionnaire and make the diagnosis if she scores highly

subtopic_detail: Neuroleptic sensitivity constraining treatment of visual hallucinations in Lewy body disease
stem:
You are the geriatric medicine registrar reviewing a 76-year-old man whose wife reports that for the past four months he has seen small children standing in the corner of the lounge room in the late afternoon, and has spoken to them. He knows afterwards that they were not there.

She also describes days when he is lucid and days when he stares vacantly for hours, and says he has acted out dreams and struck her while asleep for several years. He has had two falls in three months. On examination there is mild symmetrical bradykinesia and increased tone in both arms with no resting tremor. His Montreal Cognitive Assessment score is 21 out of 30 with prominent deficits in attention and visuospatial tasks. Screening for infection, electrolyte disturbance and hypothyroidism is negative and he takes no anticholinergic medication.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 72/min, blood pressure 138/80 mmHg lying and 108/64 mmHg standing, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.7 C
data_table.Examination: Symmetrical bradykinesia and increased tone in both upper limbs, no resting tremor, Montreal Cognitive Assessment 21/30 with attentional and visuospatial deficits, no focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, calcium, thyroid function and urinalysis within normal limits, computed tomography of the brain shows generalised atrophy only

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of his hallucinations?

options.text: Commence rivastigmine after explaining that hallucinations often improve with this treatment
Commence low dose haloperidol at night with review of the hallucinations after two weeks
Commence levodopa with carbidopa to address the parkinsonism and the associated hallucinations
Commence a regular night time benzodiazepine to reduce the dream enactment and the hallucinations
Commence low dose risperidone at night with review of the hallucinations after two weeks

subtopic_detail: Supervised administration and observation requirements when starting intranasal esketamine
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar planning treatment for a 44-year-old woman with a major depressive episode that has failed adequate trials of three antidepressants from two classes and an augmentation trial, each at therapeutic dose for at least six weeks with confirmed adherence.

She has no psychotic features, no history of mania and no substance use disorder. Her blood pressure is 138/86 mmHg on repeated readings and she has no history of aneurysm, arteriovenous malformation or intracerebral haemorrhage. She lives alone, drives herself to appointments and works part time. The team has agreed to proceed with intranasal esketamine alongside her oral antidepressant.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 76/min, blood pressure 138/86 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 C
data_table.Examination: Depressed affect, no psychotic features, no psychomotor retardation, cognition intact, no thoughts of self-harm today
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, liver function and thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: Which arrangement is essential for the first dose?

options.text: Cease her oral antidepressant before the first dose to avoid a serotonergic drug interaction
Arrange magnetic resonance angiography of the cerebral vessels before the first dose is given
Dispense it for home administration with a telephone review on the evening of each dose
Administer it in a supervised healthcare setting with blood pressure checks and prolonged observation
Admit her as an inpatient for the full induction course of twice weekly dosing over four weeks

subtopic_detail: Sequencing stabilisation before memory processing in prolonged repeated childhood trauma
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 37-year-old woman referred for trauma therapy after disclosing repeated sexual abuse between the ages of 6 and 13 by a family member. She has intrusive memories, avoidance and hyperarousal.

She also describes losing periods of time, sometimes arriving somewhere with no memory of travelling there, and a persistent sense of being detached from her own body. She has cut herself several times in the past two months when distressed and has been admitted twice this year after overdoses. She struggles to name emotions and says she either feels nothing or feels everything at once. She has stable housing and no substance use disorder.

data_table.Examination: Appears detached during parts of the interview with delayed responses, no psychotic features, oriented, no current suicidal intent though reports intermittent urges, healed and recent superficial forearm lacerations
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, liver function and thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial phase of treatment?

options.text: Begin eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing targeting the earliest abuse memory first
Defer all psychological treatment and commence an antidepressant with review in eight weeks
Begin prolonged exposure therapy immediately with detailed recounting of the abuse memories
Begin with stabilisation focused on safety, emotion regulation and grounding skills
Arrange inpatient admission for the duration of trauma processing to manage the self-harm risk

subtopic_detail: Choosing a non-stimulant for attention deficit disorder when methamphetamine use is ongoing
stem:
You are the addiction psychiatry registrar seeing a 26-year-old man attending a community drug and alcohol service. He has a well documented childhood diagnosis of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder treated with stimulants until he was 15, when he stopped medication and left school.

He has used methamphetamine three or four times a week for the past four years, most recently two days ago. He describes longstanding inattention, disorganisation and impulsivity that were present well before he began using, and that persist during his longest abstinent period of five months last year. He has no psychotic symptoms currently, though he had brief paranoia during a heavy use episode last year that resolved within a week of stopping. He wants treatment for his attention problems and is engaged with a case manager.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 88/min, blood pressure 132/82 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.7 C
data_table.Examination: Alert, restless in the chair, no psychotic phenomena, no tremor, dentition poor, cognition grossly intact
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes and liver function within normal limits, urine drug screen positive for amfetamine type substances, electrocardiogram shows sinus rhythm with normal intervals

lead_in: Which pharmacological treatment would you recommend?

options.text: Bupropion commenced at low dose with gradual increase and review of the response in six weeks
Defer all pharmacological treatment until he has achieved twelve months of confirmed abstinence
Long-acting methylphenidate dispensed daily with supervised dosing at a community pharmacy
Atomoxetine titrated gradually with review of the response after six to eight weeks
Immediate release dexamfetamine dispensed weekly with review of the response after six weeks

subtopic_detail: Benzodiazepine challenge when immobility is attributed to a severe depressive episode
stem:
You are the consultation liaison psychiatry registrar asked to see a 23-year-old woman on a medical ward, admitted three days ago for poor oral intake. She has a six week history of low mood and social withdrawal and the admitting team has diagnosed a severe depressive episode with psychomotor retardation.

She has spoken four words in three days and lies still with her eyes open. When you lift her arm above the bed it remains where you place it for over a minute. She resists passive neck flexion with equal opposing force, and repeats the last words of your questions back to you. She is afebrile with no rigidity, and there has been no antipsychotic exposure. Creatine kinase is 420 U/L (30-200), white cell count, electrolytes, calcium, thyroid function and a computed tomography scan of the brain are all unremarkable.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 92/min, blood pressure 122/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.8 C
data_table.Examination: Maintains imposed postures for over a minute, opposes passive movement with equal force, echolalia present, no lead-pipe rigidity, no tremor, no clonus, no autonomic instability
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 420 U/L (30-200), white cell count, electrolytes, corrected calcium and thyroid function within normal limits, computed tomography of the brain unremarkable

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange urgent electroencephalography to exclude non-convulsive status epilepticus as the cause
Commence an antipsychotic to treat the presumed psychotic component of the depressive episode
Refer directly for electroconvulsive therapy without any preceding pharmacological trial
Commence an antidepressant and arrange nasogastric feeding while awaiting the treatment response
Administer a parenteral lorazepam challenge and assess the clinical response within minutes

subtopic_detail: Acute confusional state arising on a background of established dementia in a residential setting
stem: An 81-year-old man in residential care with moderate vascular dementia is agitated overnight, shouting at people he sees in his room. For two days he has been drowsy by day and frightened at night. He fell four days ago, started oxycodone, and last opened his bowels five days ago.

data_table.Examination: Inattentive with fluctuating alertness, distended abdomen, bladder percussible to the umbilicus

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Give an as-required benzodiazepine and bloods in the morning
Chart regular risperidone as the nursing staff request
Treat the precipitants, draining his bladder and reviewing medicines
Attribute the change to progression of his dementia
Arrange brain imaging to exclude a subdural haematoma

subtopic_detail: First line treatment for a chronic tic disorder causing social impairment in a school aged child
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar in a child and adolescent mental health service. A 9-year-old boy is referred by his general practitioner because of 18 months of repeated eye blinking and sideways head jerking, joined 6 months ago by repeated throat clearing.

His mother says the movements are worse when he is tired or anxious and almost disappear when he is absorbed in building models. He tells you he can hold them in for a while at school but then has to let them out in a rush when he gets home.

He has no injuries from the movements. He has no repetitive hand washing, no checking and no intrusive thoughts, and his teacher reports he concentrates well and his marks are at year level. He is being mimicked in the playground and has started asking to stay home. Neurological examination is normal and he takes no medication.

data_table.Examination: Frequent eye blinking and head jerking with throat clearing, suppressible for short periods, normal neurological examination
data_table.Collateral: Teacher reports concentration at year level and marks at year level; peers mimicking him at school

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line management?

options.text: Start clonidine at a low night-time dose and titrate it over the following 6 weeks
Start aripiprazole at a low daily dose and review his movements in 6 weeks
Start risperidone at a low night-time dose and review his movements in 6 weeks
Provide reassurance about the natural history alone and review him again in 12 months
Refer for comprehensive behavioural intervention for tics with a trained therapist

subtopic_detail: Initial management of preoccupation with a perceived facial defect leading to repeated surgical consultations
stem:
A 19-year-old man is referred to your psychiatry clinic by a plastic surgeon who declined to operate on him. He has consulted two surgeons in 8 months about the shape of his nose.

He tells you he spends about 3 hours a day checking his nose in mirrors and in the reflection of his phone, and takes photographs from different angles to compare. He has stopped attending tutorials because the lighting there makes his nose look worse, and he has failed two subjects as a result.

He says his mood is flat because of how he looks, but he still enjoys gaming with friends online and his sleep and appetite are unchanged. His body mass index is 23 and he has no concerns about his weight or shape elsewhere. He accepts that others say his nose looks normal but says he can see what they cannot. There is no substance use and no suicidal ideation today. His nose appears entirely unremarkable to you.

data_table.Mental state: Preoccupied with nasal appearance, poor insight but not delusional intensity, reactive affect, no perceptual disturbance, no suicidal ideation today
data_table.History: About 3 hours daily of mirror checking and comparison photography, two surgical consultations in 8 months, two subjects failed through tutorial avoidance

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Refer him back to the plastic surgeon for a third opinion about corrective rhinoplasty
Start olanzapine at a low nightly dose to address the fixity of his appearance beliefs
Start diazepam for the distress and review him again in the clinic in 4 weeks
Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy that includes exposure and response prevention
Start sertraline at a standard antidepressant dose and review him again in 4 weeks

subtopic_detail: Management of accumulated possessions creating a fire risk in an older person with intact cognition
stem: A 72-year-old widow is referred after the fire brigade could not reach her kitchen. She says everything may be useful one day and becomes distressed at discarding anything. Her daughter has offered to clear the house next weekend.

data_table.Home visit: Shoulder-height stacks, unusable stove and bath, sleeps in an armchair
data_table.Cognition: Montreal Cognitive Assessment 28 out of 30, manages her affairs

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Arrange an aged care assessment for residential placement
Refer for hoarding specific cognitive behavioural therapy at home
Support the daughter's plan for a full commercial clearance
Start sertraline alone and review her symptoms in 8 weeks
Apply to the guardianship tribunal for a management order

subtopic_detail: Pharmacological adjunct for a body focused repetitive behaviour causing skin damage
stem: A 24-year-old woman has open sores on both forearms that antibiotics have not healed. She picks at small bumps while watching television, often noticing only when she bleeds. She says it smooths the skin, with no contamination or harm thoughts and no self-harm intent.

data_table.Examination: Excoriations at varying stages of healing on both forearms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer to dermatology for patch testing and topical antimicrobials
Start low dose olanzapine at night and review in 8 weeks
Refer to a dialectical behaviour therapy program for self-harm
Start evening diazepam for when the urge to pick is strongest
Start N-acetylcysteine 1200 mg twice daily with habit reversal training

subtopic_detail: Choosing smoking cessation pharmacotherapy for a person with stable schizophrenia
stem:
A 41-year-old man attends your community mental health clinic for his monthly review. He has schizophrenia, has been stable for 3 years on paliperidone palmitate depot, and works part time in a warehouse.

He has smoked 25 cigarettes a day for 20 years and tells you he now wants to stop because his father has just been diagnosed with lung cancer. He has tried nicotine patches twice, each time lasting about 3 weeks before relapsing, and says the cravings in the first hour of the morning defeated him both times.

He is not taking clozapine and has no other regular medications. He has had no admission for 3 years, has no current depressive symptoms, no suicidal thoughts and no history of suicide attempts. He drinks alcohol rarely and uses no other substances. His weight and metabolic screen are stable and his renal function is normal.

data_table.Mental state: Euthymic, no psychotic symptoms, no suicidal ideation, insight preserved
data_table.Medications: Paliperidone palmitate depot monthly, no other regular medications
data_table.History: 25 cigarettes daily for 20 years, two failed attempts with nicotine patch monotherapy, no admission for 3 years

lead_in: What is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Nicotine patch monotherapy again, with a higher strength patch and a longer planned course
Bupropion with a planned quit date 2 weeks after starting, and review at 4 weeks
Varenicline with a planned quit date and mental state review at 2 and 4 weeks
Nortriptyline started at a low dose and titrated, with a quit date at 3 weeks
Behavioural support alone, avoiding pharmacotherapy because of his psychiatric diagnosis

subtopic_detail: Interpreting hypercalcaemia with a non suppressed parathyroid hormone during long term lithium therapy
stem: A 58-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder has taken lithium for 12 years. She reports 6 months of constipation and increased thirst, with no bone pain and no renal colic.

data_table.Examination: No tremor or confusion
data_table.Investigations: Lithium 0.7 mmol/L, corrected calcium 2.78 mmol/L (2.10-2.60), phosphate 0.68 mmol/L (0.75-1.50), parathyroid hormone 9.8 pmol/L (1.6-6.9), creatinine 88 micromol/L, no paraprotein

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Stop the lithium and start sodium valproate instead
Give intravenous sodium chloride 0.9 per cent and zoledronic acid
Request a skeletal survey and urine electrophoresis for myeloma
Withhold two lithium doses and repeat the level in 48 hours
Continue the lithium and refer for endocrine assessment

subtopic_detail: Pharmacological management of irritability in a gene positive adult with a hyperkinetic movement disorder
stem: A 45-year-old man whose predictive testing showed a CAG repeat length of 43 attends with his wife. Over 9 months he has become quick-tempered, shouting over small frustrations, and now sits for long periods unless prompted. He denies sadness or anhedonia. He has intermittent fidgety finger movements and impersistent tongue protrusion.

data_table.Cognition: Montreal Cognitive Assessment 27 out of 30 with reduced verbal fluency

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment for his irritability?

options.text: Diazepam as required for episodes of agitation
Sodium valproate with liver function monitoring
Olanzapine at night with metabolic monitoring
Sertraline with review of irritability and initiation
Tetrabenazine with screening for depression and suicidality

subtopic_detail: Excessive daytime sleepiness with laughter induced weakness in an adolescent treated for depression
stem: A 17-year-old girl's depression has not responded to 6 months of sertraline. She enjoys her friends and art and denies guilt. She sleeps 10 pm to 7 am easily, naps an hour after school and wakes refreshed. Twice this year her knees buckled and she sank to the ground while laughing, staying fully aware.

data_table.Investigations: Epworth Sleepiness Scale 18 of 24; body mass index 23

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Increase the sertraline to the maximum tolerated dose
Arrange polysomnography then a multiple sleep latency test
Switch her from sertraline to venlafaxine and review
Arrange overnight home oximetry for sleep apnoea
Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia

subtopic_detail: Parenteral sedation for acute behavioural disturbance after novel psychoactive substance use
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar. A 23-year-old man is brought in by police at 2 am, pacing, shouting at staff and repeatedly trying to leave through the ambulance bay. His friend says he smoked a synthetic product bought online about 2 hours ago and has had nothing else.

Verbal de-escalation in a quiet room has been attempted for 20 minutes by two experienced nurses and he has refused oral medication twice. He is now pushing past staff towards the doors and there is a genuine risk of injury to him and others.

He is sweating, his pupils measure 5 mm and react, he is moving all four limbs vigorously and there is no focal neurological deficit. A blood glucose taken at triage was 5.8 mmol/L (4.0-7.8) and a 12-lead electrocardiogram recorded earlier in the evening at another hospital showed sinus rhythm with a corrected QT interval of 420 ms. He has no known cardiac history, no allergies and no alcohol on his breath.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128/min, blood pressure 158/94 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 37.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Diaphoretic, pupils 5 mm and reactive, moving all four limbs vigorously, no focal neurological deficit
data_table.Investigations: Blood glucose 5.8 mmol/L (4.0-7.8), 12-lead electrocardiogram earlier this evening in sinus rhythm with corrected QT interval 420 ms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Droperidol 10 mg intramuscularly with continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring
Midazolam 10 mg intramuscularly with continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring
Haloperidol 10 mg intramuscularly with promethazine 50 mg in the same syringe
Olanzapine 10 mg intramuscularly with continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring
Ketamine 300 mg intramuscularly with continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring

subtopic_detail: Assessing new behaviour change in a minimally verbal adult before altering psychotropic medication
stem: A 28-year-old man with severe intellectual disability and no speech lives in a group home. For 6 weeks he has struck the right side of his face, refused half his meals and woken calling out at 3 am. Nothing in his routine has changed. He has taken risperidone 1 mg daily for 4 years.

data_table.Examination: Grimaces on right cheek palpation, not the left; will not open his mouth

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Increase his risperidone to 2 mg daily
Start citalopram for a depressive episode
Arrange a dental examination under sedation
Request an abdominal radiograph for faecal loading
Commission a functional behaviour assessment

subtopic_detail: Selecting a relapse prevention strategy when adherence and substance use have both been excluded
stem: A 22-year-old man has a second schizophrenia relapse in 10 months. Every paliperidone palmitate depot has been given on time and his trough level is therapeutic. Drug screens were negative at both admissions. His mother speaks for him throughout family sessions; his father calls him lazy. Both relapses followed days of escalating arguments at home.

data_table.Mental state: Settles by day 10 without a dose change

lead_in: What is most likely to prevent further relapse?

options.text: Increase the paliperidone depot to the next dose band
Arrange behavioural family intervention for the household
Add sodium valproate and review him in 6 weeks
Switch him to clozapine with haematological monitoring
Provide weekly supportive counselling after discharge

subtopic_detail: Psychiatric opinion on repeated shoplifting in an older adult with behavioural change
stem: A 64-year-old woman faces a third shoplifting charge in 8 months, each time taking unneeded items in full view of staff. She has no financial hardship or convictions, and denies tension before or relief after. Her husband reports 18 months of craving sweets, laughing at bad news and social withdrawal.

data_table.Mental state: Unconcerned; no low mood or psychotic symptoms
data_table.Cognition: Montreal Cognitive Assessment 28 of 30; verbal fluency and trail making impaired

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Advise the solicitor that no psychiatric diagnosis is present
Diagnose kleptomania and start naltrexone with follow-up
Diagnose a depressive episode and start an antidepressant
Arrange neuropsychological assessment and brain magnetic resonance imaging
Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy targeting impulse control

subtopic_detail: Legal pathway for urgent surgery refused by an objecting patient already on a community treatment order
stem: A 58-year-old woman with schizophrenia on a community treatment order for 6 years is admitted with a black right forefoot. Below knee amputation is advised within 48 hours. She refuses: a radio voice told her the blackness is healing. She cannot repeat back that she may die. Her husband supports surgery; she does not want anyone deciding for her.

data_table.Investigations: Afebrile, lactate 1.2 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Assess capacity and apply to the guardianship tribunal
Authorise the amputation under the Mental Health Act
Obtain consent from her husband as person responsible
Proceed under the common law emergency doctrine
Accept her refusal and document that she declined

subtopic_detail: Treatment choice for severe luteal phase mood symptoms with a symptom-free follicular phase
stem:
You are the resident in a general practice clinic. A 28-year-old woman attends because for the past 2 years she has had a week each month of intense irritability, tearfulness and a sense of being overwhelmed that has twice led to shouting arguments at work.

She describes feeling completely well for the remainder of each month and has taken no time off work outside those weeks. She has no history of depressive or manic episodes, no self-harm and no substance use. She uses condoms for contraception and does not wish to become pregnant.

She has kept a daily symptom diary for the past three cycles at her general practitioner's request. It shows symptom scores rising sharply from around day 21, peaking in the 3 days before menstruation, and returning to baseline within 2 days of bleeding starting, with no symptoms recorded between day 4 and day 20 of any cycle. Thyroid function, full blood count and ferritin are within normal limits.

data_table.Investigations: Thyroid function, full blood count and ferritin within normal limits
data_table.Symptom diary: Three cycles charted: scores rise from about day 21, peak in the 3 days before menstruation, return to baseline within 2 days of bleeding; no symptoms between day 4 and day 20 of any cycle

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacological treatment?

options.text: A tricyclic antidepressant taken continuously throughout each day of the cycle
A selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor taken during the luteal phase of each cycle
A low dose atypical antipsychotic taken during the luteal phase of each cycle
A gonadotrophin releasing hormone agonist given by depot injection each month
A progestogen-only oral contraceptive taken continuously throughout each day of the cycle

subtopic_detail: First-line management of repetitive hair pulling producing visible scalp loss in an adolescent
stem:
You are the resident in an adolescent mental health clinic. A 15-year-old girl is brought in by her mother, who has noticed thinning at the crown of her scalp over 8 months.

The girl says she pulls hair out while watching television and while doing homework, often without noticing until she sees the hairs on her lap. She describes a build-up of tension beforehand and relief afterward. She denies any belief that her hair is infested or that pulling prevents harm to anyone.

She is embarrassed and has started wearing a cap at school, and she has declined invitations to swim. Her mood is reactive and she denies suicidal ideation. She eats normally and sleeps well. On examination there is an irregular area of hair loss at the crown with hairs of varying lengths and no scaling, no erythema, no scarring and no broken hair shafts elsewhere. Full blood count, iron studies and thyroid function are within normal limits.

data_table.Examination: Irregular crown hair loss with hairs of varying lengths, no scaling, erythema or scarring, no involvement of eyebrows or eyelashes
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, iron studies and thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?

options.text: A selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor titrated to a standard therapeutic dose
A topical corticosteroid scalp preparation applied to the affected area daily
Habit reversal training delivered as a structured behavioural therapy program
A low dose antipsychotic prescribed with baseline metabolic and movement monitoring
A scalp punch biopsy to establish the histological pattern before treatment is commenced

subtopic_detail: Parasomnia occurring in the first third of the night with no dream recall in a preschool child
stem:
You are the resident in a general paediatric clinic. A 4-year-old boy is brought in by his parents because three or four nights a week he sits up and screams inconsolably about 90 minutes after falling asleep.

During the episodes his eyes are open and he appears terrified, sweating and breathing fast. He does not recognise his parents and pushes them away when they try to comfort him. Each episode lasts about 5 minutes and he then settles back to sleep.

In the morning he is cheerful and has no memory of the events. His parents say there is no limb stiffening, no jerking, no tongue biting and no incontinence during the episodes, and the events never happen in the early morning hours. He started 4-year-old kindergarten 3 months ago and has been going to bed about an hour later than before. His father had similar episodes as a child. Development, growth and neurological examination are normal.

data_table.Examination: Development, growth and neurological examination normal
data_table.Event description: Onset about 90 minutes after sleep onset, eyes open, unresponsive to parents, terror with sweating and tachypnoea, duration about 5 minutes, no stiffening, jerking, tongue biting or incontinence, complete amnesia in the morning

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Arrange an electroencephalogram and start an antiseizure medicine if the recording is abnormal
Prescribe low dose clonazepam at bedtime and review the frequency of events in 4 weeks
Advise waking him fully during each episode and providing reassurance until he settles
Explain the benign nature, advise a regular earlier bedtime and safety-proof the bedroom
Refer for trauma-focused psychological assessment and review the frequency of events in 4 weeks

subtopic_detail: Sequencing bowel disimpaction and behavioural work in a school-aged child soiling daily
stem: A 7-year-old boy soils his underwear most days. His mother says he does it deliberately and hides the soiled underwear; a reward chart has not helped. He passes a very large painful stool about every 8 days and leaks small amounts of loose brown material between these.

data_table.Examination: Firm, indentable mass from the left iliac fossa to the umbilicus; normal anus and lower limb neurology

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer for family behavioural therapy with a reward program
Request an abdominal radiograph to quantify faecal loading
Arrange anorectal manometry and rectal biopsy
Prescribe a maintenance stimulant laxative and fibre advice
Commence macrogol disimpaction, then maintenance laxative

subtopic_detail: Separating drug-induced inner restlessness from an urge to move relieved by walking at night
stem: A 47-year-old man with schizophrenia started risperidone 3 mg daily 5 weeks ago. He describes a crawling urge to move his legs, worst when sitting in the evening and worse in bed, relieved by walking. His partner says he kicks in his sleep. He denies daytime mental restlessness.

data_table.Examination: Sits still through a 30 minute consultation; no tremor, rigidity or bradykinesia
data_table.Investigations: Ferritin 22 micrograms/L (30-500), transferrin saturation 14 per cent, haemoglobin 128 g/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence oral iron replacement
Reduce the risperidone dose
Commence low dose propranolol
Commence low dose benzatropine
Commence a dopamine agonist

subtopic_detail: Hyponatraemia developing weeks after starting an antidepressant in an older adult on a thiazide
stem: A 76-year-old woman has a low sodium on routine bloods. She started sertraline 50 mg daily 4 weeks ago and has taken hydrochlorothiazide for 6 years. She feels unsteady, without seizures or confusion.

data_table.Examination: Euvolaemic, no oedema, postural drop 6 mmHg
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 124 mmol/L (138 mmol/L 3 months ago), urine osmolality 480 mmol/kg, urine sodium 52 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Cease the hydrochlorothiazide, restrict fluid and recheck the sodium
Cease the sertraline, restrict fluid and recheck the sodium
Give hypertonic saline, restrict fluid and recheck the sodium urgently
