Give isotonic saline, continue current medicines and recheck the sodium
Switch sertraline to a tricyclic, restrict fluid and recheck the sodium

subtopic_detail: Selecting a replacement antipsychotic after a markedly prolonged corrected QT interval
stem:
You are the registrar in an inpatient psychiatric unit. A 52-year-old man with schizoaffective disorder has been taking haloperidol 10 mg daily for 3 weeks with good symptomatic response after a relapse with command hallucinations.

A routine electrocardiogram taken this morning shows sinus rhythm at 68 beats per minute with a corrected QT interval of 512 ms, repeated and confirmed on a second recording. His admission electrocardiogram 3 weeks ago showed a corrected QT interval of 432 ms.

He has had no syncope, no palpitations and no chest pain. He takes no other medicines and denies illicit substance use, and a urine drug screen is negative. Potassium is 4.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), magnesium 0.88 mmol/L (0.70-1.10), corrected calcium 2.34 mmol/L (2.10-2.60), thyroid function normal and renal and liver function within normal limits. There is no family history of sudden death or of unexplained drowning. Echocardiography shows structurally normal heart with normal systolic function.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 68/min, blood pressure 126/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.5 °C
data_table.Investigations: Electrocardiogram: sinus rhythm 68/min, corrected QT interval 512 ms confirmed on repeat, versus 432 ms on admission. Potassium 4.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), magnesium 0.88 mmol/L (0.70-1.10), corrected calcium 2.34 mmol/L (2.10-2.60), thyroid, renal and liver function within normal limits. Urine drug screen negative. Echocardiogram structurally normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reduce the haloperidol dose to 5 mg daily, repeating the electrocardiogram after the reduction
Cease haloperidol and commence ziprasidone, repeating the electrocardiogram after the switch
Cease haloperidol and commence aripiprazole, repeating the electrocardiogram after the switch
Cease haloperidol and commence citalopram, repeating the electrocardiogram after the switch
Continue haloperidol and give intravenous magnesium sulfate, repeating the electrocardiogram afterward

subtopic_detail: New onset misidentification delusion with fluctuating attention in an older adult
stem: A 74-year-old man admitted 3 days ago with cellulitis, now improving, insists his wife is an impostor. His daughter reports 8 months of visual hallucinations of small animals and increasing slowness, and over a year of shouting and thrashing during dreams.

data_table.Examination: Symmetrical bradykinesia and cogwheel rigidity, fluctuating attention
data_table.Investigations: Screening bloods normal; brain CT shows atrophy only

lead_in: What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?

options.text: An acute confusional state precipitated by the current infection
A primary psychotic disorder presenting for the first time in later life
A neurodegenerative disorder with cortical tau and amyloid deposition
A neurodegenerative disorder with cortical synuclein deposition
A cerebrovascular disorder producing stepwise small vessel decline

subtopic_detail: Engaging a patient presenting to dermatology with fixed belief of skin infestation and specimen collection
stem: A 58-year-old woman attends dermatology for a fourth referral in 8 months, convinced tiny parasites live under her skin. She brings a container of lint and fibres she calls the organisms, and has applied bleach and kerosene to her forearms. She functions independently. Her skin infection is being treated.

data_table.Examination: Excoriations and secondary infection on both forearms
data_table.Investigations: Microscopy of her specimen shows fibres and keratin only

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Explain the specimen has no parasites, then discharge
Prescribe topical permethrin and review in 6 weeks
Arrange involuntary assessment under the Mental Health Act
Start a serotonin reuptake inhibitor and review
Build rapport over visits, then offer an antipsychotic

subtopic_detail: Distinguishing corticosteroid-induced mood elevation from a first manic episode during an asthma admission
stem: A 34-year-old man admitted 5 days ago with severe asthma is on prednisolone 50 mg daily. For 3 days he has slept about 2 hours a night, talks rapidly, describes a business plan that will make him wealthy and telephoned colleagues after midnight. He has no personal or family psychiatric history.

data_table.Examination: Pressured speech, elevated mood, oriented with sustained attention
data_table.Investigations: Electrolytes, glucose and thyroid function normal; drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Discuss corticosteroid reduction and start an antipsychotic
Continue the corticosteroid unchanged and start lithium
Continue the corticosteroid and start an antidepressant
Order brain MRI and defer treatment meanwhile
Treat as hyperactive delirium with reorientation measures

subtopic_detail: Pharmacological choice for persistent aggression months after a moderate traumatic brain injury
stem: A 29-year-old man is 5 months after a moderate traumatic brain injury with bifrontal contusions. Several times a week he shouts, throws objects and has twice pushed staff during personal care, settling within minutes and expressing regret. A behavioural support plan has run 6 weeks with partial benefit.

data_table.Examination: No pain, constipation or retention; euthymic with no psychosis
data_table.Investigations: Electrolytes, calcium, thyroid function and electroencephalogram normal

lead_in: What medication is most appropriate to add?

options.text: Risperidone, with metabolic and movement side effect monitoring
Propranolol, with pulse rate and blood pressure monitoring
Diazepam, with sedation and respiratory rate monitoring
Sodium valproate, with liver function and platelet monitoring
Sertraline, with mood, sleep and gastrointestinal monitoring

subtopic_detail: Recognising an immune cause of first-episode psychosis when catatonia and seizures follow a viral prodrome
stem: A 23-year-old woman has 3 weeks of disorganised behaviour and believes her thoughts are broadcast. She had a flu-like illness a month ago and this week has held odd postures. She then has a witnessed generalised tonic-clonic seizure lasting 90 seconds, followed by repetitive lip-smacking and choreiform hand movements.

data_table.Examination: Intermittent mutism, resists passive movement
data_table.Investigations: CT brain, electrolytes, glucose and thyroid function normal; drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Electroencephalogram before antiseizure treatment
Serum creatine kinase for neuroleptic malignant syndrome
Lumbar puncture with neuronal surface antibody testing
Transvaginal ultrasound for an ovarian teratoma
Serum caeruloplasmin for a copper metabolism disorder

subtopic_detail: First-line treatment for difficulty discarding possessions without obsessions or compulsive rituals
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar seeing a 62-year-old woman referred by her general practitioner after a home visit. The practitioner's letter says the hallway and both bedrooms are filled chest-high with newspapers, plastic containers and unopened mail, and that the kitchen bench and the stove cannot be reached.

She tells you the items are 'all things I will need one day' and that the thought of putting any of them out makes her feel physically sick. She collects free newspapers and takes containers from recycling bins because she cannot bear to see them wasted. She has stopped inviting her sister in and eats takeaway because she cannot cook.

She describes no intrusive thoughts about contamination, harm or symmetry, and performs no checking, washing or counting rituals. Her mood is reactive, her appetite and sleep are unchanged, and she scores 28 out of 30 on the Montreal Cognitive Assessment. She holds no beliefs that the items have special powers.

data_table.Mental state: Reactive mood, no psychomotor change, no perceptual disturbance, insight that the accumulation is a problem
data_table.Obsessive compulsive features: No contamination, harm or symmetry obsessions; no checking, washing or counting rituals
data_table.Functional impact: Kitchen bench and stove unreachable; hallway and both bedrooms filled chest-high; social withdrawal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?

options.text: Start high dose fluoxetine and review her response again in twelve weeks
Arrange a council clean-out of the property and review her again afterwards
Start low dose risperidone and review her response again in twelve weeks
Refer her for cognitive behavioural therapy specifically adapted for hoarding
Refer her for neuropsychological testing and defer treatment until it is completed

subtopic_detail: Investigating excessive daytime sleepiness with episodic loss of muscle tone triggered by laughter
stem: A 19-year-old student is referred for depression. For eight months she has fallen asleep in lectures and once at the wheel. She sleeps 11 pm to 8 am and a fifteen minute nap refreshes her. When she laughs hard her knees buckle and jaw sags for seconds, with preserved awareness.

data_table.Episodic features: Sleep paralysis two to three mornings weekly
data_table.Mental state: Bright reactive mood, body mass index 22

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start a serotonin reuptake inhibitor and review
Start modafinil and arrange sleep studies if needed
Refer for polysomnography then multiple sleep latency testing
Advise sleep hygiene and review her sleep diary
Arrange oximetry and continuous positive airway pressure

subtopic_detail: Declaring serotonergic treatment failure in body dysmorphic disorder before the dose has been optimised
stem: A 23-year-old man spends three to four hours daily checking his nose in mirrors, believing it crooked and bulbous. A rhinoplasty eighteen months ago left him feeling worse. He has taken sertraline 50 mg daily for twelve months without missing doses, with no change and no adverse effects.

data_table.Examination: Nose of normal contour with a well healed scar; insight poor

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer him to a plastic surgeon for another opinion
Switch to low dose olanzapine and review in eight weeks
Increase the sertraline towards 200 mg daily for twelve weeks
Stop the sertraline and start a tricyclic antidepressant
Stop the sertraline and arrange supportive counselling

subtopic_detail: First-line intervention for electronic gaming machine losses disclosed during a consultation for insomnia
stem: A 41-year-old man asks for help sleeping, lying awake until 3 am for months. He discloses losing about 60,000 dollars on electronic gaming machines over two years, chasing the losses, concealing them and taking a mortgage redraw. Ten attempts to stop have each lasted a week.

data_table.Mental state: Patient Health Questionnaire 9 score of 8, no suicidal ideation

lead_in: What would you first recommend?

options.text: Start naltrexone 50 mg daily and review in eight weeks
Refer for gambling specific therapy with financial counselling
Start sertraline 50 mg daily and review in eight weeks
Advise venue self-exclusion alone and review in eight weeks
Refer to a residential withdrawal unit for admission this week

subtopic_detail: Consistent failure to speak at school with fluent speech at home for more than a year
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar in a child and adolescent clinic seeing a 6-year-old girl referred by her school. The teacher's report says she has not spoken a single word in the classroom or playground in the fourteen months since she started school, and communicates by nodding, pointing and writing.

Her mother says she 'never stops talking' at home, tells long stories, argues with her older brother and sings loudly. A recording made at home and played in the clinic confirms fluent, well structured speech with age-appropriate vocabulary and articulation.

At her school entry health check her hearing was normal on audiometry. She makes eye contact with you, smiles at her mother, shares a drawing spontaneously and plays imaginatively with the clinic dolls, and her teacher reports she has two friends she plays with silently at lunchtime. She freezes and looks at the floor when the teacher addresses her directly in front of the class.

data_table.School report: No speech in class or playground for 14 months; communicates by nodding, pointing and writing; freezes when addressed in front of the class
data_table.Home observation: Fluent, well structured, age-appropriate speech confirmed on a home recording
data_table.Social development: Eye contact maintained, shared enjoyment with mother, spontaneous showing behaviour, imaginative doll play, two reciprocal friendships
data_table.Investigations: Audiometry at school entry within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange audiological assessment before any other referral is considered
Start fluoxetine and review her speech at school again in twelve weeks
Refer for an autism spectrum diagnostic assessment before any treatment
Refer for graded exposure behavioural therapy delivered with the school
Advise the school to wait and review her speech again in twelve months

subtopic_detail: Choosing ADHD pharmacotherapy in an adult with concurrent methamphetamine use
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar seeing a 30-year-old man referred for assessment of attention difficulties. He says he 'cannot hold a thought long enough to finish anything' and has been dismissed from three jobs in two years for missed deadlines and lateness.

His primary school reports, which he brings with him, document inattention, fidgeting and disrupted classwork from Year 2 onwards, well before the age of 12. His partner confirms current difficulties with organisation, losing possessions and interrupting, present across work, home and social settings.

He uses methamphetamine by smoking it two to three times a week and has done so for about four years, describing it as 'the only thing that gets me through a shift'. He has no psychotic symptoms now and has never had any. He drinks alcohol rarely, has a normal physical examination, a blood pressure of 124/78 mmHg and a normal electrocardiogram.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78/min, blood pressure 124/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7°C
data_table.Developmental history: Primary school reports documenting inattention and hyperactivity from Year 2, before age 12
data_table.Current impairment: Organisation, losing possessions and interrupting across work, home and social settings; three job losses in two years
data_table.Substance use: Methamphetamine smoked two to three times weekly for four years; alcohol rarely; no psychotic symptoms ever
data_table.Investigations: Physical examination and electrocardiogram within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Start atomoxetine and refer him concurrently to a drug and alcohol service
Start immediate release dexamfetamine and refer him to a drug service
Withhold all ADHD treatment until he has been abstinent for six months
Refer him to a drug and alcohol service and defer the ADHD diagnosis
Start a sedating antipsychotic and refer him to a drug and alcohol service

subtopic_detail: Consent for continuing maintenance electroconvulsive therapy when a family member objects
stem: A 74-year-old woman has had four episodes of psychotic depression over 11 years, each remitting with electroconvulsive therapy after failed antidepressant trials. Nine months of four-weekly maintenance has kept her well and she wants it continued. Her son telephones asking that it stop.

data_table.Capacity: Understands and weighs the memory effects, anaesthetic risk and alternatives
data_table.Mental state: Euthymic; Montreal Cognitive Assessment 27 out of 30

lead_in: What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Defer the treatment until her son agrees to it
Apply to the guardianship tribunal for a decision maker
Stop maintenance treatment and continue nortriptyline
Ask her son to sign the consent form for her
Proceed on her own consent and document capacity

subtopic_detail: Arranging trauma focused therapy for a patient with limited English after a partial response to medication
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 35-year-old woman who arrived in Australia four years ago as a refugee and was granted a permanent visa eighteen months ago. Speaking through a professional interpreter, she describes nightmares almost every night, sudden intrusive images of events in a detention setting, and avoiding the supermarket because the lighting brings the images back.

She lives in stable public housing with her adult daughter, uses no alcohol or other substances, and has no current thoughts of self-harm. She is not in contact with anyone who threatens her and has no outstanding legal or immigration matters.

She has taken sertraline 100 mg daily for eight months with good adherence, and reports her sleep has improved a little and the daytime irritability has settled, but the nightmares and intrusive images are unchanged. Her conversational English is limited to short exchanges and she asks her daughter to translate when she attends her general practitioner.

data_table.Mental state: Nightmares, intrusive imagery, avoidance of supermarket lighting, hyperarousal partially improved; no suicidal ideation
data_table.Current treatment: Sertraline 100 mg orally daily for eight months with good adherence and partial response
data_table.Psychosocial: Stable public housing, permanent visa granted, no ongoing threat, no legal or immigration matters outstanding
data_table.Substance use: No alcohol or other substance use
data_table.Language: Limited conversational English; attends with her adult daughter translating at the general practice

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her treatment?

options.text: Increase the sertraline to 200 mg daily and review her again in eight weeks
Refer for trauma-focused psychological therapy with her daughter interpreting
Add low dose quetiapine at night for the nightmares and review in eight weeks
Refer for generic supportive counselling delivered in English at the practice
Refer for trauma-focused psychological therapy with a professional interpreter

subtopic_detail: Acute toxicity from an unregulated smoking product with a negative routine urine drug immunoassay
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar receiving a 22-year-old man brought in by ambulance from a share house. His flatmate says he smoked 'a herbal blend he bought off a website' about ninety minutes ago and then became terrified, shouting that the walls were closing in.

En route he vomited repeatedly and had a generalised tonic-clonic seizure lasting about forty seconds that terminated without treatment. He is now agitated, pacing and pulling at the monitoring leads, and will not sit for examination.

His pupils are 6 mm and reactive, he is diaphoretic and his skin is flushed. A urine drug immunoassay is negative for amphetamines, delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol, cocaine metabolites, opioids and benzodiazepines. Point-of-care glucose is 6.1 mmol/L and the electrocardiogram shows sinus tachycardia with a corrected QT interval of 430 ms.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 146/min, blood pressure 168/96 mmHg, respiratory rate 26/min, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 38.4°C
data_table.Examination: Agitated and pacing, pupils 6 mm and reactive, diaphoretic, flushed skin
data_table.Investigations: Urine immunoassay negative for amphetamines, delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol, cocaine metabolites, opioids and benzodiazepines; glucose 6.1 mmol/L
data_table.Electrocardiogram: Sinus tachycardia, corrected QT interval 430 ms
data_table.Event: One generalised tonic-clonic seizure of about 40 seconds, self-terminating, 90 minutes after smoking an online herbal product

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Give intramuscular haloperidol 10 mg and repeat the dose after thirty minutes
Give intravenous naloxone 400 micrograms and repeat the dose after two minutes
Give oral activated charcoal 50 g and observe him in the short stay unit
Titrate intravenous diazepam to sedation with supportive cooling measures
Give intramuscular olanzapine 10 mg and repeat the dose after thirty minutes

subtopic_detail: New onset shoplifting in middle age with preserved memory and a near normal cognitive screen
stem: A 58-year-old accountant has had a third shoplifting charge in six months, taking items he could afford. His wife says that over two years he has become socially disinhibited, laughed when their dog died, eats sweet pastries daily with 11 kg weight gain, and no longer starts conversation.

data_table.Montreal Cognitive Assessment: 26 of 30, losing points only on fluency and abstraction
data_table.Magnetic resonance imaging: Bilateral frontal and anterior temporal atrophy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer to a specialist cognitive and neurology service
Diagnose kleptomania and refer for therapy
Start naltrexone for the impulsive behaviour
Start an antidepressant and review in eight weeks
Refer to forensic psychiatry for possible feigning

subtopic_detail: first line treatment for repetitive hair pulling causing visible loss and concealment
stem: A 22-year-old student has pulled out her own hair since she was fourteen and has a bare patch at her crown she keeps covered. Tension rises before pulling and is relieved afterwards. She has no obsessions or rituals.

data_table.Examination: Incomplete alopecia at the vertex, hairs of varying lengths, no scarring
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid function and iron studies normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment?

options.text: Low dose olanzapine at night, reviewed in six weeks
Advise that this is a habit that will settle with time
Habit reversal training with a competing response
A serotonin reuptake inhibitor at the higher dose range
Dermatology referral for biopsy and a topical corticosteroid

subtopic_detail: identifying a stimulant beverage load before diagnosing a primary anxiety disorder in a young adult
stem: A 21-year-old man has four months of palpitations, tremor and restlessness, and twice left a worksite convinced he was about to collapse. Since moving to night shifts five months ago he drinks four to six energy drinks, a pre-workout powder and two to three coffees daily. He has no low mood or persistent worry.

data_table.Examination: Pulse 98 /min, fine postural tremor, no goitre
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid function, electrolytes and electrocardiogram normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first step?

options.text: Commence a low dose serotonin reuptake inhibitor
Prescribe a short course of a benzodiazepine
Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy for panic
Arrange ambulatory electrocardiographic monitoring
Arrange a graded reduction of his caffeine intake

subtopic_detail: choosing between hormone therapy and an antidepressant for new low mood during the menopause transition
stem: A 48-year-old teacher has felt flat and irritable for five months, with no previous depressive episode and no suicidal ideation. Her periods are irregular with gaps of up to sixty days, with ten to fifteen hot flushes daily and night sweats waking her three or four times.

data_table.History: No breast cancer, thromboembolism or migraine with aura
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid function normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment?

options.text: Measure follicle stimulating hormone and oestradiol before treating
Transdermal oestradiol with oral micronised progesterone
Escitalopram 10 mg daily, reviewed at two and six weeks
A low dose combined oral contraceptive pill for her cycles
Cognitive behavioural therapy for her insomnia and low mood

subtopic_detail: engaging a man sleeping rough who repeatedly disengages from clinic based appointments
stem: A 41-year-old man with schizophrenia has slept rough for eight months. Four emergency presentations this year for acute psychosis; he has attended no clinic appointment. He talks willingly to an outreach worker on the street but will not enter buildings.

data_table.Examination: Disorganised speech with persecutory beliefs, untreated leg ulcers, not detainable when last assessed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate ongoing care?

options.text: Send another appointment and discharge him if he misses it
Arrange accommodation first and treat once he is housed
Admit him from the emergency department at his next presentation
Refer to an assertive outreach team treating him where he is
Apply for a community treatment order for depot medication

subtopic_detail: disposition for an acutely suicidal patient when the nearest inpatient bed is several hours away
stem: 380 km from the nearest mental health unit, a 34-year-old shearer attends a rural clinic with his sister. He told her this morning he will end his life and has moved his rifles into his car. He intends to act tonight and refuses to stay.

data_table.Examination: Alert, breath alcohol zero
data_table.Resources: No secure room; telehealth and retrieval available

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Detain under the Mental Health Act, remove firearms, arrange retrieval
Arrange telehealth psychiatry tonight with his sister supervising
Set his disposition by a structured suicide risk scale
Start an antidepressant, give a safety plan, review tomorrow
Admit to the local ward under sedation and observation

subtopic_detail: investigating an apparent antidepressant non-response before adding an augmenting agent
stem: A 52-year-old truck driver has depression unresponsive to sertraline 200 mg for twelve weeks and venlafaxine 225 mg for ten weeks, taken reliably. He describes unrefreshing sleep and daytime somnolence, without sadness or hopelessness. His wife reports loud snoring with pauses ending in a gasp, and he has twice nodded off while driving.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 36 kg/m2, neck 45 cm, crowded oropharynx

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Switch to mirtazapine at night for his sleep
Augment venlafaxine with low-dose aripiprazole
Arrange a sleep study and advise him not to drive
Refer for electroconvulsive therapy after two trials
Add modafinil and continue the venlafaxine dose
